News.title: Iranian operative behind wave of attacks in UK & Europe ‘plotting chilling new terrorism campaign from inside jail’
News.content:
Next

A JAILED Iranian operative has allegedly been plotting terror attacks across Europe from behind bars by using “coded language”.

Saadi, 32, who has close relations with senior Iranian officials, is allegedly said to be behind eight fire-bombings at Jewish targets in London and had some involvement in the Golders Green stabbing.



US authorities have now claimed he is using “coded language” over prison phones in Brooklyn, New York, to ensure further attacks can take place.

The Iranian agent allegedly mapped out a wave of antisemitic attacks in the UK, and is accused of trying to continue with more.



The case has revealed the concerns held by the Department of Justice that Saadi is attempting to inspire others through further attacks.

During a phone call with his family in July, Saadi asked about “work” for other people and asked about a high-level member of Hezbollah, an Iranian-backed militia.



Saadi has also been accused of directing money transfers of more than $1m, and directing propaganda videos on “violent ideology and psychological warfare.”

The US authorities also accuse the terror suspect of being behind a plot to kill Jews at synagogues in America.



Saadi, whose capture followed a number of arson attacks such as the tragic torching of Golders Green ambulances, was arrested in Turkey in May.

He was then handed over from Turkey to the United States, where he faces eight charges of terrorism.

Saadi is expected to face trial next summer.

He is also suspected of running a group called Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (Hayi).



This group was behind nearly 20 attacks across Europe in less than three months, and it is allegedly a front for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

Hayi was linked to six arson attacks in London in March and April this year.

These included attacks on Jewish ambulances and synagogues and a drone attack on the Israeli embassy in April.

It also claimed responsibility for the Golders Green stabbings that same April.



The leader of the US Department of Justice (DoJ) claims Saadi told FBI agents he was a leader of “the resistance”, which included the IRGC and different proxy groups.

Since being in detention, the Iranian has challenged the special administrative measures he is under – complaining of being “illegally captured.”

He also moaned about not being given Arabic reading materials and about the quality of the halal food in detention.

Saadi is currently in near-solitary confinement and has restricted contact with his family.

US authorities have said the measures are necessary to stop him engaging in terrorism.



Federal Defenders of New York, his lawyers, said: “By keeping Mr al-Saadi in extreme solitary confinement and aggressively curtailing his access to information, the government is violating his rights under the constitution and the third Geneva Convention.

“We will continue to vigorously challenge these inhumane conditions.”

The DoJ said there were concerns he was “enlisting third parties to engage in certain conduct, including planning or even carrying out more attacks such as the European terrorist attacks”.

The probe revealed he ordered his family to wire more than $1 million in Iraqi dinars to a web of mystery individuals, and police were forced to kill the line on a separate call after overhearing chilling talk of a gun, followed by Saadi ordering: “Give him money so we can do it.”

A recording of a FaceTime call with a woman thought to be his mother also showed Saadi said that “we shall not care whether we fall upon death or death falls upon us as long as we are on the path of truth”.



This was uploaded on social media accounts that circulate IRGC propaganda, and viewed more than 96,000 times.

He also ordered his family to wire more than $1 million in Iraqi dinars to a web of mystery individuals, and police were forced to kill the line on a separate call after overhearing chilling talk of a gun, followed by Saadi ordering: “Give him money so we can do it.”

Saadi’s lawyers say the government’s harsh restrictions make no sense.

They claim his comment about a gun was just a joke to his sister about her husband being “forced” into marriage by the family.

His lawyers claim the prosecutors of Saadi are relying on guesswork and overreaching their powers.



They insist he should be treated as a prisoner of war rather than a criminal suspect.

They also hit back at claims his family were spreading terrorist propaganda online, arguing they were simply using social media to highlight his detention and how he is being treated.

The accusations follow repeated warnings from Sir Ken McCallum, the director-general of MI5, who insists Tehran is using other individuals to carry out violent plots in the UK.

At his annual threat speech last week he said the regime was determined to intimidate its opposition, Iranian media organisations, and Israeli sites.

He believed that the attempted terrorist attack was “not unique”, and had fixed its attention on UK military sites.



Jonathan Hackett, a national security analyst, said that the UK was seen as an easy target – and there were almost certainly Iranian agents carrying out orders from Saadi since his arrest.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

He said: “It’s the only ally that allows the US to put strategic bombers in the ground, so it’s seen as a place where activity can also harm the US.

“The Iranians are doing what they can within the restraints that surround them. If they had more capability we might see more spectacular and more sophisticated attacks.”

News.title: First pics of man, 35, killed alongside boy, 6, after mum drove truck onto soccer field as she is released from custody
News.content:
Next

TRAGIC photos of the man killed alongside a child after a mom drove her truck onto a soccer field have been released.

Nicholas Schafer, 35, and Cole Adrian, six, lost their lives in the horror crash on Saturday which wounded at least ten others with the driver now being released from custody.



The tragedy unfolded after an unnamed mom, 34, allegedly struck multiple people with her pick-up truck on a soccer field in Kansas.

Witnesses said the driver screamed “Oh my God, Oh my God, what have I done?” as she was pulled from her vehicle.



One of her children had been riding in the back of the Chevrolet at the time of the terrifying incident, according to the NY Post.

Her other kid had been playing in a soccer game on a different field in the Stryker Sports Complex.

READ MORE FIELD TRAGEDY Mom screamed after plowing truck onto soccer field killing 2 including boy, 6

Emergency services raced to the scene after stricken bystanders raised the alarm at around 3.25pm.

While the medics were arriving, parents and bystanders attempted to deliver “life-saving assistance” to the injured, said Wichita Police Department Chief Joe Sullivan.

He said: “It was truly amazing, but I think it’s indicative of the Wichita community.”

A girl and a boy, both 5, and another girl, 9, are among those who were injured in the tragedy.



The rest of the wounded are between 28 and 68 years old.

Police initially detained the driver, from Garden City, but released her without charges on Sunday pending a toxicology test and examination of the vehicle.

Law enforcement said: “No charges have been filed at this time, and investigators continue working to determine the circumstances that led to the crash.”



It is not yet clear whether the fatal crash was deliberate or an accident nor how fast the car was going at the time it allegedly struck players and fans.

Witness Vanessa Trammell told CNN: “We thought it was going to stop but then it like kept going.

“It was pure panic. “I didn’t know what was going on – just that people were being hit.”

Another bystander told TV station 12 News that a “black pickup truck came plowing through the youth soccer fields hitting multiple people before stopping 100-200 yards down the fields”.

The Stryker Sports Complex has canceled all events until further notice in the wake of the tragedy.



“We ask that you keep all individuals and families affected in your thoughts and prayers during this difficult time,” the facility said in a statement.

Meanwhile, investigators have interviewed over 30 witnesses and are appealing for any video from the incident.

Wichita Mayor Lily Wu said she was “heartbroken” by the incident.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

She said: “No one could have imagined the tragedy that would unfold.

“My thoughts and prayers are with everyone affected, especially the children and families involved”.

News.title: Andy Burnham faces Labour revolt as his own MPs demand end to North Sea drilling ban and Net Zero taxes
News.content:
Next

ANDY Burnham is facing desperate demands from his own MPs to lift the ban on North Sea drilling and scrap punishing Net Zero taxes.

Labour backbenchers Henry Tufnell and Steve Yemm have launched a cross-party pressure group urging the PM to green-light more oil and gas licences.



Ministers are expected to make a long-awaited decision on whether to kickstart exploration at the Jackdaw and Rosebank fields within weeks.

But Mr Burnham is maintaining the manifesto moratorium on any new North Sea licences being issued – sparking fears for the future of British industry.



The new Industry First Group is calling on Mr Burnham to slash carbon taxes and unleash more drilling off the British coast to safeguard supplies.

Mr Tufnell said: “British industry is at a crossroads.



“From chemicals and ceramics to refining and oil and gas, the industries that provide good, skilled jobs and underpin communities across the country are under huge pressure.

“We cannot afford to stand by while decarbonisation leads to deindustrialisation.

“Reducing our carbon emissions must go hand in hand with economic growth and strengthening energy security.”

Polling for the group by Yonder found that 73 per cent of voters think ministers must do more to support industry.



More than half believe the Government should issue new drilling licences.

News.title: We cannot escape our need for fossil fuels – it’s time the PM put the country before party politics
News.content:
Get drilling







Next

EVEN Andy Burnham’s own MPs are desperate for him to lift the ban on more oil and gas drilling in the North Sea and to scrap crippling Net Zero taxes.

While he dithers, British industries are being driven to the wall by unaffordable energy prices and red tape.



Jobs are threatened; ordinary people struggle to heat their homes; and the country faces increased energy insecurity at a time of dangerous global instability. So what’s the hold-up?

He didn’t want to make a decision before the Holborn and St Pancras by-election in case it put off eco-minded voters.



In the event, he needn’t have been so cynical. Zack Polanski’s Gaza-obsessed Greens were already imploding.

It’s time the PM finally put the good of the country before narrow party politics.

No one is suggesting a total halt on green energy solutions, but we cannot escape our present need for fossil fuels.

It is an exercise in national self-harm to depend on other countries to supply those same fossil fuels when we have plenty of our own.

Basket cases

CONFUSED by ever-changing guidelines on what food the state thinks you should and shouldn’t choose to eat?

You certainly will be after the latest attack on family grocery staples proposed by the nanny state.



It’s not just energy drinks, burgers and ready meals in the sights of the We Know Best brigade.

It’s bran flakes, cholesterol-lowering yoghurt drinks, soya milk, low-fat rice puddings and corn flakes which the Government now wants to demonise.

Restrictions on supermarkets advertising such products or including them in multi-deal promotions — like buy-one-get-one-free — will hit the poorest hardest because they spend the greatest proportion of their income on food.

While families need all the help they can get with the cost of living, supermarkets will be banned from including traditional favourites in money-off deals.

Labour governments always think they should be the ones to decide what you spend YOUR money on. But the latest diktats are more ludicrous than usual.



The PM should tell the Nutrient Police to BOGOF.

BBC Bites-lies

THE left-wing bias ingrained in the BBC’s news output — demonstrated with alarming regularity — is bad enough.

But indoctrinating children through its education site BBC Bitesize — with left-wing ideology on illegal migration, Net Zero and other issues — is a new low, both shocking and insidious.

It has to change. If the Corporation cannot be trusted to be impartial it should have absolutely no right to force people to fund it. Or to criminalise them if they won’t.

News.title: Make-or-break Budget threatens to burst Burnham’s bubble and expose our new PM as all talk and no trousers
News.content:
Next

FOR the past three months, all we’ve really heard from our new Prime Minister is talk, talk, talk.

Andy Burnham is in his element when speaking off the cuff, turning on the charm and offering sentimental recollections of the “good old days”.



But beneath all his long-winded monologues about doing things differently, there has so far been a distinct lack of action.

He has promised us hope, yet all he’s delivered is hype.



Apart from his positive vibes and a few cheap giveaways — like the £2 cap on bus fares — we’ve seen nothing to confront the huge problems now facing the country.

While Burnham was making rambling speeches in his socialist comfort zone last week, his Chancellor, John Healey, was thousands of miles away testing Thai snacks in a Bangkok tuk-tuk.

Meanwhile, there’s a war in Europe, our sluggish economy is stalling, fuel and energy prices are rocketing and the cost of living is hammering family budgets.

The list goes on — £3trillion of UK national debt, rising unemployment, our threadbare Armed Forces, backlogs for NHS treatment, and the small boats crisis.

Anything remotely difficult has been kicked into the long grass.

Fixing social care, adjusting the pensions triple lock and constant chatter about rejoining the EU won’t be addressed until after the next General Election.



But next week we’ll get our first good idea of whether Burnham is a man of action or all talk and no trousers.

In nine days’ time, Chancellor Healey will stand up to deliver his first Budget — and the PM’s fingerprints will be all over it.

This isn’t just a test for the Treasury, it is the moment of truth for the man in No10. It will prove whether he has what it takes to lead our country through turbulent times.



Will he be the Messiah we hoped for? Or will he be exposed, like the Wizard Of Oz when the curtain is pulled back at the end of the film to reveal a short, middle-aged man frantically pulling levers to project a grand illusion of power?

The signs are already ominous. The Treasury is busy briefing that it will be a dull and steady-as-she-goes Budget. Steady? We’re in stormy waters and another year of political drift is the very last thing this country needs.

Britain is crying out for an economic rescue plan and it would be a total cop-out to deliver just a “nothing to see here” Budget.

But every way the Chancellor looks, he is hamstrung by the PM’s indecision or fear of a backlash.

Hard-working families are feeling the combined pinch of inflation, and rising petrol and diesel prices and household energy bills — set to double in the next six months.



Labour came to power on a promise of a £300 cut to energy bills, but households are likely to see them rise by an average of around £1,000 by the end of next year.

The Chancellor can ease the pain next week by removing some of the Net Zero subsidies that artificially inflate electricity prices.

Blathering Burnham raised hopes he would give the go-ahead to drill for £40billion worth of oil and gas in the North Sea when he travelled to Lanarkshire on Friday.



But perhaps he thought he was going to Lancashire and had hopped on the wrong bus.

For the only power he talked about was political power — and transferring more of it to local councils in Scotland.

Instead of opening energy fields, Burnham only succeeded in reviving fresh demands from the SNP for a second independence referendum.

We need extra cash to rebuild our depleted Armed Forces and meet Nato commitments to spend three per cent of GDP on defence by 2030.

This is the very issue which prompted Healey to resign as Defence Secretary barely four months ago, but he’s unlikely to find the money now he’s running the Treasury.



The Chancellor is restrained over what he can do about unemployment, too.

Britain faces the worst graduate recruitment crisis since records began and nearly a million under-25s are not in work, education or training.

Working-age benefit payments are expected to rise by £30billion in this Parliament.

But all we can expect in the Budget next week is “nothing to see here”. We’ll all have to wait for the outcome of yet another review.



Nor will there be any attempt to tackle the bloated welfare bill — set to top £400billion by 2030 — and the critical issues exposed in an investigation by The Times last week.

Astonishingly, nearly two million people claiming sickness and incapacity benefits have not been re-assessed for over 18 months.

Healey wants to press ahead with a third runway for Heathrow Airport, which would create up to 100,000 jobs UK-wide and spread growth across the nation.

Burnham wants to “hear the voice of the people there first”.



Is he seriously telling us he hasn’t made his mind up on this issue of national importance which has been rumbling on for decades?

He suggests, instead, an airport expansion for his beloved Manchester.

But millions of tourists and business people want to fly into London — and Manchester does not need the extra capacity.

The PM swaggered into No10 with big ambitions and people are slowly beginning to ask if he’s got what it takes.

Next week, we’ll find out. Or maybe he’ll be found out.



WOKE panto chiefs have ditched the happy ending where Sleeping Beauty is awakened by love’s first kiss because it is non-consensual.

Whatever next? Cinderella’s two facially challenged sisters?

I’m off to see Jack And The Beanstalk, starring a person of exceptional verticality.

ANDY BURNHAM spent 16 years plotting to seize power. Now that he’s finally got it, he seems determined to give it all away.

He’s spent his first few months as PM looking less like a man in charge than one desperate to hand over the controls to someone else.



Within days of his arrival at No10, he vowed to pass more authority to regional mayors and give back control to Brussels by unpicking Brexit.

Last week, he was at it again – on a visit to Scotland, he offered to put decision-making in the hands of city regions and communities north of the border.

He talks about putting “power in every postcode” but his mass devolution risks creating a postcode lottery where service quality will depend on where you live.

The UK already has three devolved assemblies, 14 regional mayors, 382 local authorities and 305 arms-length bodies and quangos.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

If he gives much more power away, he’ll soon have nothing left to govern.



Or perhaps that’s part of his masterplan. If he doesn’t run anything, nobody can blame him when things go horribly wrong.

News.title: Noisy commuters face £100 fines for blasting music on buses and trains in new crackdown
News.content:
Next

LOUTISH passengers could be fined £100 for blasting noise from their phones on ­public transport, the PM will announce today.

Andy Burnham will unveil a fresh campaign against “loudcasters” who put other people’s backs up with their selfish din on buses and trains.



Earphone-dodgers will be warned of the possible fines, with forthcoming alerts on trains urging: “Share the carriage, not the noise.”

The new guidance will also target vaping and littering.



Mr Burnham will say today: “We’ve all been on the train when someone starts blasting music or videos from their phone. It can quickly spoil the journey.

“So, we’re launching a nationwide campaign reminding passengers to use headphones on trains.

“On top of that, we’re giving local leaders new powers to tackle loud music, vaping and littering on buses.”

Given a lack of train personnel, it is unclear how many fines will be imposed.

Bus drivers will not be expected to dole them out, however, and the responsibility will fall to police and traffic officers.

Selfish passengers can already be asked to leave a train if they are causing a nuisance and be fined up to £1,000 if they refuse.



Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander will say: “It is so frustrating when the actions of an inconsiderate few spoil journeys for the rest of us, whether that is vaping, littering or blasting music out loud.

“Small changes in behaviour can make a big difference to people’s experience on public transport.”

News.title: Water company reveals emergency plan to import drinking water from NORWAY as 280,000 Brits face running dry
News.content:
Next

A WATER company has plans to ship drinking water from Norway after a severe drought was declared.

Around 280,000 residents served by South East Water face running out next month.



And the firm’s extreme drought proposals include using sea tankers to bring in supplies from overseas.

South East’s emergency Level Four will be hit when Ardingly reservoir, which is just 19 per cent full, nears empty.



No water company has ever imported drinking water from abroad, though Southern Water has previously drawn up similar plans.

South East Water bosses say just four to six weeks’ supply remains at Ardingly, West Sussex, following the hottest summer on record.

The extreme proposals include: “Import of potable water using sea tankers. Supplies are typically from overseas, such as Norway.”

The company’s other severe drought schemes include standpipes on the street — last seen in 1976 — and shipping container desalination plants, turning seawater into ­drinking water.

Nick Price, the head of water resources at South East Water, said: “While importing water from ­Norway is listed within our drought plan, it is strictly a last-resort ­contingency option.

“It is not an action currently being considered.



“We have more teams than ever working to find and fix leaks, have undertaken changes to our network and implemented other measures, including reducing the amount of water released from Ardingly.”

The company has also applied to extend hosepipe restrictions.

News.title: ‘Monster’ who tied up and raped woman in ‘sustained & terrifying manner’ which left her fearing she’d die is jailed
News.content:
'UTTERLY CHILLING' ‘Monster’ who tied up and raped woman in ‘sustained & terrifying manner’ which left her fearing she’d die is jailed







Next

A RAPIST who tied up and gagged a woman before repeatedly raping her has been sentenced to 11 years in prison.

Toby Snow, 28, unleashed a frenzied attack on a woman in Scunthorpe which left her fearing for her life.

He was found guilty of rape and assault by penetration at Hull Crown Court.

During the trial, Dale Brook, prosecuting, said that Snow was intoxicated from a night out when he targeted the woman.





“He lost control of himself,” he said, attacking her in a “terrifying manner”.

Snow began by apologising to the woman for what he was about to do, before physically assaulting her.

“He then proceeded to rape her,” said Mr Brook.

“Her ordeal went on for what seemed like a long time.



“She thought he was going to kill her.”

He added that she made it “crystal clear” to Snow that she did not want it and there had been “no ambiguity”.

“She told him again and again but he did not care and he raped her repeatedly to satisfy his sexual urge and, no doubt, to demonstrate his power over her while she was pulling away from him,” he said.

He described the attack as “utterly chilling” and one that left the woman deeply traumatised and “utterly terrified”.



The vile rapist initially snatched her phone off her to prevent her from calling the police, before eventually giving it back.

Mr Brook continued: “She was confused and scared and did not immediately call the police but she did not wait long.”

After confiding in a work mate the following day, she reported the harrowing attack to the cops, leading to Snow’s arrest.

He accepted that the two of them had had sex but claimed it was consensual.

In her victim statement, the woman described giving evidence as the “worst day of my life” that brought the trauma of the degrading attack flooding back.



“I will always be questioning why it happened,” she said, adding that she still suffers from night terrors.

Defending, Craig Lowe said references on his client’s behalf were inconsistent with the horror of the attack and “out of character”.

He had previously been described as “caring and having a strong work ethic”, with no previous convictions.

He added that his client’s dad had died in 2024.

Judge Richard Woolfall said: “It was an horrendous ordeal. It was a sustained incident.”



He added: “She described you as a monster.”

Snow was jailed for 11 years, with an extended sentence of four more years on licence due to the risk of reoffending.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The judge said Snow will serve two thirds in prison before being considered for release by The Parole Board.

He ordered him to be on the Sex Offender Register for life.

News.title: Macron expresses 'anger and shame' after 2,400 arrested in violent France protests
News.content:
Macron expresses 'anger and shame' after 2,400 arrested in violent France protests

French President Emmanuel Macron has spoken of "anger" and "shame" as nationwide protests in France over the cost of living crisis and school conditions turned violent, resulting in at least 2,400 arrests across Paris and other cities.

View Image Breaking News (Image: Express)

French President Emmanuel Macron has voiced the nation's "anger" and "shame" over sweeping protests against soaring living costs and deteriorating school conditions, which have led to at least 2,400 arrests.

‌



‌



Mr Macron echoed fellow government officials in attributing much of the violence to far-left activists, accusing them of targeting police and public buildings in a bid to stoke disorder.

‌



"Those who looted will have to pay back for the damage, and those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable," Mr Macron declared in a televised address to the country.

‌



He condemned "unrestrained violence" by "insurrectionist elements from radical far-left groups, joined by numerous criminals".

Mr Macron had earlier convened an emergency meeting with senior government figures, a day after masked groups set buildings ablaze and stormed public properties, including town halls, across several cities.

He revealed he had directed prefects to collaborate with mayors to safeguard public buildings and businesses over the coming weeks, including imposing protest bans where necessary.

‌



In the central town of Limoges, fire tore through the 19th-century City Hall, causing its roof to cave in and leaving the building on the verge of total destruction.

Hundreds of demonstrators once again gathered on Sunday at the Place de la Republique in Paris, amid a significant police presence.

Officers deployed tear gas as sporadic tensions flared across the area, with small clusters of individuals attempting to set bicycles and bins alight. "The right to protest is a fundamental right. Deliberately and collectively sowing disorder through violence is not," interior minister Laurent Nunez wrote on X, pointing to the ransacking of hundreds of businesses across cities including Paris, Marseille, Lyon and Bordeaux.

‌



Official figures put Saturday's march attendance at approximately 550,000, while organisers claimed the figure was closer to 800,000.

Protesters heeded calls from a trade union, student groups and activists seeking to reignite the "yellow vest" movement, which first emerged in 2018 as a demonstration against social inequality.

Large-scale demonstrations in France are frequently tarnished by violence on the periphery of otherwise peaceful marches, resulting in confrontations with police. The number of arrests reported on Sunday came close to the nearly 2,000 recorded across the country during a single day of yellow-vest protests back in December 2018.

‌



One individual suffered a fatal heart attack, according to a statement from Paris police, though no further details were provided. The Paris prosecutors' office confirmed it had launched an investigation.

Around Paris' Place de la République on Sunday morning, the aftermath of the unrest was plain to see, with uprooted cobblestones, smashed shopfronts and shards of broken glass littering the streets.

Reports of looting and damage emerged from around the square and several other tourist and shopping districts in the city centre.

‌



Paris police confirmed 855 arrests in the capital region, with the city's prosecutor's office stating that 557 people remained in custody. "I am actually stunned by the level of destruction and violence that was expressed," said Marie Peyreigne, a 57 year old government employee, as she tried to make sense of the chaos that had unfolded.

Surveying the wreckage, scores of Parisians photographed the partially demolished base of the central monument at Place de la Republique - a statue of Marianne, an enduring symbol of France.

Jean Foissy, 74, said he had intended to join the demonstration but encountered "a wall of riot police and fires everywhere", and turned back.

‌



"I was very scared," he said. "I've been a Parisian since I was born, so when I got here, it almost made me want to cry because I find it so bad, it hurts me."

Margaux Eude, 26, said she backs the protest movement but "didn't think it would escalate like this".

"It's the troublemakers who came, and it breaks my heart because it delegitimises the movement", she said.

‌



Political figures across the divide moved swiftly to exploit the fallout from Saturday's unrest for political gain, with one eye firmly on next spring's presidential election.

Far-right leader and presidential contender Marine Le Pen rounded on far-left rival Jean-Luc Melenchon, who had taken part in the Paris march.

"Looting, ransacking, destroying and attacking law enforcement: Rioters have again spoiled the October 17 demonstrations for the protection of purchasing power," Ms Le Pen wrote on X.

‌



Her running mate, Jordan Bardella, said on X that "if the silent majority of French decide it, we will re-establish order for the long-term". Mr Melenchon, for his part, exchanged sharp words with the prime minister, accusing Mr Lecornu of "playing with fire" and claiming that "by banking on degradation, you have only succeeded in uniting all youths and workers' unions".

Mr Melenchon stated that "my message is clear: those who share our fight have no business in looting or destruction".

US President Donald Trump posted "France is burning!" on his Truth Social platform, apparently linking the unrest to "the immigration of people from an entirely different world".

‌



"Close your borders and take control, before it is too late!" he wrote.

French authorities and police have drawn no connection between immigrants and the rioting, repeatedly attributing elements of the violence to "radical far-left groups" and opportunistic looters.

Paris mayor Emmanuel Gregoire announced the establishment of an emergency unit to help businesses evaluate the extent of the damage.

‌



"The scale of the damage is considerable and unprecedented," Mr Gregoire wrote in an open letter.

"Paris is a city of freedoms, debate and demonstrations. It must remain so. But it must also be a city where everyone can work and run a business safely."

The mayors of Paris, Marseille and Lyon, France's three biggest cities, called for an urgent meeting with the prime minister in the coming days "given the extent of the damage and the seriousness of the situation."

‌



In the southern coastal city of Marseille, demonstrators temporarily stormed the entrance hall of City Hall, while a group wearing hoods and masks vandalised a police station. In Lyon, flames erupted within a tourist office.

In Limoges, a band of "radical troublemakers" broke into City Hall while elected officials, staff, security personnel and members of the public were inside, Maurice Barate, prefect of the Haute-Vienne region, said.

"Despite the presence of so many people, they deliberately set the building on fire. It is an extremely serious and unspeakable act," he said.

Article continues below

In eastern France, the Mulhouse prosecutor's office said an investigation has been launched after a 17 year old girl sustained injuries during the protests and lost an eye.

On Saturday, another investigation was launched after a young demonstrator lost a hand in Saint-Etienne.

The injuries emerge as police face intense criticism over their deployment of grenades and other riot-control weapons during recent demonstrations.

News.title: Man, 93, accused of stabbing his wife, 76, inside popular shopping centre
News.content:
Man, 93, accused of stabbing his wife, 76, inside popular shopping centre

Witnesses say that the woman tried to seek refuge in the Repair Shop - she has since been taken to hospital where she remains in a critical condition after the incident

View 2 Images Emergency crews were called to Westpoint on Patrick St in Blacktown, in Sydney, about 10am on Sunday after reports of a knifeman and an injured woman. (Image: 7News)

Police have charged a 93-year-old man who allegedly stabbed his wife in a shopping centre in Sydney, Australia.

Emergency services were called to a shopping centre on Patrick Street, Blacktown, at around 10am on Sunday, October 18 following reports of an armed offender.

A spokesperson for New South Wales Police stated that officers attended Westpoint shopping centre in Blacktown and were told a woman had allegedly been stabbed multiple times.

View 2 Images The shopping centre in Blacktown, Sydney (Image: Sandara/Wikimedia Commons)

A 79-year-old woman was treated at the scene - witnesses say she had attempted to seek refuge in discount retailer The Reject Shop. The woman was treated by paramedics at the scene before she was transported to hospital, where she remains in a critical condition.

Article continues below

A 93-year-old man – believed to be known to the woman – was arrested nearby and taken to Blacktown Police Station. The Daily Mail is reporting that the woman is understood to be the man's wife.

A spokesperson for New South Wales Police said: "He was charged with reckless wounding (DV) and two counts common assault (DV).

"He was refused bail and will appear before Blacktown Local Court tomorrow (Monday 19 October 2026)."

News.title: Air Force commander plunges to death in front of horrified fans at football game
News.content:
Air Force commander plunges to death in front of horrified fans at football game

The air force member was performing a stunt as part of the pregame coin toss when he slid down a rope and hit the ground before being rushed to hospital

View 2 Images (Image: @Qu4k3r0ats/X)

An Air Force commander who fell 170 foot in front of thousands of horrified football fans has died.

‌



‌



The airman was rappelling from the roof of the Alamodome stadium at the University of Texas game on Saturday when he slipped and plunged to the ground.

‌



The service member was part of a pregame demonstration at the school's “Salute to Armed Forces and Veterans” game.

‌



View 2 Images An airman rappels from the Alamodome stadium rafters during an earlier demonstration (Image: @UTSAFTBL/X)

Videos posted on social media appear to show the moment the man loses control and slides down the rope. He then received medical treatment on the field for around 10 minutes before being rushed to a local hospital.

UTSA staff formed a semicircle around him before he got taken off the pitch on a stretcher.

‌



He sadly died at the hospital.

“Everyone was quiet, the band stopped performing. Everybody was dead silent,” Adrian Corey, who witnessed the fall, said to KSAT .

The military demonstration was part of the pregame coin toss and featured four members carrying out the stunt, who are trained in descending from helicopters at heights over 100 feet.

‌



UTSA officials expressed concerns for the man at the time of the fall. A university spokesperson said: “We are deeply saddened by the incident that occurred at the start of tonight’s football game. Our heartfelt thoughts and prayers are with the soldier who was affected, his family and his military colleagues.

“We recognize that members of our campus community may be emotionally affected by this incident and are activating wellbeing services to support our faculty, staff and students.”

“I’ve never had to deal with anything like that before,” coach Jeff Traylor stated. “It just puts things into perspective. It really does.”

Article continues below

The American Conference also posted a statement saying they're “deeply saddened” by the incident.

“We consulted with representatives of both participating member institutions, Alamodome management, local authorities and a working group to review the information available."

News.title: Andy Burnham faces significant demand to join EU after Donald Trump 'unreliability'
News.content:
Andy Burnham faces significant demand to join EU after Donald Trump 'unreliability'

Andy Burnham is facing a significant demand to consider EU membership for Britain amid the unpredictability of Donald Trump and the US’s waning support for Ukraine

View 2 Images An influential left-wing think tank has called Britain to make EU membership its goal, amid the 'unreliability' of the US (Image: AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson)

Andy Burnham is facing a significant demand to consider EU membership for Britain amid the unpredictability of Donald Trump and the US’s waning support for Ukraine.

‌



‌



Relations between the US and Ukraine have dramatically deteriorated in recent weeks, with fears rising over the American President's commitment to European security.

‌



In a major intervention today, influential left-wing think tank the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) has called Britain to make EU membership its goal, amid the "unreliability" of the US.

‌



It follows a series of erratic moves from Mr Trump, including a surprise move on Friday to block a number of sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to come into force. Mr Zelensky on Saturday accused Mr Trump of rewarding and encouraging Vladimir Putin.

Russia and Ukraine continued to strike one another's energy infrastructure over the weekend. Kyiv launched more than 1,000 drones across Russia in what has been described as one of its largest ever aerial bombardments. Smoke was seen billowing above Saint Petersburg on Sunday following air attacks on the city's oil terminal and the city’s Ruchi oil depot. Volodymyr Zelensky yesterday said Russia had continued to bombard Ukraine overnight.

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

‌



View 2 Images Relations between the US and Ukraine have dramatically deteriorated in recent weeks (Image: AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson)

Yvette Cooper's thinly veiled swipe at Donald Trump over Russia sanctions block as UK sends warning to Putin READ MORE :

Zelensky sends biting coded message to Trump in post about him easing sanctions on Russia READ MORE :

The intensified action comes despite Mr Trump last week unveiling a supposed energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine. At the time, Mr Zelensky said the President's announcement had come as a surprise but that he'd honour it if Putin did. But after continued strikes, and worsening relations with the US, he later said: “The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done.”

In a post on social media on Sunday, the Ukrainian President warned Mr Trump: " America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements. On the contrary, they take every signal of an opportunity to make money as proof that their bet on war is paying off and they can keep fighting."

‌



On Saturday afternoon, Mr Zelensky said the American side had signalled that negotiations could take place next week. He said: "The American negotiating track will continue. We’re counting on them to put more pressure on Putin, not on us. Otherwise, it’s simply unfair. As for our meetings with the American side – we expect to meet and are ready to meet in Ukraine or in Europe. If they want to meet in America, let them invite us. We’re ready to negotiate anywhere."

In other recent troubling developments, Mr Trump announced plans to import Russian diesel to the US, called for Mr Zelensky to be replaced and declined to say whether Russia was responsible for the war. It has also been alleged the White House slowed down the US-provided Starlink satellite system used by Ukraine to shoot down Russian drones.

Former CIA Director and retired US General David Patraeus said US sanctions would be "really helpful" in putting pressure on Russian despot Putin. He told Sky News yesterday: “US sanctions would really be helpful in addition to the 21 or 22 rounds of EU sanctions that have been imposed, then I think you can actually see it's possible that Vladimir Putin might look in the mirror one morning and conclude that he really cannot continue this war."

‌



Yesterday, Cabinet minister Yvette Cooper said the UK takes a “different view” to Mr Trump on Ukraine, warning that the UK will continue to increase sanctions. Speaking to Sky News’s Sunday Morning, Health Secretary Ms Cooper - who was Foreign Secretary until recently - said: “We’ve been very clear that Ukraine’s security is also our security. It’s Europe security. It’s also UK security. So look, of course, we have taken a different view on the issue about the need to keep increasing sanctions, and we will continue with that.”

But she stopped short on using the word "wrong" when pressed on Mr Trump's decision to pause sanctions on Russia, adding: “I can tell you my strong personal views around the support for Ukraine, I can tell our collective views about the Government’s support for Ukraine. But we do also have to recognise the crucial diplomatic role that the Prime Minister and the rest of the Government have to play in pulling everybody together in order to support Ukraine, and that’s crucial.”

In a report published on Monday, IPPR - which is independent but is close to the Burnham administration - has warned “Britain’s assumptions about its place in the world no longer hold, upturned by Russian aggression, American unreliability and Chinese coercion”.

Article continues below

It added: “The EU that Britain left no longer exists, and the country cannot ‘rejoin’. Instead, the UK must become a member of a transformed union.” It also released polling, with Persuasion UK, showing more than half (52%) of voters want to join the EU, compared with less than a third (29%) who want to stay out.

Mr Burnham last week said it would be a "dereliction of duty" to reject closer ties with the EU. Ahead of the UK-EU summit next month, he told the Commons: “If we are serious about promoting growth, controlling immigration, upholding our values and security, it is a conversation we must have. Sticking with the status quo is not good enough for Britain.

"Worse, it would be a major dereliction of duty to turn away. We need to take a calm, clear-eyed, rational look at the world as it is today to consider what is best for our country."

News.title: Trump launches attack on 'foolish' Zelensky in extraordinary rant urging Ukraine to surrender
News.content:
Trump launches attack on 'foolish' Zelensky in extraordinary rant urging Ukraine to surrender

The US president has launched a fresh attack on Zelensky as he claims Ukraine is "in shambles" and that the Ukrainian president "doesn’t want to end this war"

View 2 Images Trump launched a new attack on Zelensky (Image: AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson)

Trump has launched a fresh attack on President Volodymyr Zelensky in a further attempt to pressure Ukraine to surrender to Russia as he has slammed the country a "shambles".

‌



‌



Tensions have heightened between the two presidents after Donald Trump made a controversial deal with Moscow to import diesel and branded the Ukrainian president "more difficult to deal with than Putin".

‌



On Sunday night, Trump posted on Truth Social claiming that the US is "in the process of negotiating peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine " as he added that Zelensky "doesn’t want to end this war".

‌



View 2 Images Tensions have been rising between Donald Trump and Volodymyr Zelensky (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Ukraine launched a new wave of strikes on Russian oil refineries this week, which Zelensky has claimed is standing up to the diesel deal he cannot accept.

Russia's defence ministry said on Sunday it had destroyed 1,015 Ukrainian drones over 15 Russian regions, the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black Sea.

‌



Trump's post defended his decision to prevent new sanctions from being placed on Moscow despite criticism and stated he does not “want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table”.

He said of the sanctions: “I can sign it later, or any time that I want!” The US president also attacked the Ukrainian president, stating "Zelensky doesn’t care" and "his country is in shambles".

Zelensky told NBC on Sunday that waiving sanctions against Russia would strengthen Putin’s war effort, and be a “historic mistake” for Washington.

‌



He told NBC: “People want to forget what’s going on. But we can’t give this possibility to forget, or to change reality, or to change the truth.

“We can’t compare me and Putin. He’s aggressor. He occupied us. He killed adults and children, his soldiers. He’s a terrorist. And that’s why I hope that President Trump will be very clear with this position.”

Zelensky later posted on X that he had spoken with US presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner following a meeting between US and Ukrainian negotiating teams in Miami on October 9, as well as “next steps in diplomacy”.

Article continues below

Earlier this week Ukraine did pause attacks on Russian oil facilities, but after Russia reportedly attacked Ukraine’s energy, oil and gas sectors 76 times in the week since Trump’s announcement Zelensky resumed strikes.

Putin has allegedly proposed that he, Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping meet next month to talk about Ukraine in an attempt to end the four-year conflict. Zelensky would not be involved in these talks.

The US president concluded his post on Sunday "I WANT THIS WAR END!"

News.title: Westminster Bridge shut and major 999 response due to 'ongoing incident'
News.content:
Westminster Bridge shut and major 999 response due to 'ongoing incident'

The bridge has been shut this evening

View Image Westminster Bridge is shut (Image: Maureen McLean/REX/Shutterstock)

There's a police presence on Westminster Bridge which has been closed due to an incident.

‌



‌



Met Police were called to the area at around 4pm today (Sunday) due to receiving reports of concern for the welfare of a man.

‌



Emergency services were seen around the vicinity as of 8pm while diversions were put in place around Victoria Embankment, London.

‌



Footage shared on social media shows dozens of emergency vehicles in attendance around Big Ben, including police cars, ambulances and fire engines. A police cordon also appears to stretch across the road.

The London Ambulance Service said its teams were dispatched to the scene, The Standard reports.

Article continues below

A Met spokesperson said: "Police were called at 15:41hrs on Sunday, 18 October following concerns for the welfare of a man on Westminster Bridge.

"Emergency services remain at the scene and Westminster Bridge, along with a number of surrounding roads, has been closed while officers respond to the incident.

"Motorists and pedestrians are advised to avoid the area where possible."

News.title: Priest dies after giant crucifix crushes him during mass
News.content:
Priest dies after giant crucifix crushes him during mass

There were audible gasps after the large wooden cross fell onto Father Sánchez Molinari as he gave a sermon inside the church - the archdiocese later confirmed he died

View 3 Images Father Sánchez Molinari was delivering a sermon when he was hit by the falling cross

A priest has died after a giant crucifix fell onto his head during a livestreamed mass.

‌



‌



Father Sánchez Molinari was crushed to death when the giant cross was fell while he delivered a sermon in Guayaquil, Ecuador, on Saturday. Tragically, the incident was being recorded and went out to those watching online.

‌



The large wooden cross mounted on the wall behind Father Molinari somehow detached and swiftly fell on him. Father Molinari collapsed onto the floor the instant the cross made contact with his head.

‌



There were audible gasps as it dawned on those present that the priest had been seriously injured. "Father, father...call an ambulance," one female member of the congregation was heard screaming.

View 3 Images The priest tragically died after being struck by the falling cross

Others present were also heard screaming as the video continued to be sent out via a livestream. It is unclear what caused the crucifix to fall from the wall.

‌



"We inform you that our brother, Father Patricio Alfredo Sánchez Molinari, who served as parish priest of the Perpetual Help Church, central vicariate, has departed to the House of the Father to enjoy His presence and His glory," said Cardinal Archbishop Luis Cabrera Herrera.

"The Archdiocese of Guayaquil joins in prayer for the eternal rest of his soul and expresses its solidarity, affection, and love to the Redemptorist family, his relatives, and friends. May he rest in peace."

View 3 Images Father Molinari was praised by other religious leaders in Ecuador

Article continues below

The San Lorenzo parish in Vinces in the region of Los Rios, also paid respect to the late priest. A message posted on social media said: "With hope placed in God’s love and mercy, we share the news of the passing of Father Patricio Sánchez Molinari, who served with dedication and pastoral love for several years as parish priest of our Vinces community."

Father Molinari was a member of the Congregation of the Most Holy Redeemer, founded in 1732. His duties included carrying out pastoral and missionary work in the area, reports La Prensa Grafica.

According to local outlets, the Archdiocese of Guayaquil lost two priests last year. Alfonso Aviles and Pedro Anzoategui both drowned while attempting to rescue an altar boy.

News.title: Inside 'boulder-house' with huge windows and natural outdoor pool after owner finally wins planning row
News.content:
Inside 'boulder-house' with huge windows and natural outdoor pool after owner finally wins planning row

The eco-friendly property, designed to resemble natural rock formations, will feature irregularly-shaped windows, a courtyard and a natural outdoor pool

View 5 Images The 'boulder-house' will be built on Ilkley Moor

A contentious contemporary home designed to resemble stone boulders has been granted planning permission to be constructed on a nature reserve on moorland, despite facing significant opposition.

‌



‌



Plans for the eco-friendly property, set to be built on Heber's Ghyll Drive in Ilkley, near Bradford, had previously been rejected before an appeal was lodged with the Planning Inspectorate.

‌



The dwelling, designed to mimic large, irregular natural rock formations, will feature uniquely shaped windows, a courtyard and a natural outdoor pool.

‌



Ilkley Town Council recommended rejecting the planning application, submitted by businessman David Rasche, arguing it would be a "visual anomaly to the moorland".

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 5 Images Plans for the eco-friendly property had previously been rejected

‌



Ibiza airport flooded as mum found dead and torrential rain batters holiday hotspot READ MORE :

Britain's biggest warship HMS Prince of Wales sets sail for the North Atlantic READ MORE :

Councillors contended that the land formed part of several protected areas of interest, including the South Pennine Moors Site of Special Scientific Interest and the South Pennine Moors Special Protection Area and Special Area of Conservation.

Ilkley Moor also forms part of the Bradford Pennine Gateway National Nature Reserve, which is backed by Natural England.

The council further highlighted that the proposed development sat in close proximity to the Swastika Stone, a prehistoric rock carving and one of hundreds of Scheduled Ancient Monuments found on Ilkley Moor.

‌



View 5 Images The home will feature uniquely shaped windows, a courtyard and a natural outdoor pool

However, architects Shaw and Jagger maintained that the property, which will be built on green belt land, takes "cues from the surrounding rocks and escarpments synonymous with the landscape."

They added: "The building depicts a series of monolithic elements embedded in the earth as the wild, dramatic environment looms around, attempting to overcome them."

‌



The original application was turned down by Bradford Council planners on grounds of 'non-determination', meaning a verdict wasn't reached within the stipulated timeframe.

View 5 Images The building has been at the centre of a planning row

However, the decision was challenged and the developers secured approval from the Planning Inspectorate in August via the country house clause.

‌



The country house clause demands an isolated design of "exceptional quality" in that it "is truly outstanding", would "significantly enhance its immediate setting and be sensitive to the defining characteristics of the local area".

View 5 Images The property has been christened Fomorian

Neighbouring Ilkley Quarry is home to the renowned rock formation "Cow and Calf" which takes its name from its resemblance to the animals.

Article continues below

The property has been christened Fomorian - referring to a mythical race of giants in Irish folklore - and takes its inspiration from a creature called Rombald who is believed to have inhabited the moor.

News.title: Watch: Russian saboteur working for Ukraine shares reconnaissance videos
News.content:
A Russian man secretly working for Ukraine's intelligence services has shared videos of surveillance work he says he has done for Kyiv inside Russia.

The man, who we are calling Ivan, claims to have played a role in Ukrainian drone attacks on strategic bombers and munitions factories on his home soil.

He features in a BBC World Service documentary about the shadowy world of Russian saboteurs.

Ivan was cautious about how much detail he shared, making it impossible to verify the activities he claims to have carried out.

News.title: Burnham says youth employment and training crisis is a 'moral failure'
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has warned the UK faces an "economic catastrophe and moral failure" due to the nearly one million young people not in education, employment or training.

Writing in the Times newspaper, external, Burnham has laid out his case for the government to "invest in the success of our young people" rather than "pay for failure through the benefits system".

"Benefits will become the backstop, not the starting point," Burnham wrote in his piece published in Monday's paper.

Later this week, the government is expected to announce plans to give young people thousands of job opportunities. The Conservative Party has labelled the government's youth employment strategy "a disaster".

According to the latest data from the Office for National Statistics, there are almost a million people aged 16 to 24 known as Neets - not in education, employment or training.

In his opinion column, the prime minister said this reflected a "generation being denied its chance to get on in life".

"This is an economic catastrophe and a moral failure. And it must change," he wrote.

Burnham said two years of Covid lockdowns, social media that erodes "confidence and sense of belonging", an education system focused on the "university route", job markets with "too few opportunities" and failures of previous governments have all contributed to the Neets crisis.

"Today, the welfare system provides an assessment, a payment and, after that, goodbye," Burnham wrote. "Too often there is no support, no offer of skills and no opportunity to get a job."

He flagged a shift in the approach to welfare, which he said "will no longer begin by establishing which benefits a young person is entitled to" but rather "begin with their ambitions and the help they need to achieve them".

The prime minister added: "The safety net will always be there for those who cannot work. But if someone can work with the right help, the government has a duty to do everything in its power to make that happen."

Ministers are this week set to release plans for tens of thousands of new youth apprenticeships and placements in the construction industry, and at accounting, consulting and legal firms.

Shadow Business and Trade Secretary Julia Lopez said: "Labour have been a disaster for youth jobs. Their tax hikes and red tape have made it harder for businesses to hire, invest and grow, destroying opportunities for young people looking to take their first step on the career ladder."

News.title: People playing loud music on buses could face £100 fine
News.content:
Passengers who play loud music on buses in England could be fined up to Â£100 under an attempt by the government to crack down on antisocial behaviour.

The measures also seek to tackle littering, vaping and threatening behaviour to help improve journeys on all forms of public transport.

Offenders on buses could be issued with the fines under new powers for local authorities.

A national campaign asking rail passengers "share the carriage, not the noise" is also being launched. The proposed crackdown has been welcomed by campaigners, but some have questioned how it can be enforced.

"We've all been on the train when someone starts blasting music or videos from their phone. It gets on your nerves and can quickly spoil the journey," said Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

Under existing powers, those who are asked to stop and refuse could be removed from a train or fined up to Â£1,000.

The phenomenon has been given many terms - including loudcasting or sodcasting - and in recent years, Ofcom, YouGov and Transport for London (TfL) have all published polls showing the vast majority of people dislike it.

Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said small changes in behaviour "can make a massive difference to people's experience on public transport".

The government said it had issued new guidance to local authorities on powers - which were introduced earlier this year - to help them crackdown on loud music and other antisocial behaviour on buses in England.

These new powers allow them to impose new rules on buses, but still need to be signed off by the Transport Secretary

Those who commit offences could face fixed penalties of up to Â£100.

The government says bus drivers will not be responsible for enforcing the new rules. It says authorised officers, including Transport Safety Officers and the Police, will deal with the incidents.

Meanwhile a new national campaign aims to remind rail passengers to "share the carriage, not the noise", to improve journeys for everyone

The campaign will be launched across operator websites, social media, and in carriages. The government said this would end the current "patchwork" of approaches across different rail operators, and help create "a clear, consistent message across the network".

The general secretary of the TSSA transport union, Maryam Eslamdoust, said tackling antisocial behaviour on public transport was "a step in the right direction".

However, she added that the government must also "urgently confront the violence, threats and abuse faced by passengers and transport workers".

"Increasing the budget for British Transport Police is vital to protect people, respond to incidents and bring violent offenders to justice," she said.

Michael Solomon Williams from the Campaign for Better Transport told the BBC antisocial behaviour could be a "real deterrent" to people using public transport, especially those with different accessibility needs.

He also questioned how the new measures will be enforced. "When local authorities are required to do the enforcement there are perhaps some question marks about how a local police force might be called upon on bus services, for example, where we don't tend to see British Transport Police."

Richard Holden MP, Shadow Transport Secretary, said: "After we led the charge against antisocial behaviour on public transport last summer, Ministers have worked out that nobody wants to endure pounding techno or blaring hip hop on a packed train or bus.

"But passengers and railway staff face far more serious problems. Assaults against rail staff have risen by 68%, while prosecutions have slumped under Labour. It's time for Andy Burnham to get serious about enforcement, tackling violence and protecting those who work on our railways."

Liberal Democrat Transport spokesperson, Olly Glover MP said: "Tough talk means nothing without enforcement.

"Unless the Government funds transport safety officers on the ground, these new rules won't be worth the paper they're printed on."

Independent watchdog Transport Focus said research it had published in June showed personal safety and security was now fundamental to passengers' confidence in the railway.

"Four in 10 passengers say that anti-social behaviour has made them feel vulnerable when travelling," said Alex Campbell, Transport Focus's director of policy and insight.

"Measures that reduce nuisance behaviour, such as playing loud music and vaping, can help improve people's experience and encourage more people to choose public transport."

News.title: Home sellers cut asking prices on 3,000 properties a day
News.content:
Home sellers cut asking prices on more than 3,000 properties a day on average in Britain during September, according to figures from Rightmove shared exclusively with the BBC.

The property website said the total was the highest of any month for 15 years and was driven, in part, by a glut of homes on the market and some sellers setting unrealistic expectations.

The proportion of listed homes that eventually had a price cut peaked in 2023 and has remained relatively high since.

Property portals say buyers are now having to be choosy, with many working to a tight budget as mortgage rates have risen to three-year highs.

"Once a home has been on the market for a while and then has a price reduction, some buyers start asking questions, even when there is nothing wrong with the property," said Colleen Babcock of Rightmove.

"In a market with so much choice, first impressions matter."

News.title: Cindy Crawford 'beyond heartbroken' after death of son Presley at 27
News.content:
Supermodel Cindy Crawford has said she and her family are "beyond heartbroken" over the death of her son Presley Gerber.

"He is a sweet, beautiful soul who loved and is loved, now and forever," she posted on Instagram, next to a black-and-white photo of him. "We are so proud of how he showed up in the world, with kindness and vulnerability."

The 27-year-old died on 20 September at a rehab facility in California. Police said officials are investigating his death as a suspected overdose.

Gerber had been a model like his mother and younger sister Kaia, making his catwalk debut for Italian label Moschino aged just 16.

Crawford wrote in the post on Sunday: "We feel so blessed to have had Presley in our lives for 27 years."

"We are grateful for the outpouring of love and support from so many who know and love our family and even strangers who feel our pain," she also posted.

"Til we meet again our sweet boy. We love you forever, Mom, Dad and Kaia," she wrote in closing, with an emoji of angel wings.

The tribute also listed the dates of his birth and death.

The Los Angeles County Medical Examiner lists Gerber's case as pending additional investigation. The Santa Monica Police Department has said there is no indication foul play was involved in his death.

Gerber's sister Kaia also dedicated a post to him on Sunday which included a video of the two siblings as children dancing together, a photo of them standing near the ocean, and a four-page letter to "prez" typed out on a blue background.

In the letter, she said she had been scared of getting her ears pierced, so "you went first".

"But when I held the earring they took from your body, all I could think was: That belongs to you," she wrote.

"I am learning how to love you when I cannot see you," she also wrote. "How to tell you something without picking up my phone to call you. How to be your sister in a world that I can't reach for you in," she wrote.

In recent years, Gerber had spoken openly about his mental health challenges and drug use and frequently posted videos on Instagram himself for what he called "Mental Health Mondays".

His father Rande Gerber, a well-known businessman, co-founded the Casamigos tequila brand with George Clooney.

If you're affected by any of the issues in this article you can find details of organisations who can help via the BBC Action Line.

Details of help available in many countries can be found at Befrienders Worldwide, external, external.

News.title: Suspects hunted after police officer injured in shooting
News.content:
Detectives are searching for two suspects who fled after a police officer was shot in Nottingham city centre.

Nottinghamshire Police said the officer had approached two suspects in Angel Row shortly before 04:50 BST on Sunday.

The officer is in a stable condition in hospital, where he is receiving treatment for a wound to his foot, the force added.

Detectives said a man and a woman had fled the scene and that a firearm, which could be seen within the cordon, had been found.

Angel Row remained closed by a large police scene until Sunday evening.

Police cars were parked along the road, which is lined by fast food stores and shops, and orange traffic cones had been laid out alongside items left on the road.

The cordon had also been extended to St James's Street, where an officer is standing guard.

The force said there would be a heightened police presence as the investigation continued.

News.title: Chance of storms this week as Atlantic jet stream roars into life
News.content:
The UK may see its first named storm of the autumn as forecasts show the potential for a deep area of low pressure to cross the UK later this week.

A strengthening jet stream triggered by temperature contrasts across North America will cause turbulent conditions to develop.

All areas will experience rain at times, including those currently in drought, but amounts of rain will depend on the exact track of a stormy low pressure system later in the week.

After a chilly weekend, temperatures will generally remain slightly below average for mid-October.

News.title: GTA 6: Can you cheat on someone with a video game character?
News.content:
Imagine your partner spending hours flirting with someone else, trying to hold their hand and taking them on dates. Most people would have questions.

But what if that someone only exists inside a video game?

The latest instalment in Rockstar's blockbuster Grand Theft Auto franchise is set to be the biggest entertainment launch of the year when it is released next month.

Judging by previews, the connection between its two main characters is a central feature.

Rockstar has hinted that the Bonnie and Clyde-type protagonists Jason and Lucia do not have to become a full-on romantic couple.

But their relationship can grow by spending time together outside of the main crime and life-on-the-run storyline â through shopping, visiting bars and restaurants and working out together.

Smaller interactions like holding hands and quickly responding to each other's texts can help build a bond.

The idea has restarted a debate almost as old as gaming itself: if you are that invested in a fictional relationship, is your real-life partner entitled to be upset?

News.title: Polanski says he will not overturn Green Party's 'Zionism is racism' motion
News.content:
Zack Polanski has said he will not overturn a motion passed by Green Party members that declared Zionism a form of racism.

The Green leader told Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that, while he would like to make amendments, it would be party policy until 2028.

The motion, passed at the party's conference earlier this month, described Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state in historic Palestine to the exclusion and/or domination of the non-Jewish population".

It divided the party and sparked a major backlash from MPs, Jewish campaigners, the government and the European Green movement, with the equality watchdog writing to the party for more information on it.

The fallout from the motion overshadowed the final days of Polanski's campaign in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, in which he came second to Labour, and threatened his leadership.

He came under criticism for not voting on the motion which was passed by 1,022 votes to 813 - a small fraction of the party's 230,000 members - in Brighton earlier this month.

The motion also asserted the party's backing for "a single democratic state throughout historic Palestine", a full arms embargo on Israel and a commitment to Palestinian liberation.

Asked if he would now step in as leader to overturn it, Polanski said: "I'm not going to try to overturn it.

"At the first available opportunity, I do want to amend it - I want to move away from one state, towards saying that Israelis and Palestinians should decide that future for themselves."

He said this would not be until 2028 as "you can't [amend it] within the rules, so when you vote on something in our party conference that's then policy for two years".

Kuenssberg asked if he would therefore change the rules as leader, but Polanski said: "I think if members have made a decision, then I respect the democratic will of our members."

Former Green Party co-leader and current MP Adrian Ramsay responded by calling for action to be taken sooner.

"I don't think it's tenable for us to continue the next two years with this policy that's been adopted given the huge political distraction that it's been for our councillors across the country," he told the BBC News Channel.

"One way forward could be to have a ballot of all party members to establish very clearly where does the party as a whole stand - my view is we would see a different answer."

Polanski had previously said he would not have voted for the motion without two amendments.

The first of these would have avoided "determining there was a single democratic state", and the other would have specified that the motion should not be used to discipline Jewish Green members who attend synagogues that consider themselves Zionist.

Both of these amendments were voted down by members at the party's conference.

Green MPs, including Ellie Chowns, have called for the party's member-led decision-making procedures to be reviewed given how few people took part in the vote.

News.title: Ending corridor care in hospitals for children a priority, says health secretary
News.content:
The health secretary has asked the NHS to draw up urgent plans to speed up ending hospital "corridor care" for children.

Yvette Cooper told the BBC there would be new standards for caring for children in A&E in England, with figures collected on corridor care by age for the first time.

She was speaking on Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg where the programme highlighted the case of two-year-old Finlay Roberts who died in 2024 after spending hours in a hospital corridor before being discharged.

The health secretary has announced Â£140m to improve urgent care in England ahead of what she said would be a "more difficult" winter than usual.

The government has already pledged to end corridor care for all patients by the end of this parliament, and now Cooper has said eradicating it for children would be prioritised.

Corridor care refers to patients receiving treatment or waiting in corridors, waiting rooms or other hospital areas due to a lack of appropriate space.

The health secretary was also asked if the government would meet a key manifesto pledge that 92% of patients would start treatment within 18 weeks of booking a hospital appointment by 2029.

"That remains our manifesto commitment and of course we're going to keep working towards it," Cooper said.

Pushed further on whether the target was achievable, she replied: "The whole point about having the targets is about having something stretching that we work towards."

The 18-week target has consistently not been met for more than a decade.

Cooper said that the NHS was dealing with a number of challenges after record A&E admissions following heatwaves over the summer.

According to the latest figures for England, an estimated 7.37 million treatments were waiting to be carried out at the end of August, relating to 6.24 million patients.

On the programme the story of Finlay Roberts, was highlighted. He died after being discharged from hospital in 2024 following hours spent in an A&E corridor in north London.

Finlay's father David told the BBC the situation was a "terrible mess", with the family moved into a room with a bed before being moved back into the corridor.

"He just clung to me, as we now know, slowly dying," he said.

Liz Roberts, Finlay's mother, said corridor care "robs people of their dignity when they are at their most vulnerable". She recalled being told to administer a suppository to her son in the corridor.

Cooper apologised to Finlay's parents on behalf of the NHS, saying: "No child should be treated in a corridor. No patient should be treated in a corridor."

News.title: Man, 80, who died in light aircraft crash near Loch Lomond named
News.content:
An 80-year-old man who died in a light aircraft crash is understood to be flying instructor Ian Haggis.

He and a 16-year-old boy died when their plane came down near Loch Lomond. The teenager's identity has not been released.

The pair had flown out from Glasgow Airport at 16:17 and stopped transmitting at 16:37, a few miles north east of the village of Drymen near Stirling.

Emergency services were called to the crash at about 16:45 on Friday.

Both of them were pronounced dead at the scene.

Temporary airspace restrictions are currently in place over the area while the Air Accidents Investigation Branch (AAIB) carries out its inquiries.

Old Drymen Road, near the scene of the crash, remains closed with vehicles being turned around and hillwalkers rerouted.

News.title: NHS data breaches a disgrace, health secretary says
News.content:
NHS staff accessing the medical records of the Nottingham attacks victims and possible breaches over a man killed by a tiger is a "disgrace", the health secretary has said.

Speaking to the BBC, Yvette Cooper said she expected action to be taken against staff who had breached NHS data and privacy standards.

Her comments came after Nottingham University Hospitals (NUH) NHS Trust confirmed it had sacked a total of 15 members of staff and Yorkshire Ambulance Service said William Chapman's medical records may have been accessed illegitimately.

Dr Manjeet Shehmar, NUH medical director, previously said there was "simply no excuse for accessing the records of a patient without a legitimate reason".

Speaking to the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Cooper said "there's got to be proper respect for patients" from NHS staff.

"Let me be really clear about this," she said. "There are proper data and privacy standards across the NHS."

Students Barnaby Webber and Grace O'Malley-Kumar, and grandfather Ian Coates, were stabbed to death on 13 June 2023 by Valdo Calocane, who was diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 2020.

NUH said in May that it had sacked 11 members of staff for inappropriately accessing the victims' medical records, and had informed the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) and Nottinghamshire Police of the investigation.

At the time, the ICO told the BBC it would "assess any evidence provided by the trust in due course and consider our next steps", while police said there was "no criminal investigation".

In its update about further dismissals on Friday, NUH said it had taken action against "doctors, nurses, registered healthcare professionals and other staff", and that independent regulators such as the Nursing and Midwifery Council and General Medical Council, the ICO and Nottinghamshire Police had been informed.

NUH added a new system, currently under testing, was being implemented to protect patient records in future and alert the trust to potential breaches.

News.title: Man and woman in their late teens die in collision
News.content:
Two people in their late teens died in a collision involving two cars, Suffolk Police said.

Officers were first called by the ambulance service to Debenham Road near Little Stonham at 10:15 BST.

Fire crews and the air ambulance were also called to the incident that involved a red Peugeot 107 and a silver Volkswagen Passat.

Police said a male passenger in the Peugeot died at the scene. The female driver was taken to Addenbrooke's Hospital in Cambridge by land ambulance, but has since died as a result of her injuries.

The occupants of the Passat suffered minor injuries, the police spokesperson added.

The road was expected to reopen later in the evening.
