World.title: Venezuela opposition renews support for Maria Corina Machado as leader
World.content:
The exiled Nobel laureate has petitioned for new elections in Venezuela and for the country to allow her return.

Share Venezuela opposition renews support for Maria Corina Machado as leader on social media

An alliance of Venezuelan opposition parties has reaffirmed its commitment to exiled Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Corina Machado as its leader.

On Sunday, members of the opposition’s Unitary Democratic Platform (PUD) agreed in a meeting in Caracas to “recognise and support the leadership of Maria Corina Machado”.

The coalition also renewed its demand for free elections in Venezuela, following a series of contested presidential votes in 2024 and 2018.

Sunday’s statement included 14 proposals for a democratic transition, including freedom for political parties, the release of all political prisoners and the safe return of those who went into exile.

The announcement also increases pressure on authorities to allow Machado’s return. She has been living in exile since leaving Venezuela last December to receive her Nobel Prize.

“The will of the Venezuelans must once again govern the destiny of our nation,” the opposition’s former presidential candidate Edmundo Gonzalez wrote on social media supporting the proposals.

“We will not accept political prisoners, persecution or a governing power that disregards the mandate of its citizens. Living in freedom and under a genuine constitutional order is a legitimate demand of our society.”

No election set

Venezuela has yet to declare a date for a new presidential vote. Since January 3, the country has been led by interim President Delcy Rodriguez of the long-governing United Socialist Party of Venezuela (PSUV).

PSUV leaders have been accused of carrying out human rights abuses against political dissidents, including arbitrary arrest, imprisonment and torture.



Still, after the United States launched a military operation to abduct and jail former President Nicolas Maduro, the PSUV has remained in power with the support of the White House.

US President Donald Trump has backed Rodriguez’s leadership, despite her having been Maduro’s vice president.

His administration has maintained an active role in Venezuela, exerting control over its oil resources and pressuring the Rodriguez government for reforms.

But critics point out that Trump has been reluctant to push Rodriguez for new elections, opting instead for a three-phase plan that focuses first on stabilising the country and economic recovery before pursuing a political transition.

Machado, meanwhile, has told The Financial Times she would like to see Venezuela hold elections by July next year.

“The US government and the Venezuelan people all agree ⁠⁠that the only way to make ⁠⁠this sustainable and ⁠⁠a real victory is to turn Venezuela into a stable democracy,” she told the newspaper earlier this month.

A thwarted return

Venezuelan authorities blocked Machado’s repeated attempts to return to the country, according to her party, Vente Venezuela.

Machado has also reportedly attempted to petition the Trump administration for help re-entering Venezuela.

Separately, she gifted Trump her Nobel Peace Prize in January, during a visit to Washington, DC. Media reports, however, have suggested friction between the Trump administration and Machado.

In interviews with Reuters and Axios, US administration officials have anonymously expressed frustration with the opposition leader’s repeated efforts to return home, particularly after a pair of deadly earthquakes in Venezuela last July.

Axios quoted one official as calling Machado’s push “political opportunism”.

Machado, however, remains one of the most popular figures in Venezuela’s opposition.

In October 2023, Machado won the opposition coalition’s presidential primary, but in January 2024, Venezuela’s courts blocked her from running in the upcoming race.

The courts upheld a 15-year ban on her holding public office, reportedly due to her support of US sanctions against the Maduro government.

Gonzalez ultimately replaced Machado as the opposition candidate in the 2024 race. Maduro claimed victory for a third term as Venezuela’s president in that election cycle, despite widespread criticism that the vote did not meet democratic standards.

The opposition released vote tallies that appeared to show Gonzalez had won the race.

The US had recognised Gonzalez as the country’s rightful president-elect and denied the legitimacy of Maduro’s election claims.



Machado was previously removed from the National Assembly in 2014, due to her activism against the Venezuelan government.

A third round of talks between the Rodriguez government and the opposition began in Venezuela this month.

But instead of including Machado, the negotiations have involved members of the 2015 National Assembly, which was led by the opposition and dissolved under Maduro.

Still, in a statement this month, the US State Department praised the talks as aiding the Venezuelan government’s reform.

“Political reconciliation talks between the interim Venezuelan government and 2015 National Assembly representatives are producing tangible reforms in civil liberties and political rights, laying the groundwork for credible elections and a democratic transition,” the State Department said.

World.title: Alberta independence referendum: Will separatists survive a loss?
World.content:
Alberta’s independence movement faces likely defeat, but history suggests losing a referendum may not end the fight.

Cory Morgan has spent more than 25 years fighting for Canada’s oil-rich province of Alberta to become an independent country. On Monday, Albertans will head to the polls to vote on the issue for the very first time. But even if the answer is no, Morgan said he’s in it for the long haul.

“I would respect the will of the voters,” he told Al Jazeera. “If they’ve decided it’s not time to go that route yet, then so be it. But that doesn’t mean I’ll stop.”

Morgan, the founder of the advocacy organisation Pathway to Independence, is among a group of longtime separatists who have managed to push what was once a fringe idea onto the ballot.

Monday’s provincial referendum asks Alberta residents to weigh whether they would like to pursue a binding resolution in the future on the question of independence.

Polls indicate the pro-independence side has little chance of succeeding, with four of five people in the province saying they want Alberta to remain a part of Canada. But Morgan’s focus is on the one in five who don’t.

“That’s not a movement that’s leaving,” he said.

What the referendum will mean for the separatist movement and for Canada as a whole, however, is a more complicated question.

What exactly are Albertans voting on?

Monday’s ballot gives Albertans two options: to remain part of Canada or begin the legal process for holding a future referendum on separation.

A vote in favour of the second option doesn’t mean Alberta immediately becomes an independent country.

Any province that tries to secede would first have to go through complex negotiations with the federal government in Ottawa, other provinces and Indigenous peoples who live in and around Alberta.



Some separatist organisers have been using that distinction to encourage people to vote for the referendum — even if they don’t necessarily want independence.

“Strategic separatists and their leaders have been using that ambiguity, that lower-bar threshold, to entice folks to vote not to leave, but rather to send Ottawa a message that Albertans need to be heard,” said Jared Wesley, a political science professor at the University of Alberta.

He told Al Jazeera that the message may be resonating with some voters.

Data collected by Viewpoint Alberta, a University of Alberta-based research initiative, suggests that two-thirds of voters who support the referendum say they’re doing so for strategic reasons, to send a message to Ottawa.

These are people Morgan calls “reluctant separatists”, people who are “at the end of their rope” and simply want Ottawa to pay attention.

But Prime Minister Mark Carney has warned Albertans against this strategy.

“Don’t be fooled by the idea you can ‘send a message’ with your vote,” he told a pro-Canada rally in Calgary on Thursday. “This is not poker. A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep division and great uncertainty.”

What’s driving Alberta’s separatist movement?

Monday’s referendum has been decades in the making. Separatists have long felt that Alberta, home to the world’s fourth-largest proven oil reserves, sends too much money to Ottawa, subsidising the rest of the country while receiving little in return.

They also take issue with federal energy policies that they feel limit the potential of the province’s oil industry.

For Morgan, the resentment stretches back to the 1980s when the National Energy Program was introduced by the government of Pierre Trudeau, former Prime Minister Justin Trudeau’s father.

The policy used price controls, taxes and ownership rules to keep Canadian energy affordable while directing more of Alberta’s revenues to Ottawa.

It has since become a central symbol of “Western alienation”, a term used to describe the sense of disenfranchisement felt among Canada’s westernmost provinces.

Those tensions resurfaced decades later under Justin Trudeau, whose term began in 2015. His climate policies, including a national carbon tax and a limit on emissions, angered Alberta’s oil sector.

“We’ve been fighting about the same things for 50 years,” said Morgan.



Then came the COVID-19 pandemic. Experts say demonstrations against health restrictions mobilised a new generation of conservative activists, breathing new life into Alberta’s separatist movement.

Trudeau ultimately resigned as Liberal Party leader and prime minister in 2025, amid sinking poll numbers. Carney was elected his replacement.

Last year, under growing pressure from separatist groups, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith’s government made it easier to start referendums, helping bring the question of Alberta’s independence onto the political agenda.

For Wesley, the moment is less about growing public support for independence and more about pressure from within Smith’s governing United Conservative Party, whose members show higher support for separation than Albertans generally.

“We’re having a referendum because Danielle Smith wants us to have a referendum,” Wesley said. “She is looking to solve internal party matters by throwing a question to the broader public.”

Though she called Monday’s referendum, Smith has said she opposes the independence effort, and on October 14, she announced she had voted against seceding.

“In my view, now is not the time to give up hope in our country, not when we have fought so long and come so far,” Smith said in a social media video, explaining her vote.

Could defeat make the movement stronger?

Smith’s political gamble has drawn comparisons with the 2016 Brexit referendum in the United Kingdom, including from Carney.

At the time, then-UK Prime Minister David Cameron called a vote over whether the country should leave the European Union, in hopes of settling a debate dividing his own Conservative Party.

Voters ultimately chose to leave the bloc, triggering years of political unrest.

But Ian Cooper, a political scientist who grew up in Alberta and now lives in Ireland, says a more useful comparison might be a different UK referendum in 1975, when British voters chose overwhelmingly to stay in what was then known as the European Economic Community.

That vote, he said, did little to deter those who wanted the country out.

“The activists who were in favour of Brexit — this is before anybody called it Brexit — they really played the long game,” he said. “It took them 25 years, but they finally achieved it.”

Cooper suspects that, even if Alberta separation is roundly defeated, separatists could take a similar approach, pursuing the issue over the long term to gain prominence and support.

“My impression is that they really are true believers, and it’s really ideologically driven,” he said.

If Monday’s separatist vote fails, Morgan said separatists would need to take a hard look at why they had fallen short and work towards making a stronger case for independence in the future.

He does not believe the underlying grievances can be resolved by working within the Canadian system or by electing a more sympathetic federal government.



Carney, who grew up in Alberta, acknowledged at Thursday’s rally that “the frustrations that many Albertans have felt are real”. He added that Ottawa had made people in the province feel “like our resources weren’t our own”.

The prime minister has tried, amid an ongoing trade war with the United States, to improve relations with Alberta, including through commitments to building a new pipeline to Canada’s west coast and major infrastructure projects.

Morgan admits that, for those whose goal is simply to get more leverage in Ottawa, “it’s pretty clear the movement has been effective”.

“We’ve seen more love from a federal prime minister in the last year than we’ve seen in the last 10,” Morgan said. “The problem though, when it comes to stubborn independence folks like me, is nothing has changed in the system.”

Prime ministers come and go, he added. “We’re just one election away from another hostile one.”

Why the other referendum questions matter

But the referendum could also offer an opportunity to challenge the premise that Alberta’s grievances cannot be addressed within Canada.

The independence question is just one of 10 on Monday’s ballot. Other proposals include restricting temporary residents’ access to healthcare and education, as well as allowing Alberta to choose its own judges.

Smith has encouraged Albertans to vote in favour of the nine other proposals, arguing that they will give her more negotiating power in Ottawa.

“Many Albertans I speak with tell me they want to send Ottawa a message, and I would suggest the best way to do that is to give us a strong mandate on the other nine questions,” she said on social media.

If Albertans back those proposals but Ottawa refuses to make concessions, Cooper, the political scientist, said the movement would have fresh ammunition to argue that meaningful change within the current system is impossible.

“Buried in the nine other questions are the seeds for a future referendum,” Cooper added.

What could keep the movement alive?

Not everyone agrees, however, on whether the separatists can emerge from the vote as a united force.

Wesley explained that people have been drawn to the separatist cause for a variety of reasons.

If there’s a sense that independence is not a realistic prospect, there may be little to keep that group of activists together, he said. They could turn their attention to other conservative issues, such as immigration.

Other experts question whether Alberta’s separatist movement, which is united more by economic grievances than by a shared cultural identity, can endure the way Quebec’s has.

Just two weeks ago, the largely French-speaking province elected the separatist Party Quebecois, which has promised a third referendum on independence after Trump leaves office.

Morgan, however, argues that Alberta does have a distinct culture, shaped by generations of people who have moved to the province in search of prosperity.

“The type of person drawn to do that is often an individualistic type of person,” he said. “They want the opportunity to go out and succeed or fail on their own.”

“And that builds a kind of a distinct culture on its own, even if it’s not a long-built one, as you would see in a distinct area like Quebec with a linguistic difference or in another country.”

Even if Albertans reject separation, he believes the movement has succeeded in forcing Ottawa to take the province’s frustrations more seriously.



“Hopefully some people understand that eventually something has to give,” he said. “So whatever the results are … I do hope, at the very least, they’ve served as a wake-up call to a lot of people.”

World.title: Macron condemns violence after riots lead to looting and mass arrests
World.content:
NewsFeed Macron condemns violence after riots lead to looting and mass arrests

French President Emmanuel Macron says protesters who attacked government buildings need to pay for their crimes. His address comes after hundreds were arrested across France during violent protests against the rising cost of living and poor school conditions.

World.title: Macron calls for 'calm and order' after riots across France
World.content:
French President Emmanuel Macron has called for "calm and order" after a major day of protests turned into rioting and looting on Saturday, and as some disorder continued in Paris on Sunday.

In a national address from the ÃlysÃ©e Palace, he warned those who had taken part not to "escalate", adding: "We all feel anger and shame."

Some 550,000 demonstrators took to the streets for largely peaceful protests against rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools.

Macron said a distinction must be drawn between the "legitimate demands" of protesters and "those who destroyed, smashed and looted".

Police have arrested about 2,400 people, according to France's interior ministry.

The French president said "nothing justifies" the "unbridled" violence seen and said those involved would face justice.

Groups of rioters, some dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas, also came out in Paris, Marseille and other towns and cities, with some setting fire to cars and buildings.

World.title: 'Very upsetting': Residents in shock after historic French town hall set alight
World.content:
A historic town hall in the French city of Limoges has been damaged in an apparent arson attack following a day of nationwide protests on Saturday.

Dramatic footage shared online shows the 19th-century building engulfed in flames, with the spire of its clock tower later collapsing.

On Sunday, stunned residents watched as firefighters, who had battled the blaze through the night, assessed the building's structural integrity. Officials have not yet confirmed whether the town hall is at risk of collapse.

"Damaging heritage buildings because you're angry with the government is selfish", one resident told the BBC.

BBC correspondent Chris Bockman reports from Limoges.

Read more about the protests across France.

World.title: Major fire at Canada military base leaves four dead, dozens injured
World.content:
Four members of the Canadian military have died and dozens were injured in a major fire at a base in the province of Alberta.

Addressing the nation on Sunday from Ottawa, Prime Minister Mark Carney described it as "one of the worst tragedies for the forces on Canadian soil in peacetime".

The fire broke out at about 16:00 local time (22:00 GMT) on Saturday at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, one of the country's busiest military training bases, and is now contained. Its cause is still unclear, but officials said it did not appear tied to "terrorist activity".

"The nation is in mourning for those brave members of our armed forces who we have lost," said Carney.

The BBC has confirmed that Sgt Morgan Wong, Pte Shaun Farrell, Pte Aidan Goulding and Pte Hayden Lykkemark have died.

Of the 39 injured people being cared for in hospital, at least 19 are in a critical condition, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said at a press briefing on Sunday evening.

Fire and rescue teams are remaining at the scene to contain any potential flare-ups, Wainwright Mayor Bruce Pugh told the BBC.

Members of the infantry had been conducting "high-intensity combat training with live munitions" at a grenade range and attack range, where 10 soldiers practise attacking a simulated enemy, Maj-Gen Wade Rutland told reporters at the briefing.

"There was a multitude of ordnance moving through the Wainwright training area," he said, including a grenade launcher, grenades, small arms and ammunition.

A grass fire ignited about 1km (0.6 miles) away, with the cause currently under investigation, and moved toward the attack range.

"What I would say is there was multiple training activities happening throughout the training area at the time," he said. "Uncommonly strong winds caused the fire to spread rapidly and shift direction towards the range administrative area."

Cannon fire had been heard coming from the base on Saturday before it suddenly stopped, Mayor Pugh told the BBC, noting it's not uncommon to hear cannons being fired there.

News then came through that local emergency services had been deployed to an "all hands on deck" situation.

Carney said military and emergency crews fought the flames throughout the night in "some of the worst conditions imaginable".

The people who were hurt were on the attack range and included reservists and soldiers from the Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry, officials said.

In a statement early on Sunday, the Canadian Armed Forces said that "while the incident remains under investigation, at this time, there are no indications that it was the result of any terrorist activity".

Rutland told the briefing: "We do not believe this [incident] to be a result of any oil and gas infrastructure nor any outside interference".

World.title: Trump says suspension of Russia sanctions is to keep peace negotiations going
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has said his decision to suspend several Russian sanctions is an effort to keep Moscow at the negotiating table.

"I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine," Trump said on his Truth Social messaging platform, adding that he didn't want to "do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table".

Trump blocked numerous sanctions on Russia on Friday night, two days before they were due to take effect, as a row with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky deepened.

Zelensky told NBC News on Sunday that siding with Russian President Vladimir Putin would be a "historic mistake".

Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev has responded to Trump's order by calling it "an important and truly historic moment". He said the sanctions, which were passed by the US Congress and signed into law by the US president in September, would have inflicted "serious damage" on the US and global market.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has described the suspension of the sanctions as a 60-day pause during which their potential impact on the US and global economies would be analysed.

In his Truth Social post, Trump also said Zelensky "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did", adding "he could have made a better deal two years ago than he can now".

Zelensky has pushed for an end to fighting, and has repeatedly said that Putin doesn't want peace, since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Relations between Washington and Kyiv frayed after the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel last week.

Despite the international sanctions, Russia has still been able to export oil, much of it to China and India - often at attractive discounts. According to the think-tank Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), China has taken about half of Russia's crude exports, with India accounting for about 37%.

In remarks to a European Union summit, after Trump announced the deal to buy diesel from Russia and said Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with" than Putin, Zelensky said it was nice to be among "real leaders".

World.title: Inside the shadowy world of anti-Putin sabotage from within Russia
World.content:
"You will get a file... from me or a colleagueâ¦ with the proposed target. The file will contain [the target's] photo, his data, his details, date of birth, age, and a description of him. There'll be information on his car, if he has one. When you go to the target, don't take a phone," he told his volunteers.

Foma was once part of the Russian elite, so he claims to have a unique set of contacts and constant flow of insider information.

He showed Mamon on his laptop how he mapped military targets.

"This shows a database... the location of storage warehouses, and military units. Where generals liveâ¦ Where the pilots of strategic bombers who shell Ukraine live.

"In order to break the system, you need to understand how it works. Then you can aim for their weak points."

He said there were about "three dozen" people in his network split between Russia, Ukraine and elsewhere in Europe, with the contingent outside Russia providing logistical support, such as tracking targets' digital footprints.

Foma stressed that the GUR suggests the targets to be surveilled, but that he and his team check for themselves that these individuals should be considered military criminals.

"As a ruleâ¦ we also check the data [on that person]â¦ Only after that we say whether we work or not."

But he argued that his team's actions were justified.

"I want people who do terrible things on behalf of Putin and Russia in Ukraineâ¦ to understand that they'll have to pay for it. I want them to get scared."

Foma stressed that he only passed on intelligence to the Ukrainians, and his network did not carry out any assassinations themselves.

Of the assassination of Gen Sarvarov, killed in December 2025, he later texted Mamon to say: "Keeping track of him took quite an effort. He lived alternately with his mistress and his colleague. Covered his tracks and constantly changed his schedule."

But Foma did not share any plans with Mamon and the BBC in advance.

Ivan, however, was tight-lipped about the work he had been involved with, even after the event.

Foma did his own digging on Ivan.

After checking with his military intelligence contacts in both Ukraine and Russia, he thought it likely that Ivan had been involved in a plan to strike Russia's largest military drone factory at Yelabuga in June last year, external. One person was reported to have been killed in the incident.

Ivan stressed that the aim is always to try to avoid harming civilians.

Operations have clearly been risky for Ivan too.

"The most serious case was when my car was stopped for inspection and I had the handmade explosives on me. The risk was very high - however as you can see, I was not detected," he said.

To mitigate the risk of being compromised, "there is no clear structure" to the work, he said, adding he had never met and did not know the identity of others he had been working alongside.

Foma has the same rule for his operatives.

"As soon as you start gathering people in groups, in general chatsâ¦ leaving a mark on the internet, with a high probability this whole group will be quickly detained or destroyed," he said.

Ivan stressed there were few people left in Russia suitable for this kind of work.

"Most of the ideological people have either left the country or are already behind bars," he said.

Many Russians involved in sabotage work on their native soil are therefore either oblivious - for example lorry drivers unaware that their cargoes have been compromised - or are individuals who have been paid, the BBC understands.

Ivan, on the other hand, says he is doing this work for ideological reasons - he used to be a member of the political opposition. As such, his movements would be expected to be monitored closely by the Russian authorities.

So it was a surprise that he managed to frequently leave Russia and return.

World.title: Inside Chicago's battle against the synthetic drugs flooding the US
World.content:
Warning: This video contains descriptions of drug-taking and distressing images

A new wave of synthetic drugs is sweeping across the United States, raising fear of a worsening drug crisis.

Earlier this year, President Donald Trump pledged a crackdown on drug cartels, proscribing many as terrorist organisations.

Drug overdose deaths have fallen from a peak of around 110,000 in 2022, down to roughly 70,000 last year.

However, America's decades-long drug crisis may be accelerating and authorities are increasingly concerned about cheaper, more powerful synthetic drugs, including an animal tranquilliser called tranq.

The BBC's Quentin Sommerville reports from the frontlines in South Side, Chicago, where communities are battling the crisis.

Camera journalist: Darren Conway

Read more about the synthetic drug crisis sweeping the US.

World.title: EU tariffs aimed at China hitting Ukraine, steel boss says
World.content:
The boss of one of Ukraine's biggest steel companies has called on the European Union to drop import restrictions on products made from the country, arguing it has been "bundled together" in measures aimed a curbing cheap imports from the likes of China.

Yuriy Ryzhenkov, chief executive of Metinvest, told the BBC the recently-imposed tariffs on imported steel to the EU were "unfair" and had been put in place "without any consideration for the situation Ukraine is in".

He said he wished to see "at least a carve out" for Ukraine to access the EU market.

A spokesperson for the European Commission said the EU "took into account the difficult situation" of Ukraine when deciding its steel policy.

The trading bloc has recently imposed restrictions on steel imports in an effort to protect steel manufacturers of member nations.

It has capped the amount of steel which can enter the EU tax free at 18.3 million tonnes per year - a 47% reduction from 2024 levels.

There are some country-specific quotas in the policy, but the overall aim is to cut the amount of steel that can be imported due to member nations struggling to compete with cheap imports from the likes of China and Turkey.

Despite a free-trade agreement (FTA) being in place between the EU and Ukraine, the FTA does not stop the EU from introducing separate trade protection measures.

"Ukraine has been bundled together into those measures without any consideration for the situation Ukraine is in," Ryzhenkov said, pointing to the war with Russia.

"Access to the European market is crucial for survival," he added. "The restrictive measures that have been put in place by the authorities in the European Union, they don't help.

"I think it's unfair that Ukraine has been treated in the same way as all of the other importers into the European Union."

The Ukraine steel industry estimates steel exports to the EU could ultimately fall by about 50â60%.

The EU said Ukraine's specific steel quota guaranteed exports of the metal, but acknowledged this was at a "level lower than in the past years".

"Despite the war effort, Ukraine remains an important exporter of steel to the EU," a spokesperson said, adding it had "offered compensations" to its largest suppliers, which included Ukraine.

World.title: Oil facilities hit in deadly overnight attack on St Petersburg
World.content:
At least one person has been killed in an overnight attack on St Petersburg that successfully targeted two of the city's oil facilities.

The region's Governor Alexander Beglov said fires were being extinguished at the St Petersburg Oil Terminal and the Ruchyi oil depot following the attack, which also injured at least five.

A logistics centre belonging to Ozon - known as Russia's Amazon - and a data centre belonging to Facebook equivalent VKontakte were also hit.

Kyiv has not yet commented on the strikes. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Saturday morning that Russia had targeted his country's energy sector 76 times since Donald Trump declared an "energy ceasefire" last week.

Ukraine had paused its strikes on Russian oil facilities - which it says are to limit the main revenue stream for Moscow's war effort - for three days after the announcement, while accusing Russia of continuing.

It then resumed strikes earlier this week, drawing the ire of Trump, who called for a truce to facilitate a deal he struck with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin to supply diesel.

Ukraine has struck St Petersburg before, though regions closer to Ukraine are threatened more often. The city's oil terminal was last hit in July.

Russia's defence ministry said it had shot down more than 1,000 Ukrainian drones over Russian territory overnight into Sunday.

St Petersburg's governor said 12 apartment buildings and two homes were damaged in the attacks on the city, while Pulkovo Airport was temporarily closed.

He also said mobile internet service disruption was possible.

Social network VK confirmed a drone had targeted its regional data centre, but stressed its services were available "as usual" after users reported outages in the early hours of the morning.

Ozon also confirmed its local logistics centre had been targeted by a drone, sparking a fire.

It said staff were evacuated and no one was injured, and that it was not accepting shipments from sellers at the location "as it is currently serving other operational purposes".

As well as numerous oil facilities across Russia, Ukraine has also mounted strikes aimed at disrupting the Russian economy more broadly. Earlier this month, it launched a series of attacks on Yandex, Russia's largest search engine, that led to service disruptions.

Relations between Washington and Kyiv have frayed since the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel in the hope of bringing down US energy prices, which have skyrocketed during the Iran war, ahead of the midterm elections.

Zelensky suggested the deal was tantamount to the US investing in Russia's war effort.

Trump's decision to temporarily suspend a raft of sanctions against Russia has brought fresh criticism, including from some US Republicans.

However, on Sunday, Zelensky said on Telegram he had had conversations with Trump's top negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.

He said their teams are in constant communication and preparing the next diplomatic steps.

Both Russia and Ukraine have been striking one another's energy infrastructure with increasing intensity ahead of the winter, as Moscow's full-scale invasion drags on in its fifth year.

Russia says it hits targets used by Ukraine's military, though the UN noted on Friday that the first two weeks of October had been the deadliest for Ukrainian civilians in years.

Russian strikes on energy facilities have left hundreds of thousands without power, raising concerns about civilians enduring another freezing winter.

Zelensky said on Saturday that tens of thousands of people were still without power. Russia launched nearly 2,700 drones, 1,700 aerial bombs and 66 missiles in the past week, most of which were aimed at energy facilities, he said.

World.title: Burkina Faso, Niger, Mali resume talks with ECOWAS after withdrawal from regional bloc
World.content:
Burkina Faso, Niger and Mali have resumed formal discussions with the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS), agreeing to work towards establishing a framework for cooperation despite their withdrawal from the regional bloc.

The three Sahel countries officially left ECOWAS in January 2025 after forming the Alliance of Sahel States (AES), amid growing disagreements with the bloc.

Saturday’s meeting, held in Dakar, is believed to be the first official ministerial-level engagement between the two sides, although discussions had been ongoing since January 2025.

In a joint statement issued on Saturday evening, both sides welcomed the discussions, citing fraternity, mutual respect and openness as guiding principles. They also emphasised the importance of good neighbourly relations and respect for national sovereignty.

The parties agreed to establish joint thematic working groups to develop a framework cooperation agreement.

Burkina Faso’s Foreign Minister, Karamoko Traore, led the AES delegation, while Senegal’s Foreign Minister, Cheikh Niang, headed the ECOWAS team.

Insecurity across the Sahel

Across the AES countries and other parts of the Sahel, armed groups continue to carry out attacks and expand towards coastal West African countries. Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger have battled jihadist insurgencies for more than a decade, with al-Qaeda- and Islamic State-linked groups exploiting weak state presence, porous borders and local grievances.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

In Mali, coordinated attacks on 25 April targeted several locations, with the violence involving Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM), an al-Qaeda affiliate, and the Azawad Liberation Front, a separatist movement. The country’s Defence Minister, Sadio Camara, was killed during the attacks.

In Burkina Faso and Niger, armed groups have also sustained pressure on security forces and civilians, while violence has increasingly threatened northern Benin and Togo.

Also, Nigeria, the largest economy in the region, faces overlapping security threats, including Boko Haram and Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP) insurgencies, banditry and mass kidnappings.

With armed groups operating across borders, strained relations between Nigeria and the AES countries risk weakening intelligence-sharing and joint counterterrorism operations. Niger’s withdrawal from the Multinational Joint Task Force in March 2025 gave a clear implication of the collapsed regional cooperation.

The challenge of regional cooperation

The AES countries have pursued an independent security and political course, distancing themselves from France and strengthening ties with Russia.

READ ALSO: ECOWAS Court gets four new judges

Their withdrawal from ECOWAS has complicated regional cooperation, despite shared threats that require intelligence-sharing, effective border controls and coordinated military responses.

The diplomatic disputes have also been fuelled by allegations from Sahelian leaders that neighbouring countries and foreign powers are supporting armed groups. Such claims remain contested, and allegations should not be treated as established facts without independently verifiable evidence.

It is not yet clear whether the renewed talks envisage the AES states returning to the regional bloc. If this is not part of the agenda, it will be interesting to see how ECOWAS, which has traditionally emphasised democratic governance, navigates diplomatic engagement with the junta-led countries while addressing mounting security threats across their shared borders.

World.title: ‘Please forgive me’: Fatai Okoya begs billionaire father after 40 years apart
World.content:
More than four decades after becoming estranged from his father, Fatai Okoya has publicly appealed to billionaire industrialist Razaq Akanni Okoya for forgiveness and an opportunity to rebuild their relationship.

Mr Fatai, who identifies himself as the Eleganza Group founder’s first child, appealed in an open letter that circulated online.

He said the years they had spent apart weighed heavily on him and urged his father to allow them to make peace while they still had time.

“More than four decades have passed, and today, I write with a humble heart, putting aside all pride to say: Dad, I am truly sorry. Please, find it in your heart to forgive me,” he wrote.

The letter, signed “Your First Child, Fatai Okoya,” has generated reactions online, with some people expressing sympathy and others questioning what caused the prolonged estrangement.

‘Pain of separation’

Mr Fatai said he had made previous attempts to reach his father and resolve their differences, but the separation continued to cause him pain.

“Over the years, I have tried to reach out and make peace because the pain of our separation and the precious years we have lost weigh heavily on my heart,” he said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“No matter what has happened, you remain my father, and I will forever be your first child.”

He asked Mr Okoya to look beyond the events that separated them, saying they could not recover the years already lost but could decide what happened next.

“Dad, we cannot turn back the hands of time, but we can choose to make the years ahead different,” he wrote.

“Life is precious, time waits for no one, and I do not want us to lose any more opportunities to love, forgive and reconnect.”

Although Mr Fatai repeatedly referred to past pain and differences, he did not explain what caused the rift or why the separation lasted for more than four decades.

‘Let us begin again’

Mr Fatai said he wanted a chance to heal their relationship and restore their bond.

“I am simply asking for a chance a chance to heal, to make peace and to rebuild the bond between a father and his child,” he wrote.

He said he was prepared to pursue reconciliation with humility and an open mind.

“Dad, please, let love speak louder than the pain of the past. Let forgiveness open a door that has been closed for far too long. I am ready to take that step with humility, sincerity and an open heart.”

He ended the letter with another apology, saying that despite their years apart, he still wanted his father back in his life.

“I love you, Dad. I miss you, and deep down, I still long for the blessing of having my father back in my life,” he wrote.

“Dad, I am truly sorry. My heart is open, my hands are extended, and my hope for reconciliation remains alive. Please, let us begin again.”

The Okoya family

Razaq Okoya founded the Eleganza Group, a manufacturing conglomerate known for producing household and consumer goods.

He began his business career as a trader before expanding into manufacturing and establishing Eleganza in the early 1970s.

The industrialist has a large family, although the precise number of his children has not been publicly confirmed by him.

In February 2026, one of his sons, Raheem Okoya, popularly known as Siraheem, said in an interview that his father had 26 children with nine women.

The singer described himself as the 23rd child and said the eldest was about 60 years old.

However, the information available for this report does not independently establish Mr Fatai’s claim that he is the billionaire’s first child.

Mr Fatai’s mother’s identity also remains unclear. He did not name her in the letter, and PREMIUM TIMES found no reliable public record identifying her.

The circumstances surrounding the estrangement also remain unclear. Beyond saying he had previously sought peace, Mr Fatai did not provide details of his reported attempts to contact his father.

As of the time of this report, Mr Okoya had not publicly responded to the letter.

World.title: Presidency disputes Makinde’s claim of N250 billion NLNG dividends per state
World.content:
The presidency has disputed Oyo State Governor Seyi Makinde’s claim that the federal government is withholding N250 billion in Nigeria Liquefied Natural Gas Limited (NLNG) dividends meant for each state, describing the allegation as “false.”

Bayo Onanuga, special adviser to President Bola Tinubu on information and strategy, said in a statement on Sunday that the amount claimed by the governor was inconsistent with the revenue-sharing formula and the history of NLNG’s dividend payments to the Federation.

Mr Onanuga argued that a one-off payment of N250 billion to each of Nigeria’s 36 states would amount to N9 trillion, excluding the federal government, the Federal Capital Territory and the 774 local government areas.

“Under the Federation Account Allocation Committee (FAAC) formula, states receive 26.72 per cent of the distributable Federation Account revenue. For the states’ share alone to reach N9 trillion, total NLNG dividends paid into the Federation Account would have to exceed N33.68 trillion (about $25 billion) in a single declaration,” the statement read. “NLNG has never paid $25 billion in dividends to the Federation Account in a single payout.”

Mr Onanuga urged the public to disregard the claim. “Makinde’s latest claim that the Federal Government is withholding the NLNG dividend windfall is false and should be disregarded.”

However, the presidency’s statement did not provide a transaction-by-transaction reconciliation of the specific NLNG dividend proceeds referenced by Mr Makinde or a breakdown of the sums allegedly due to individual states.

The dispute followed remarks by Mr Makinde at the 2027 Budget Stakeholders’ Consultative Engagement in Ibadan on Friday, where he alleged that the Federal Government had spent the dividend proceeds instead of distributing the states’ shares.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“They fooled us. The Nigeria LNG paid dividends to the Federal Government, which went straight into the Federation Account, but they spent it,” Mr Makinde said,

He stated that the amounts due to the states had been reconciled and that each state was expected to receive more than N250 billion.

Mr Makinde, the presidential candidate of the Allied People’s Movement for the upcoming 2027 elections, further alleged that the release of the funds had been postponed until after the 2027 general elections, questioning why political considerations should take precedence over the needs of citizens.

“Each state was supposed to get N250 billion. We had already identified projects that would expand Oyo State’s economy. But they have now said the money will not be paid until after the election. Is the election more important than the people of Nigeria?” the governor said.

Presidency’s argument

Responding, Mr Onanuga said states receive 26.72 per cent of distributable Federation Account revenue under the Federation Account Allocation Committee (FAAC) sharing formula.

He argued that for the states’ combined share to reach N9 trillion, the total NLNG dividends paid into the Federation Account would have to exceed N33.68 trillion ($25 billion), in a single declaration.

“NLNG has never paid $25 billion in dividends to the Federation Account in a single payout,” the presidency’s statement read.

According to the statement, NLNG has paid approximately $21.5 billion in dividends to the Federation over the past 25 years, with less than $3 billion realised since Mr Tinubu assumed office.

Mr Onanuga argued that the amount allegedly being withheld would therefore exceed the company’s entire historical dividend payments to the Federation.

“Therefore, any claim that a single payout exceeds the company’s entire lifetime distribution to the Federation—and is being withheld—defies basic logic and economic reality,” he said.

World.title: Protect indigenous seeds, farmers’ rights, HOMEF tells FG on World Food Day
World.content:
The Health of Mother Earth Foundation (HOMEF), an environmental advocacy organisation, has called on the federal government to protect indigenous seeds and farmers’ rights, warning that industrial agricultural practices and restrictive seed policies could undermine food sovereignty, biodiversity, and nutrition.

The organisation made the call on Friday to mark World Food Day, observed annually on 16 October, arguing that hunger and malnutrition persist in resource-rich countries because of political and economic choices that disadvantage smallholder farmers and local food systems.

In a statement made available to PREMIUM TIMES by its Media and Communications Manager, Kome Odhomor, HOMEF said food security requires more than increasing agricultural output. It called for policies that protect local seed varieties, promote ecological farming and give farming communities greater control over what they grow and how they produce food.

The organisation also called on Nigerians to pay closer attention to the origins and nutritional quality of their food, warning that climate change, economic instability, and conflict continue to threaten food production and distribution.

Food sovereignty

Nnimmo Bassey, HOMEF’s executive director, said Nigeria’s food system was overly dependent on monoculture and cash-crop production, which he noted weakened food supply chains, depleted soil health and reduced farmers’ control over agricultural production.

“World Food Day should be a day of reflection. It must also be a day of structural reckoning,” Mr Bassey said, calling for a shift from industrial uniformity towards diverse and ecologically sustainable farming systems.

He said indigenous seeds are critical to adapting to climate change because they preserve genetic diversity that can support drought resistance, pest management, and improved nutrition.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“We must move beyond the short-sighted goal of ‘yield at any cost’ and support a transition to agroecology,” he said.

Agroecology applies ecological principles to agricultural production, emphasising soil health, biodiversity, local knowledge, and sustainable relationships between farming communities and their environment.

Mr Bassey said protecting indigenous seeds was essential to preventing biodiversity loss and sustaining ecosystems, arguing that food systems should not sacrifice environmental health for short-term production gains.

Seed laws, farmers’ rights

HOMEF’s Director of Programmes, Joyce Brown, said hunger in resource-rich African countries reflected failures in political and economic decision-making.

She said that food should not be treated merely as a commodity for profit but as a fundamental human right connected to public health, cultural identity and community livelihoods.

Ms Brown called on governments and international institutions to review policies that, she said, privilege industrial exporters over small-scale farmers who supply local communities.

She specifically raised concerns about Nigeria’s Plant Variety Protection Act, 2021, explaining that restrictions on farmers’ ability to save and reuse seeds could threaten the food and nutritional security of vulnerable communities.

The law provides a framework for protecting the rights of breeders of new plant varieties. The debate over its implementation includes questions about how breeders’ rights should be balanced with farmers’ traditional practices and access to seeds.

Ms Brown said agricultural policies should recognise farmers’ rights and ensure that communities closest to the land retain meaningful authority over what they grow and how they use their resources.

‘Industrial agriculture not the only solution’

Mariann Bassey-Olsson, deputy director of Environmental Rights Action/Friends of the Earth Nigeria, described seed-saving and exchange as essential to farmers’ independence and the preservation of cultural heritage.

She rejected the argument that industrial agriculture was the only viable way to feed the world, saying smallholder farmers had sustained communities for generations through locally adapted farming practices.

Ms Bassey-Olsson said indigenous seeds embodied generations of farmers’ knowledge and adaptation to local soils and climatic conditions.

She warned that losing control of local seed varieties could make farmers increasingly dependent on foreign corporations and weaken their ability to adapt to changing environmental conditions.

She also opposed genetically modified crops, saying it could threaten farmers’ seed rights and biodiversity and increase dependence on foreign companies.

Her position reflects HOMEF’s call for increased investment in agroecology and locally controlled food systems, rather than approaches that put industrial agricultural interests at the centre of food production.

Food security, climate change

HOMEF said future food systems should prioritise nutritional quality, environmental sustainability and farmers’ livelihoods, rather than focus narrowly on increasing yields.

It called for better access to agricultural knowledge, tools and resources for smallholder farmers and marginalised communities, warning that climate change and other socioeconomic pressures could further destabilise food supplies.

The organisation also asked governments to support diverse local food systems that can withstand climate shocks while protecting biodiversity and improving soil health.

World Food Day is an annual international observance that raises awareness of hunger and food insecurity and promotes access to safe, nutritious, and affordable food.

World.title: NCDMB, Heritage Energy train 48 Nigerians in subsea engineering
World.content:
The Nigerian Content Development and Monitoring Board (NCDMB), in partnership with Heritage Energy Operational Services Limited (HEOSL) and Global Oceon Engineers Nigeria Limited, has launched a Human Capacity Development programme to train 48 Nigerians in subsea engineering.

The kick-off ceremony took place on Friday, 16 October, in Port Harcourt, Rivers State, as part of the Board’s efforts to address critical skills gaps and strengthen indigenous technical expertise in the oil and gas industry.

The programme combines six months of classroom instruction with six months of structured on-the-job training, giving participants specialised knowledge and practical experience in subsea engineering. The curriculum covers risers and hydrodynamics engineering, offshore structures design and engineering, pipeline engineering, and computer-aided design and drafting (AutoCAD).

In his keynote address, the Executive Secretary of NCDMB, Felix Omatsola Ogbe, a Fellow of Nigerian Society of Engineers, represented by the General Manager, Human Capacity Development, Ms Emelle Alexis, said the programme would equip the trainees with the technical expertise required for complex subsea operations and the safe, efficient and reliable operation of modern oil and gas facilities.

“Today marks the beginning of a transformational journey for 48 young Nigerians in a highly specialised field that demands precision, discipline and accountability. Through intensive classroom instruction and structured on-the-job training, the participants will gain hands-on experience in subsea engineering,” he said.

Ogbe stressed that subsea operations require technical competence, professionalism and an unwavering commitment to safety.

“The competencies you acquire through this programme are critical to the safe, efficient, reliable and environmentally responsible operation of modern oil and gas facilities. Beyond technical proficiency, the training is designed to develop your problem-solving skills, teamwork, professionalism and commitment to safety,” he stated.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The Executive Secretary urged the trainees to make the most of the opportunity and demonstrate the discipline and commitment required to succeed in the industry. He expressed confidence that they would emerge with the skills and professional standards needed to contribute to the sector.

In his remarks, the Manager, Nigerian Content Development at Heritage Energy, Felix Osiwo, reaffirmed the company’s commitment to indigenous skills development. He noted that a skilled Nigerian workforce is essential to delivering current and future energy infrastructure projects and sustaining industry growth.

Earlier in his welcome address, the Managing Director of Global Oceon Engineers Nigeria Limited, George Ebuh, represented by Ifedolapo Aderibigbe, described the programme as a strategic investment by Heritage Energy, NCDMB and Global Oceon in developing indigenous subsea engineering expertise. He noted that skilled local professionals are vital to the safe and reliable operation of offshore and deepwater infrastructure.

The trainees expressed appreciation for the opportunity to acquire specialised subsea engineering skills, identifying safety training and AutoCAD as important areas of learning. The programme is part of NCDMB’s Top 10 Field Readiness Human Capacity Development initiatives, designed to address critical skills gaps in the oil and gas industry. It supports the Board’s efforts to develop specialised Nigerian expertise for offshore and deepwater operations, facilitate technology transfer and increase local participation in high-value industry activities.

The ceremony was attended by representatives of NCDMB, Heritage Energy Operational Services Limited and Global Oceon Engineers Nigeria Limited, as well as the trainees, facilitators and other industry stakeholders.

World.title: Utomi says Akwa Ibom ex-governor Victor Attah has attained ‘immortality’
World.content:
Nigerian professor, entrepreneur, and former presidential candidate Pat Utomi has described Akwa Ibom State’s Governor Victor Attah as a leader who has attained “immortality”, citing the enduring influence of his development vision.

Mr Utomi, also a professor of entrepreneurship at Lagos Business School, assessed this in a Facebook post on Friday after travelling from Ikot Ekpene to Victor Attah International Airport to welcome former President Olusegun Obasanjo for the unveiling of a media platform in Uyo.

Reflecting on the journey, Mr Utomi said the experience reminded him of the foundations Mr Attah laid during his eight-year tenure as governor and how his development initiatives continued to influence the state beyond his time in office.

“I was reminded of the foundation that one decent, visionary man of character, Obong Victor Attah, laid as Governor of Akwa Ibom State, and the fruits of his labour, so evident even in the work of his successors, both good and bad,” he wrote.

Mr Utomi said the experience gave him a renewed appreciation of transformational leadership, particularly the ability to envision a future beyond immediate political considerations and persevere in pursuing it despite opposition.

“These are the people who see tomorrow and persevere to bring it about, even in the face of determined opposition,” he said.

He added that Mr Attah had “attained immortality, like Chief Obafemi Awolowo, Dr Michael Okpara and Sir Ahmadu Bello,” while continuing to live simply.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Attah’s enduring legacy

Mr Attah, an architect and politician, governed Akwa Ibom from 29 May 1999 to 29 May 2007, becoming one of the principal figures in the state’s development following Nigeria’s return to civil rule in 1999.

His administration pursued major infrastructure and economic development projects, including establishing an international airport, the Ibom Power Plant, developing the Ibom Hotels and Golf Resort, and planning an Ibom Deep Seaport. The state later renamed the airport Victor Attah International Airport in 2018 to recognise his contributions to the state.

Mr Attah initiated the Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul facility at Victor Attah International Airport. Still, the project was abandoned before his successor, Udom Emmanuel, revived it and inaugurated it in May 2023.

Subsequent reports showed that outstanding construction and operational requirements remained under Governor Umo Eno, whose administration was still pursuing a partnership to bring the facility into full operation in August 2026.

Beyond infrastructure, Mr Attah became a prominent advocate of resource control and fiscal federalism, insisting that oil-producing states should receive a fairer share of revenue generated from their natural resources.

His advocacy was particularly noteworthy in the Niger Delta, where communities and state governments had long demanded more benefits from petroleum wealth extracted from the region.

The struggle over derivation revenue became a major constitutional and political issue during the administration of Mr Obasanjo, who was president from 1999 to 2007, the same period Mr Attah governed Akwa Ibom.

Mr Attah’s campaign for resource control helped put revenue allocation and the rights of oil-producing states at the centre of national debate. The constitutional principle of derivation provides for a share of revenue from natural resources to be returned to the areas from which the resources are derived.

READ ALSO: Utomi faces backlash over defence of Kila despite academic credentials controversy

Beyond monuments

Mr Utomi’s remarks place Mr Attah’s legacy within a bigger debate about the meaning of leadership and how political performance should be assessed after an administration leaves office.

By comparing the former governor with Awolowo, Okpara and Ahmadu Bello, Mr Utomi suggested that a leader’s lasting importance lies not only in the projects completed during his tenure, but also in the institutions, ideas and development pathways that survive him.

Late Awolowo, the former premier of Western Nigeria, was associated with major social welfare and education programmes. Okpara, who led the former Eastern Region, was known for agricultural and industrial development. At the same time, Ahmadu Bello, the Sardauna of Sokoto, was a central political figure in Northern Nigeria’s development and administration.

Mr Utomi’s assessment goes beyond the physical infrastructure associated with Mr Attah’s administration. It frames the former governor’s legacy by how far his vision continued to shape the state under successive governments.

However, Mr Utomi’s tribute was a personal assessment of Mr Attah’s leadership, rather than a comprehensive evaluation of the former governor’s record.

Mr Attah, born on 20 November 1938, turned 87 in November 2025. His political and professional career has continued to attract public attention, including at the 2025 launch of a biography chronicling his life and career.

World.title: LASU professor Tunde Akanni inducted as peace studies fellow
World.content:
Tunde Akanni of Lagos State University (LASU) has been inducted as a Fellow of the Society for Peace Studies and Practice (SPSP).

Mr Akanni, a professor of Journalism in LASU’s Faculty of Communication and Media Studies, received the fellowship at the society’s 20th International Conference and General Assembly held at Lead City University, Ibadan, from 5 to 9 October 2026.

The fellowship recognises his contributions to journalism, conflict-sensitive communication and development communication, according to reports on the investiture.

FCCPC congratulates Akanni

The Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC), where Mr Akanni is currently on sabbatical, also congratulated him on the recognition.

In a letter dated 7 October 2026, the commission described the fellowship as a testament to his scholarly contributions to journalism and his commitment to conflict-sensitive journalism.

The letter, signed by Yisau Adepoju, Head of the Administration Department, on behalf of the FCCPC’s Executive Vice Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, Olatunji Bello, said Mr Akanni had consistently demonstrated commitment to development communication and its role in promoting social change.

The commission said the recognition was “timely and richly deserved”, and expressed confidence that Mr Akanni would continue to contribute to Nigeria and the global academic community.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“This auspicious milestone is a clear testimony to your laudable scholarly contributions to the field of journalism. As a thoroughbred professional and accomplished academic, you have consistently demonstrated passion and unwavering commitment to the promotion of Conflict- Sensitive Journalism. You have tenaciously identified with this strand of Development Communication that is renowned for fostering sustainable social change and advancing the overall quality of life, particularly in developing nations,” FCCPC noted.

About Tunde Akanni

Mr Akanni is a Professor of Journalism at LASU. The university’s official academic profile lists his specialisation as Journalism and Development Communications and his PhD in Media and Conflict Resolution Studies from the University of Ibadan.

He joined LASU’s Department of Journalism in 2001 as an Assistant Lecturer and rose through the academic ranks. In March 2025, the university’s Governing Council approved his elevation to full professor of Journalism and Development Communication. At the time, he was an Associate Professor and pioneer Director of LASU’s Digital Media Research Centre.

Before joining academia, Mr Akanni worked in Nigeria’s print media industry, including at The Punch and National Concord, where he rose to Acting Features Editor. Following the proscription of Concord titles in 1994, he became Head of Campaigns at the Civil Liberties Organisation.

His academic interests include journalism practice, media ethics, development communication, political communication, media and conflict, strategic communication and the impact of artificial intelligence on media systems.

He has undertaken academic and professional training at institutions including Columbia University in the United States, the University of Leicester in the United Kingdom and the Institute of Social Studies in The Hague, Netherlands. He is also a British Chevening Scholar and a recipient of the Netherlands NUFFIC Fellowship.

World.title: Court of Appeal upholds N12m damages against EFCC over Ubani’s detention
World.content:
The Court of Appeal in Abuja has dismissed an appeal by the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) challenging a judgement awarding Monday Ubani, a Senior Advocate of Nigeria (SAN), N12 million in compensation for his unlawful detention in 2019.

Delivering judgement on the appeal on Thursday, a three-member panel of judges unanimously upheld the award.

The appellate court also ordered the commission to pay N300,000 in costs, according to a statement shared with PREMIUM TIMES on Sunday.

Mr Ubani, a lawyer and former vice-president of the Nigerian Bar Association (NBA), was not yet a SAN when the EFCC detained him in March 2019. He attained the rank in 2024.

How the dispute began

The dispute began after the EFCC declared Ngozi Olejeme, a former chairperson of the Nigeria Social Insurance Trust Fund (NSITF), wanted over allegations of financial crimes relating to her time at the agency.

Mr Ubani said he helped persuade her to return to Nigeria to answer the allegations. She was subsequently granted administrative bail, with him and former Senator Christopher Enai standing as sureties.

A surety guarantees that a person granted bail will comply with the conditions of their release, including appearing when required by investigators or a court.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

However, the EFCC later said it could no longer reach Ms Olejeme and demanded that her sureties produce her. The commission arrested Mr Ubani and Mr Enai in March 2019.

Mr Ubani maintained that he was not responsible for her disappearance. He said he had helped bring her back to Nigeria and questioned why the commission held him responsible after its operatives visited her home and could no longer reach her.

Later that month, Judge Sylvanus Oriji of the FCT High Court in Apo ordered the EFCC to charge the two men in court or release them on bail. The judge also granted them bail subject to conditions.

However, the commission did not comply with the order by the deadline, prompting their lawyer, Mike Ozekhome, also a SAN, to initiate contempt proceedings against the then acting EFCC chairman, Ibrahim Magu.

In January 2022, Judge Oriji ruled that the EFCC’s arrest and detention of Mr Ubani violated his fundamental rights.

The judge held that a surety could be required to show cause or forfeit the bail bond if the person for whom they stood surety could not be produced, rather than being arrested and detained.

Consequently, he declared the detention illegal and awarded Mr Ubani N12 million in damages but declined to order the EFCC to issue a public apology.

Dissatisfied with the judgment, the commission appealed to the Court of Appeal, challenging the trial court’s jurisdiction and the amount awarded as compensation.

The appellate court has now dismissed the appeal and upheld the trial court’s jurisdiction.

World.title: CAN to citizens: ‘We all, not leaders alone, are guilty’
World.content:
Most Rev. Daniel Chukwudumebi Okoh, CAN President

By Luminous Jannamike

The Christian Association of Nigeria, CAN, has urged Nigerians to share responsibility for the country’s challenges, including insecurity, corruption and economic hardship, rather than blame political leaders alone.

Read Also: DisCos’ revenue rises 450% as debt profile hits N700bn

The association called for collective repentance and a renewed commitment to national restoration, saying the Church and citizens must acknowledge their shortcomings and contribute to rebuilding the country.

Vice-President of CAN, Rev. Stephen Panya-Baba, stated this in a homily at a special thanksgiving service in Abuja weekend to mark the association’s 50th anniversary, with the theme, “Working Together in Faith.”

“The truth, brethren, is that we all stand guilty before God as a Church. This, therefore, requires collective responsibility from all of us to do what is right and support our leaders in the difficult task of rehabilitating and restoring our beloved country,” he said.

Panya-Baba said the anniversary provided an opportunity for the Church to reflect on its journey, shortcomings and responsibility to Nigeria’s peace, progress and prosperity.

“We have no other country we can call our own. Nigeria is our home, and we have no alternative but to work towards its restoration,” he declared.

The CAN vice-president, however, stressed that the association must continue to hold government accountable, noting that speaking truth to power did not mean becoming an opposition party.

“CAN has a responsibility to speak truth to power on critical national issues, privately or publicly, as circumstances demand. However, it must never assume the role of an opposition party to the government,” he said.

Tracing the association’s origins, Panya-Baba recalled that Christian leaders met in Lagos in August 1976 at the instance of the then Head of State, General Olusegun Obasanjo, and resolved to speak with one voice. He attributed the account to Professor Yusuf Turaki.

He said CAN adopted the anniversary theme from the biblical call for unity in John 17:21, with its ecumenical philosophy anchored on unity in essentials, liberty in non-essentials and charity in all things.

Panya-Baba said the association had contributed to peacebuilding, the defence of religious freedom, national engagement and public discourse over the past five decades. He also highlighted its support for victims of religious crises and efforts to promote moral values and encourage the participation of women and youths through Women in CAN and Youth in CAN.

The cleric acknowledged challenges, including leadership disputes, religious persecution, insecurity, interreligious tensions, financial constraints and public criticism.

Despite these difficulties, he urged members to remain united and committed to CAN’s mission. He also appealed to members whose contributions might not be recognised during the anniversary celebrations not to become discouraged.

“The journey is not over, and God keeps a much more perfect record,” he said.

Panya-Baba paid tribute to past leaders and others who contributed to the association’s growth, while acknowledging the support of its national officers and state and local government structures.

He urged Nigerians to examine their individual and collective roles in the country’s difficulties, citing Proverbs 14:34 to emphasise the need for righteousness, repentance and a willingness to confront wrongdoing.

The CAN vice-president also called on the association to mobilise Nigerians to pray for the country and seek God’s intervention, while sustaining its advocacy for justice, equity and fairness irrespective of religion, ethnicity or region.
