World.title: IMF, World Bank hail Oyedele’s G-24 leadership
World.content:
Taiwo Oyedele

By Henry Ojelu

Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Taiwo Oyedele, has received commendation from the leadership of the International Monetary Fund, IMF, and World Bank for his leadership of the Group of 24 (G-24), highlighting Nigeria’s growing voice in global economic discussions.

The commendation came during the 2026 IMF and World Bank Group Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, where Oyedele chaired the G-24 Board of Governors meeting and led calls for a fairer global financial system, affordable development financing and faster resolution of sovereign debt crises.

IMF Managing Director, Kristalina Georgieva, and World Bank Senior Managing Director, Axel van Trotsenburg, representing World Bank President Ajay Banga, joined other G-24 governors in commending Oyedele’s leadership of discussions on the financing challenges confronting developing economies.

The recognition was reinforced by Banga’s meeting with Oyedele and Central Bank of Nigeria Governor, Olayemi Cardoso, during which he acknowledged Nigeria’s reform progress, pointing to private capital inflows that reportedly increased from about $300 million in 2023 to nearly $6 billion in 2026.

Oyedele’s performance at the meetings extended beyond diplomatic engagements. As G-24 chairman, he drew attention to the burden of rising debt-servicing costs on developing countries, warning that they were undermining investment, job creation and inclusive growth.

A Reuters report quoted him as saying developing economies were paying approximately $500 billion more in debt servicing than developed countries.

He urged international financial institutions to provide more accessible and affordable concessional financing to vulnerable economies.

The minister also argued against imposing additional tax burdens on vulnerable households and productive sectors amid global economic uncertainty, advocating improved revenue mobilisation.

reduced waste and a careful balance between taxation and borrowing.

At the Africa’s Golden Future Forum in Bangkok, he also presented Nigeria’s experience with fuel subsidy removal, foreign exchange liberalisation and tax reform as lessons for African countries pursuing sustainable growth.

He highlighted cash transfers and education support as measures intended to cushion vulnerable citizens.ing HYPREP’s work and extending environmental remediation to other polluted parts of the region.

He described the Ogoni cleanup as a pilot scheme, adding that the committee had involved HYPREP, the Federal Ministry of Environment and other relevant stakeholders in developing the bill.

“Very soon, the bill will come up. What we intend to do with that is to sustain what HYPREP is doing and see how it can be taken to all other parts of the Niger Delta,” Dekor said.

He commended HYPREP for its commitment to the project, noting that the sites inspected were more than 80 per cent complete.

Although the projects were still ongoing, he said the progress recorded was encouraging, expressing confidence that the renewed drive within HYPREP would ensure timely completion and quality delivery.

Dekor also praised the project’s skills acquisition component, saying it had equipped young Ogonis with specialised skills sought after internationally.

He said about 2,400 youths had been listed among those trained at various centres, adding that the programme would help develop a pool of skilled professionals in Ogoniland.

Meanwhile, HYPREP Project Coordinator, Prof. Nenibarini Zabbey, said the project had more than 130 sites across its intervention areas, covering remediation, shoreline cleanup, potable water provision, healthcare improvement and skills development.

He said the initiative had created direct and indirect employment opportunities for Ogoni residents, including youths and women.

Zabbey highlighted the specialist hospital project, which he said would provide tertiary healthcare services to residents of Ogoni and other people in the region. The facility includes an oncology unit for cancer screening and treatment.

He also disclosed that HYPREP had conducted a human health biomonitoring study coordinated by the World Health Organisation’s International Agency for Research on Cancer to examine the relationship between exposure to hydrocarbon contaminants and the health of residents.

According to him, the committee’s visit provided an opportunity for lawmakers to assess the projects firsthand and make recommendations to improve the implementation of the cleanup.

World.title: Electricity: Geometric Power puts Aba ahead of Nigerian cities
World.content:
Prof. Bath Nnaji

By Emma Ujah, Abuja Bureau Chief

For decades, unreliable electricity supply has undermined Nigeria’s industrial growth, forcing businesses to close, driving up production costs and making life increasingly difficult for households.

Read Also: DisCos’ revenue rises 450% as debt profile hits N700bn

From textile mills in Kaduna, Kano, Lagos and Onitsha to vehicle assembly plants, tyre factories and footwear manufacturers, several once-thriving industries have struggled or shut down, partly because of inadequate power supply.

Now in Aba, Abia State, a different experience is emerging, as the Geometric Power-owned Aba Power distribution network provides electricity to businesses, institutions and households, enabling some to reduce dependence on costly petrol and diesel generators.

The development is reshaping business operations in the commercial hub, with manufacturers reporting uninterrupted production, traders extending working hours and households enjoying improved food preservation and lower running costs.

Geometric Power Chairman, Professor Barth Nnaji, described the Aba Integrated Power Project, an investment exceeding $900 million, as a dream come true.

He said the company was committed to providing reliable and affordable electricity to customers, irrespective of their social or economic status.

“Our services are for all people, regardless of class or status. Electricity is a fundamental right of the Nigerian people, and we are happy to provide reliable and affordable electricity to all our customers,” Nnaji said.

He added that, unlike other legacy distribution companies, Aba Power was wholly privately owned and had not received Federal Government subsidies.

Role of Afreximbank

The decision of the African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank) to provide a $50 million facility to Geometric Power Limited after a seven-year delay was what made Aba Power a reality today.

The Group Managing Director of Geometric Power, Mrs. Agatha Nnaji, said the bank provided the lifeline that enabled the project to be commissioned, saying, “Afreximbank is the bank that provided the funding that enabled us to complete and commission the project.”

“As you may know, politics got in the way, human error impacted the project, and it was delayed just as we were about to commission it. So, for seven years, we were simply maintaining the facilities that were already in place. We had staff who had to be paid to keep maintaining them.

“Eventually, when we determined the exact amount needed to complete the project—after President Jonathan intervened and his successor, the late President Muhammadu Buhari, directed his team to resolve the issues arising from the privatization—we were thrilled that Afreximbank stepped in. They shared our vision and understood the impact the project would have on the community.

“I believe that was the turning point for them. Seeing Aba’s potential as an industrial hub in Africa made them far more willing to find a way to make the project work. Although subsequent challenges prolonged completion, Afreximbank ultimately came to the rescue.

“At that crucial juncture, we needed $50 million, and they provided it. Honestly, Afreximbank’s role in all of this was remarkable. Ordinarily, a bank or financier would walk away from a project facing the kinds of hurdles we had at the time.

“We were operating in an environment where the government had breached the terms of our signed agreement. We were dealing with civil and public service officials who knew what needed to be done but refused to act.

“There was little to offer them comfort beyond the sheer determination of our lead investor. For him, it wasn’t merely a financial venture; his drive to see the project through was fueled by a desire to create a lasting, positive impact on people’s lives.”

Infrastructure built for reliability

The company says its investment in distribution infrastructure is central to its efforts to maintain stable electricity supply.

According to the Director of Commercial Operations, Engineer Victor Ngwoke, Aba Power deliberately invested in heavy-duty tubular steel poles designed to withstand extreme conditions and minimise disruptions.

“We wanted to have a very sturdy and reliable infrastructure. We, therefore, deliberately invested in heavy tubular steel poles,” he said.

Ngwoke explained that the poles have deeply buried concrete foundations and are designed to withstand substantial impact, including collisions with vehicles.

He said the company also maintained standards for conventional concrete poles and worked to restore damaged infrastructure quickly whenever faults occurred.

On metering, the director said approximately 98 per cent of Aba Power’s customers had prepaid meters, helping to reduce disputes associated with estimated billing.

With prepaid meters, customers can monitor their consumption and manage electricity expenses more effectively.

Ngwoke also disclosed that the company deployed smart meters and monitoring teams to detect and prevent electricity theft, including illegal connections and meter bypasses.

He said residents had also supported efforts to protect the network, recognising the benefits of reliable electricity to their businesses and livelihoods.

Excess capacity, wider reach

Aba Power currently takes an average of 50 to 60 megawatts from an installed generation capacity exceeding 140MW, according to the company.

The available capacity has enabled it to extend electricity supply to parts of neighbouring Rivers State, where some communities are underserved by the Port Harcourt Electricity Distribution Company.

The company says it hopes to extend its reach across Abia State, subject to the necessary infrastructure and operational requirements.

Polytechnic cuts energy costs by 80%

One of the institutions benefiting from the improved supply is Ogbonnaya Onu Polytechnic, Aba, whose Rector, Professor Christopher Okoro, said the development had transformed academic and administrative activities.

Okoro, who assumed office in 2024, said one of the first challenges he encountered was a huge outstanding diesel bill, which he considered unsustainable.

He contacted Nnaji for assistance, and the institution was connected to Aba Power within 48 hours.

Before the connection, he said, academic activities, research and other operations were constrained by unreliable electricity, with staff often leaving the campus by 2pm.

With the improved supply, students and staff now remain on campus until late in the evening, despite the institution not being residential.

“Before now, staff used to leave by 2pm. They cannot work without electricity. You cannot carry out research without electricity,” he said.

The rector said the institution’s energy costs had fallen by about 80 per cent.

Manufacturers, traders extend working hours

At Damson Industries, a manufacturer of shoe components, Chairman David Mmadueke, said reliable electricity had enabled the company to operate day and night shifts without routinely shutting down because of power outages.

“We have light here morning and night. The only time we didn’t have light was when the company had a problem with gas supply for about three days. Apart from that, this factory has never closed because there is no electricity,” he said.

Similarly, the President of Aba North Shoe Plaza, Obioma Onyebuchi, said the plaza, which houses more than 2,000 shops, switched to Aba Power on January 14 and had since enjoyed steady supply.

According to him, traders no longer depend on individual petrol or diesel generators, as the company has ensured that customers are metered.

“With the constant electricity supply from Aba Power, we can now work throughout the day. This has increased the productivity of our members,” he said.

Although some traders consider the electricity tariff high, Onyebuchi said the cost remained preferable to the substantial sums previously spent on fuel.

He expressed the plaza’s readiness to support the company to sustain reliable supply.

Steady power eases household expenses

Beyond factories and commercial centres, improved electricity supply is also changing how some households manage their finances.

Mrs Ada-Ngizi Greg-Ilobinso, a wife, mother and teacher, said reliable electricity had made household management easier, particularly in food storage and budgeting.

She explained that she could now purchase food items in bulk, preserve them in a freezer and reduce the frequency of shopping trips.

“Aba Power has really affected my life positively in so many ways. As a mother and a wife, and also as a housekeeper, a house manager, if I may say, it has really helped me because now we have steady light,” she said.

While the experiences of residents, manufacturers and institutions point to significant gains, the wider impact will depend on the consistency, affordability and reach of the electricity service.

World.title: DisCos’ revenue rises 450% as debt profile hits N700bn
World.content:
File image.

*Supply grows by 4.8% *Available plant capacity falls by 41% *13 years of privatisation yield little results *FG turns to bonds to tackle N6trn debt *Power supply has improved, Power Minister insists *Consumers, experts react

Revenue collected by Nigeria’s electricity Distribution Companies (DisCos) rose by about 450 per cent in eight years, from N218.16 billion in the first half of 2018 to N1.2 trillion in the corresponding period of 2026, far outpacing growth in electricity supply over the period.

Read Also: NLC, Falana, activists rally Nigerians against petrol price hike, hardship

Data from the Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission (NERC), analysed by Financial Vanguard, showed that while DisCos’ revenue increased by about N983.04 billion, total electricity supply grew by only 4.8 per cent, from 16,861 gigawatt-hours (GWh) in the first half of 2018 to 17,668GWh in the first half of 2026, even as their debt profile in the last six months hits N700billion.

The data also indicated that average available generation capacity declined by 41 per cent, from 7,565.5 megawatts (MW) in the first half of 2018 to 4,456MW in the corresponding period of 2026.

On an annual basis, DisCos’ revenue increased by about 666 per cent in ten years, from N302.93 billion in 2016 to N2.32 trillion in 2025, highlighting the widening gap between revenue growth and improvements in electricity supply.

NERC data showed that while DisCos’ annual revenue rose by about N2.016 trillion over the period, average daily power generation increased by approximately 36 per cent, from 3,276MW in 2016 to 4,475MW in 2025.

The disparity has raised concerns about the extent to which increased revenue collections have translated into improved electricity supply and service delivery to consumers, 13 years after the privatisation of the power sector.

In the same vein, data from NERC showed that in the first half of 2026, DisCos failed to collect N700.53 billion. It indicated that while the utilities received N1.9trillion worth of energy from the market, they collected N1.2trillion from consumers, leaving a balance of N700 billion.

The Rural Electrification Agency (REA) has estimated that about 85 million Nigerians still lack access to electricity.

In 2016, DisCos collected N302.925 billion, while total annual electricity supply stood at 23,742GWh. By 2025, revenue had risen by about 666 per cent to N2.3188 trillion, while annual electricity supply increased by 31.6 per cent to 31,251GWh.

DisCos’ revenue rose to N370.456 billion in 2017, before increasing to N448.749 billion in 2019 and N542.729 billion in 2020. Collections further climbed to N775.336 billion in 2021 and N841.811 billion in 2022.

The upward trend accelerated in subsequent years, with revenue reaching N1.0775 trillion in 2023, N1.6597 trillion in 2024 and N2.3188 trillion in 2025.

By comparison, annual electricity supply increased from 23,742GWh in 2016 to 33,489.17GWh in 2019 and 35,242.17GWh in 2020. It rose further to 36,710.60GWh in 2023 and peaked at 37,093.70GWh in 2024 before declining to 31,251GWh in 2025.

The divergence was particularly evident in 2025, when annual electricity supply fell by about 15.7 per cent from 37,093.70GWh in 2024, even as DisCos’ revenue increased from N1.6597 trillion to N2.3188 trillion.

13 years of privatisation yield little results

The bulk of the power sector was privatised in November 2013, with generation plants and 11 distribution companies handed over to private investors, while the Federal Government retained control of the transmission segment.

The arrangement formed the basis of the Nigerian Electricity Supply Industry, NESI.

However, 13 years after privatisation, concerns remain over the pace of growth in electricity supply despite over N10 trillion public investment in the sector.

NERC data showed that in 2016, three years after privatisation, the average available generation capacity of 27 power plants was 7,527MW, while actual average generation stood at 3,276MW.

By 2025, with installed generation capacity of more than 13,000MW, average available capacity had fallen by 28.3 per cent to 5,398MW, while average generation rose to 4,475MW.

FG turns to bonds to tackle N6trn debt

With the Federal Government’s debts to power generation companies hitting the N6 trillion mark at the end of 2025, the government has gone to the bond market to raise funds to make up for its inability to fund electricity subsidies from the national budget.

NERC, in its 2025 industry report, put the Federal Government’s gross tariff subsidy obligation at N1.928 trillion for the year, representing 57.44 percent of the total NBET invoice.

The amount translates to an average subsidy obligation of N160.69 billion per month. The government’s subsidy obligation was distributed across the four quarters, with N536.40 billion recorded in the first quarter, N514.36 billion in the second quarter, N458.76 billion in the third quarter and N418.79 billion in the fourth quarter.

The 2025 figure represented a slight decline from the N1.949 trillion subsidy obligation recorded in 2024.

The government had in September 2026 signed the N728.979 billion Series 2 bond under its N4 trillion Power Sector Debt Reduction Programme, in a fresh move to settle verified legacy debts owed to electricity generation companies and restore liquidity to Nigeria’s power sector.

The transaction comprised N402 billion in cash bonds raised from the domestic capital market and N326.979 billion in non-cash bonds allotted to participating generation companies.

The Managing Director/CEO, Nigerian Bulk Electricity Trading Plc, Akin Odeyemi said,

at the backdrop of weak growth in power supply the GenCos appear to be shackled by indebtedness by the Federal Government with outstanding debt put around N6 trillion at the beginning of this year.

Consequently, the government had in September 2026 signed the N728.979 billion Series 2 bond under its N4 trillion Power Sector Debt Reduction Programme, in a fresh move to settle verified legacy debts owed to electricity generation companies and restore liquidity to Nigeria’s power sector.

The transaction comprised N402 billion in cash bonds raised from the domestic capital market and N326.979 billion in non-cash bonds allotted to participating generation companies.

Odeyemi said at the weekend that NBET has commenced the settlement of participating Generation Companies (GenCos) and their associated Gas Companies following the successful issuance and signing of the N728.979 billion Series 2 Bonds under the N4 trillion Power Sector Multi-Instrument Issuance Programme.

He noted that the milestone “represents a significant step in the implementation of the Presidential Power Sector Debt Reduction Programme, under the visionary leadership of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, and in furtherance of the objectives of the Renewed Hope Agenda.

“The settlement is being undertaken through a combination of N402,000,000,000.00 in Cash Bonds and N326,979,000,000.00 in Non-Cash Bonds, in accordance with the approved settlement framework”, he added.

Power supply has improved, Power Minister insists

Despite concerns over the sector’s performance, the Minister of Power, Mr. Joseph Tegbe, has insisted that electricity supply has improved over the past three months.

Tegbe, who acknowledged that some parts of the country continued to experience poor supply, said the government was working to address the challenges.

According to him, “Operational record reports show generation and transmission above 5,000MW over the past couple of weeks, compared to the 3,700 to 4,700MW range before June, and a generation peak of 5,330MW during August and September.

“Our next task is to sustain these gains and translate them into more dependable supply at customer level. We are aware that a national peak alone cannot describe the experience of every community.”

He said the government’s efforts to address the challenges were anchored on three pillars: stabilising the value chain, restoring market discipline and strengthening governance.

“Under the first pillar, the 375MW Alaoji open-cycle power plant was restored to the national grid after three years offline.

“A number of substations have been upgraded. For instance, new transformers have been commissioned at Apapa, Ijora, Alausa and Lekki in Lagos, unlocking 672MW of transmission capacity, while a new 300MVA transformer has been energised at Katampe in Abuja, unlocking another 240MW of transmission capacity.

“These interventions restored existing assets and strengthened the network serving major centres of demand.”

The Minister said the government was also working to diversify the country’s energy mix, with emphasis on solar power.

He said the completed electrification portfolio under the REA and its partners comprised 62 solar and mini-grid installations across 30 states, representing about 43.6MW of installed solar capacity and 41,735 new connections, with an estimated reach of more than 208,000 people.

Reform remains unfinished — Babalola

Speaking on the state of the power sector, Special Adviser to the President on Power and Chairman, Presidential Task Force on Power Sector Reset and Restoration, Dr. Lanre Babalola, said the reforms initiated by the government remained incomplete.

Babalola noted that Nigeria’s electricity challenge was not simply a lack of generation capacity.

“Our deeper problem is that we have not yet built a system capable of consistently converting available capacity into reliable electricity, commercial value and sustainable investment,” he said.

According to him, “We must also recognise that Nigeria’s electricity reform remains an unfinished transition.

“We unbundled the old vertically integrated utility. Generation and distribution assets were privatised. A bulk trader was established. And we expected private capital and commercial discipline to progressively transform the industry.

“But we never fully completed the transition to the competitive electricity market envisaged by those reforms.

“The single-buyer model was conceived as a transitional mechanism. NBET provided a credible intermediary while market participants developed the creditworthiness required for direct contracting.

“But a transitional mechanism becomes a structural constraint if the transition never happens. The objective cannot be to preserve the institutions of transition indefinitely. The objective must be to complete the transition.”

‘Nigerians have been paying for darkness’ — Fadipe

Reacting to the figures, lawyer and Lead Consultant at Sage Consulting on Power Sector, Mr. Bode Fadipe, said the data raised questions about whether consumers had received commensurate value for the money paid for electricity.

“What this data has just confirmed is that Nigerians have been paying for darkness,” Fadipe said.

He identified inadequate investment as one of the major challenges responsible for the limited improvement in electricity supply, arguing that the figures also justified NERC’s directive requiring DisCos to retain part of their revenue for investment.

“You will recall that the DisCos vehemently protested this order, but NERC thankfully insisted on the implementation of the order,” he said.

Fadipe, however, said the level of compliance with the investment directive remained a separate issue that needed to be established.

He called for closer monitoring of DisCos and strict enforcement of NERC’s investment directives.

“NERC must dutifully enforce its order on investment. NERC must also set timelines for certain levels of improvement,” he said.

He further advocated forensic audits of investments by DisCos to determine whether funds earmarked for infrastructure were being properly utilised, while urging NERC to work with market participants on debt recovery.

Consumers demand stronger protection

Also reacting, consumer rights advocate and Executive Director, Electricity Consumer Protection Advocacy Centre, Chief Princewill Okorie, said the revenue figures raised questions about the quality of service delivered to consumers.

Okorie said the decentralisation of the electricity sector under the new legal framework had brought regulation closer to consumers in the states, but argued that enforcement of consumer protection provisions remained a major challenge.

According to him, consumers continued to face issues including estimated billing, infrastructure charges and alleged non-compliance with regulatory directives.

He alleged that in some communities, consumers had been compelled to contribute money for transformers and other distribution infrastructure despite regulatory obligations on DisCos.

“Consumers are not paying” has often been cited as a reason for poor service, Okorie said, but argued that the quality and basis of bills issued to consumers must also be examined.

“The appropriate question to ask is: how did they generate these bills? Were they justifiably, accountably and transparently generated?” he said.

He called for stronger enforcement of electricity regulations and greater protection for consumers, particularly in rural communities.

Okorie also advocated a dedicated mechanism for investigating alleged electricity-related violations and improving consumer awareness of their rights.

He questioned why the Federal Ministry of Power did not have a dedicated consumer protection unit and urged stronger involvement by consumer protection authorities in educating electricity users about their rights.

He also questioned claims that the Federal Government was paying subsidies in the sector, noting that electricity consumers provide much of the equipment used by DisCos, including poles, cables and transformers, without reimbursement from the utilities.

World.title: Despite inflation trend down, stocks sustain losses amid selling pressure
World.content:
CBN Governor, Yemi Cardoso

The Nigerian Exchange Limited, NGX dropped further Week-on-Week, WoW, amid selling pressure across sectors despite the fourth consecutive month of decline in headline inflation rate for the month of September 2026.

Read Also: Nigeria’s Oil Assets: Oye demands probe into NNPC’s ₦11.2trn receivables

Specifically, the NGX market capitalisation, which represents the total value of equities listed on the Exchange, dropped to N260.725 trillion last Friday from N161.260 trillion the previous week, as investors lost over N535 billion.

Similarly, another market gauge, NGX All Share Index, ASI nosedived by 0.3% to close last Friday at 247539.73 points from 248,363.55 points the previous week.

Analysis of trading showed that the market closed lower for the third consecutive week, as losses in Zenith Bank by -6 .5%, MTN Nigeria -1.8%, First HoldCo -3.9% and GTCO -4.4% contributed significantly to drag the ASI down WoW, bringing the Month-to-Date, MtD and Year-to-Date, YtD returns to -1.5% and +59.1%, respectively.

On market activity, trading volume and value declined by 39.0% WoW and 38.0% WoW, respectively.

On sector performance, the Banking declined by -3.1% and Insurance Index -0.1% , while the Oil & Gas Index rose by 3.1% and Consumer Goods 0.1% respectively. The Industrial Goods index closed flat.

Commenting on the market outlook, analysts at Cordros Capital Limited, stated: “Looking ahead, we expect market sentiment to improve, supported by bargain hunting following recent price declines. Secondly, anticipation of third quarter, Q3 earnings releases and positioning ahead of upcoming dividend qualification dates, which could drive selective buying interest.”

On their part, analysts at InvestData Consulting Limited, said: “The oil market’s movements may also influence expectations regarding inflation, energy costs and broader economic activity. Changes in crude prices can affect transportation, production and distribution costs, with potential implications for businesses across several sectors.

However, the implications for individual companies will vary according to their exposure to energy prices, operating structures and ability to pass higher costs on to customers. Investors should therefore assess the potential impact of oil-price movements within the context of individual company fundamentals and the wider economic environment.”

World.title: Nigeria’s Oil Assets: Oye demands probe into NNPC’s ₦11.2trn receivables
World.content:
The Chairman of the Alliance for Economic Research and Ethics, AERE, Dele Oye, has called for an independent probe into the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited’s ₦11.201 trillion receivables from the federation, demanding a transparent breakdown of the claims and the actual cost of securing the nation’s oil and gas assets.

Read Also: NLC, Falana, activists rally Nigerians against petrol price hike, hardship

Oye, who made the call in a policy analysis titled, “The ₦11.2 Trillion Bodyguard: A Receivable in a Security Uniform,” said the figures disclosed in NNPC’s 2025 annual report raised critical questions about the composition of the outstanding balance, the documentation of the underlying transactions and the reconciliation of obligations between the national oil company and the Federation.

He, however, cautioned against interpreting the ₦11.2 trillion balance as money spent on security in 2025, stressing that the figure represents year-end receivables rather than expenditure incurred during the financial year.

According to the report, NNPC’s other receivables from the Federation stood at ₦11.201 trillion at the end of December 2025, up from ₦8.840 trillion in 2024. The company broadly attributed the balance to advances to the Federation and costs incurred in protecting oil and gas assets under a government-approved framework.

But Oye said the published accounts did not provide sufficient details to establish how much of the balance related to physical security, advances to government or other financial obligations.

He said the government and NNPC must open the books to public scrutiny, insisting that the management of petroleum revenues and obligations should not be obscured by broad accounting descriptions.

“The ₦11.2 trillion bodyguard is not a 2025 security bill,” Oye declared.

₦8.67trn energy-security balance reconciliation

Explaining the accounting treatment, Oye said NNPC’s Note 24.2 recorded no energy-security expense for 2025, while an opening energy-security receivable of ₦8.672 trillion, carried forward from 2024, was reconciled in September 2025.

The amount was offset against royalties, taxes and dividends due to the Federation as of December 2024, contributing to a reduction in total Federation receivables from ₦17.512 trillion to ₦11.201 trillion.

He said the reconciliation did not remove the need for greater transparency, arguing that a receivable involving public funds, petroleum operations and government obligations required more detailed disclosure.

“That does not end the transparency question; it finally starts it properly. A receivable from the Federation is not an invoice from a private customer. It sits at the intersection of public finance, petroleum operations and sovereign authority. When the label is broad, scrutiny must become narrow,” he said.

Oye also explained that the energy-security framework was not limited to the protection of pipelines and other petroleum infrastructure. Under the Petroleum Industry Act framework cited by NNPC, the label also covered its supplier-of-last-resort role and, during the regulated petrol period, price-under-recovery obligations.

He described under-recovery as the difference between the actual landing cost of imported petrol and the regulated selling price, noting that exchange-rate movements could widen the gap. However, he said NNPC’s 2025 report did not separately quantify the foreign-exchange component.

In his view, the broad classification combined physical asset protection with oil-market and public-finance arrangements that should be accounted for separately.

Demands public register of costs

To address the disclosure gaps, Oye called for a publicly accessible register separating physical oil and gas asset security costs, supplier-of-last-resort and price-under-recovery obligations, and advances to the Federation.

He proposed a three-column reconciliation showing, for each category, the legal authority, beneficiaries, supporting invoices, cash status, amounts offset against government obligations and measurable outcomes.

“Nigeria should therefore insist on a three-column public reconciliation: physical asset security; supplier-of-last-resort/price-under-recovery support; and advances to the Federation. Each column should show the legal authority, beneficiary, invoice, cash status, offset status and measurable result,” he said.

The AERE chairman said the disclosures should be supported by verifiable evidence of the protection and maintenance of the infrastructure concerned, enabling Nigerians to distinguish actual security expenditure from other financial arrangements recorded in the company’s books.

He argued that a credible accountability framework must document the costs incurred, transactions completed, obligations settled and results achieved.

Questions over NNPC’s profit growth

Beyond the receivables, Oye raised questions about the composition of NNPC’s reported profit after tax of ₦7.183 trillion in 2025, compared with ₦5.414 trillion in 2024.

He acknowledged the company’s reported achievements, including peak crude and condensate production of 1.77 million barrels per day, its highest level in five years, and a declared dividend of ₦5.8 trillion.

However, he noted that revenue fell 24 per cent to ₦34.517 trillion, while gross profit declined by about 20 per cent to ₦9.374 trillion, even as profit after tax increased.

According to him, the accounts showed that other income rose from ₦3.392 trillion in 2024 to ₦8.416 trillion in 2025, while an impairment charge of ₦753.557 billion in 2024 became a reversal of ₦325.432 billion in 2025.

Oye said NNPC attributed its largest other-income category, described as “sundry income”, to items including Trans-Forcados pipeline income, crude-processing fees, miscellaneous income from joint-venture operators and a write-back connected to an Amenam-Kpono stock-overlift claim.

He stressed that the figures did not invalidate the reported profit but warranted further explanation of the factors driving the increase.

“None of that makes the profit unreal. But it does make the simple victory dance incomplete. When a company’s profit grows while core revenue and gross profit retreat, citizens deserve to know which cash-generating operations did the lifting, which accounting estimates moved, and which one-off items may not return for an encore,” he said.

Oye added: “The numbers deserve applause before they receive interrogation.”

He said Nigerians should be able to see, line by line, how value was generated, what was owed, how obligations were settled and what benefits were delivered.

Pipeline maintenance disclosure

The AERE chairman also questioned the presentation of pipeline maintenance costs in NNPC’s accounts, warning against drawing conclusions from a single expense category without examining the broader cost structure.

He noted that the line item for pipeline maintenance costs fell from ₦149.478 billion in 2024 to ₦13.813 billion in 2025, a decline of 90.76 per cent.

However, he said “other direct costs” rose from ₦566.540 billion to ₦1.277 trillion over the same period. According to NNPC’s disclosures cited in the analysis, the broader category includes the maintenance and operation of wells, production facilities, pipelines and processing infrastructure, as well as integrity management, repairs and field support.

Oye said the figures did not establish that physical pipeline maintenance had fallen by 90 per cent, but exposed a reporting gap that made it difficult for the public to determine whether work had been postponed, reclassified, captured under another cost centre or performed more efficiently.

“So the accounts do not prove that physical maintenance collapsed by 90%.

They prove that the public cannot tell, from the published categories, whether work was postponed, reclassified, embedded in another cost centre or carried out more efficiently. That distinction is not a footnote; it is the governance issue,” he said.

He called on NNPC to publish an asset-integrity scorecard for each major trunk line, detailing planned and actual maintenance, incidents, downtime, integrity spending and independent inspection results.

“A pipeline is not a metaphor. It either holds pressure or it holds a press conference,” he added.

Calls for accountability, not publicity

Oye said NNPC’s reported financial and production achievements should be acknowledged but accompanied by stronger disclosure of the financial arrangements, future obligations and operational results behind the figures.

He also called for greater transparency over forward-sale commitments, arguing that a public commitments calendar was necessary to clarify obligations associated with future deliveries and their implications for domestic supply.

He cautioned that memoranda of understanding and public announcements could not substitute for verifiable operational performance, particularly where refinery operations were concerned.

“NNPC’s 2025 accounts contain real achievements: stronger reported profit, improved production and a notable dividend declaration. They also show a financial architecture in which major public questions can still hide inside broad labels, offsets and future-delivery obligations,” he said.

“The ₦11.2 trillion figure is not proof that ₦11.2 trillion was spent on security in 2025. It is a very large Federation receivable whose composition deserves a public ledger.”

He added that the maintenance figures did not prove that pipeline upkeep had disappeared, but highlighted a disclosure structure inadequate for a strategic national asset.

Oye urged the government and NNPC to strengthen the documentation and reconciliation of petroleum revenues, expenditure and obligations, insisting that public accountability must extend beyond headline profits and production figures.

“Nigeria does not need another acronym, another relaunch or another headline with a ribbon around it. It needs a receipt: names, dates, invoices, barrels, offsets, performance and cash,” he said.

World.title: NLC, Falana, activists rally Nigerians against petrol price hike, hardship
World.content:
File image

*Accuses FG of enriching few to starve citizens *Say workers, masses under siege *N70,000 minimum wage now a cruel joke

By Victor Ahiuma-Young & Henry Obetta

Labour leaders and pro-democracy activists weekend called on Nigerians to unite against rising fuel prices, worsening economic hardship and government policies that have impoverished workers and the masses while enriching a privileged few.

Read Also: Buhari saw Tinubu as ‘Bad News’ for Nigeria — Baba-Ahmed

They warned that the continued increase in the pump price of Premium Motor Spirit, PMS, popularly known as petrol, has eroded workers’ purchasing power, intensified poverty and pushed millions of Nigerians into a daily struggle for survival.

The Nigeria Labour Congress, NLC, human rights lawyer, Femi Falana, SAN, members of the Joint Action Front, JAF, among others, made the call at the first memorial celebration and symposium in honour of late activist Abiodun Aremu in Lagos.

President of the NLC, Joe Ajaero, who was represented by the union’s Acting General Secretary, Benson Upah, said the removal of petrol subsidy had inflicted devastating consequences on the working class and the wider population, insisting that organised labour would continue to demand relief from the federal government.

In the address delivered on behalf of the NLC President, the labour movement described the prevailing economic situation as a crisis of survival, arguing that workers could no longer cope with the combined effects of rising transport fares, food prices, electricity tariffs and the depreciation of the naira.

“The removal of fuel subsidy has devastated Nigeria’s working class and masses,” NLC President stated.

According to him, transport costs have risen sharply, forcing many workers to choose between paying exorbitant fares and walking long distances to their workplaces.

NLC President also cited the increase in the price of essential commodities, noting that a bag of rice, which previously sold for about ₦30,000, now costs more than ₦80,000, while the price of a loaf of bread had risen from approximately ₦500 to ₦1,500.

He argued further that escalating electricity tariffs had forced some small businesses to shut down, while the depreciation of the naira had increased the cost of imported medicines, industrial inputs and other essential goods.

Ajaero attributed the worsening conditions to what it described as anti-people economic policies implemented without adequate consultation with Nigerians or effective measures to cushion their impact.

“The government has effectively declared war on its own people, pushing the majority to the fringes of survival,” he declared.

The NLC President noted that the crisis was not accidental but reflected economic policies that enriched the ruling class while deepening the hardship experienced by ordinary citizens.

NLC’s ultimatum over fuel prices

He disclosed that NLC had on October 9, issued a two-week ultimatum to the federal government, demanding an immediate reduction in the price of petrol.

According to him, the ultimatum is intended to compel the government to address the growing disconnect between workers’ earnings and the cost of living.

Ajaero said: “Most recently, the NLC issued a two-week ultimatum to the Federal Government, demanding an immediate reduction in the price of Premium Motor Spirit (PMS), also known as petrol.

“This ultimatum is not a mere bargaining chip but a solemn warning. If the government does not act within the stipulated timeframe, the NLC will have no choice but to seek remedial steps with all of us in this hall today.”

He argued that fuel prices should be reduced to a level consistent with the purchasing power of workers earning the national minimum wage of ₦70,000 monthly.

NLC recalled that when the minimum wage was set at ₦70,000 in July 2024, petrol sold for approximately ₦668.30 per litre, compared with prices exceeding ₦1,400 per litre in many parts of the country at the time covered by the address.

“A worker earning ₦70,000 a month cannot afford to buy petrol at ₦1,400 per litre. The government has effectively rendered the minimum wage meaningless.

“The ₦70,000 minimum wage was inadequate when it was announced. It is now a cruel joke. The NLC will not accept a situation where Nigerian workers are expected to survive on starvation wages while the cost of living continues to rise,” the NLC President declared.Beyond the demand for a reduction in petrol prices, the NLC urged the “government to take concrete measures to stabilise the naira, reduce inflation and strengthen domestic refining capacity.

“The removal of the subsidy was justified on the grounds that it would attract investment in local refining. Where is that investment?

Falana questions government’s approach to fuel pricing

Falana, who was the Chairman of the event, challenged the argument that withdrawing petrol subsidy was the only viable option available to the government, pointing to the continued use of subsidies in other countries.

He said “As you are all aware, countries across the world, including major capitalist economies, such as the United States, Germany and France, subsidise not only fuel but also education, healthcare and other essential services.

“That is the reality today. A simple internet search will reveal announcements of various subsidies in different countries.”

The senior advocate argued that governments should be prepared to consider different policy options to protect citizens from economic shocks, rather than treating the withdrawal of subsidies as an unavoidable solution.

He also referred to international developments concerning energy supplies and sanctions against Russia, and argued that countries routinely reconsidered their economic positions in response to changing circumstances.

Falana criticised the federal government’s position on fuel prices, saying Nigerians continued to face high costs, despite official discussions about reducing the landing cost of the commodity.

He said: “Here in Nigeria, with elections approaching, the government is telling us that the best it can offer is that the landing cost of fuel will be ₦1,350 per litre.

“When the government talks about landing cost, we must consider what that means for Nigerians in Abuja, Jos, Maiduguri and other parts of the country, where additional transportation and distribution costs may apply. That is what this administration has offered the Nigerian people.

“Among those seeking to take over power, only a few, including Omoyele Sowore and Donald Duke, have reportedly stated that, if given the opportunity, they would ensure that fuel sells for less than ₦500 per litre,” he said.

₦70,000 wage can buy only 50 litres of petrol — JAF

Among other speakers, Rashidat Adesina of the Joint Action Front (JAF) highlighted the dramatic increase in fuel prices since the announcement of subsidy removal in 2023, arguing that the consequences had been particularly severe for low-income earners.

She recalled that petrol sold for approximately ₦165 per litre before subsidy was removed, after which the price rose to about ₦500 and subsequently ₦600 per litre.

“We are now discussing prices of ₦1,350 to ₦1,400 per litre, depending on the location and filling station,” she said.

Adesina challenged Nigerians to consider what the increase meant for workers whose monthly earnings remained far below the cost of maintaining a household.

“What does this mean for workers and poor Nigerians?” she queried.

She illustrated the situation by comparing the minimum wage with the prevailing petrol price, noting that a worker earning ₦70,000 monthly could purchase only 50 litres of petrol at ₦1,400 per litre.

“The national minimum wage is ₦70,000 per month. At ₦1,400 per litre, an entire month’s minimum wage can purchase only 50 litres of petrol. That calculation does not include rent, school fees, food, transportation or other essential expenses,’’ she said.

For Adesina, the calculation demonstrated the extent to which rising energy costs had undermined the ability of workers to meet basic needs, even before accounting for other expenses required to sustain a family.

She referred to figures attributed to the National Bureau of Statistics, NBS, that placed the national poverty threshold at approximately ₦345 per person per day, although the specific figures and their reference periods required independent verification.

She argued that the reported poverty levels reflected the vulnerability of households already struggling with rising prices and stagnant incomes.

“The consequences for ordinary Nigerians are severe. While workers and poor households struggle, sections of the business community continue to accumulate enormous wealth,” she said.

Her remarks reinforced the central argument advanced at the symposium that the burden of economic adjustment was falling disproportionately on workers, traders, artisans, young people and other low-income groups.

Activists demand a change in economic priorities

The speakers’ interventions converged on a demand for the federal government to review policies they said had increased the cost of living without providing adequate protection for vulnerable citizens.

They argued that reducing petrol prices, reviewing the minimum wage, stabilising the naira and investing in domestic refining should form part of a broader response to the economic crisis.

World.title: 2027: I won’t step down for ADC, Kwankwaso declares
World.content:
Kwankwaso

…says party no better than APC

By Luminous Jannamike

ABUJA – Senator Rabiu Musa Kwankwaso, vice-presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress, NDC, has ruled out withdrawing from the 2027 presidential race in favour of the African Democratic Congress, ADC, declaring that the opposition party offers no better alternative to the ruling All Progressives Congress, APC.

Kwankwaso’s declaration comes amid opposition manoeuvres ahead of the election, with the NDC chieftain accusing the ADC Presidential Campaign Council, PCC, of promoting claims that his ticket with Peter Obi is working for the APC or may step down for the ADC candidate at the last minute.

In a statement on Sunday, Kwankwaso accused the ADC campaign team of directing unnecessary attacks at him, Obi and the NDC instead of selling its own candidate to Nigerians.

“We will not withdraw our candidature for the ADC or any other party,” he declared.

Kwankwaso also dismissed suggestions that the NDC ticket was acting on behalf of the ruling party, insisting that it remained committed to contesting the election.

“The OK ticket is neither working for nor acting on behalf of the APC or any of its candidates. We see no possibility or reason to withdraw from the presidential race in favour of the ADC candidate or any other,” he said.

Turning his attention to the ADC campaign council, Kwankwaso urged it to address allegations levelled against its presidential candidate by Vice-President Kashim Shettima rather than attack the NDC ticket.

He also rejected the ADC’s claim to being an alternative to the APC-led government, which he accused of failing Nigerians.

“The APC-led government has failed Nigerians. The ADC offers no better alternative,” Kwankwaso declared.

Presenting the NDC as a stronger opposition platform, he said his ticket with Obi had the credibility, capacity and nationwide support to unite the country and tackle insecurity, education, agriculture, infrastructure, healthcare and economic challenges.

Kwankwaso urged supporters and well-meaning Nigerians to remain committed to the party’s electoral victory, describing the NDC as the country’s most formidable opposition party.

“I therefore urge all our supporters and well-meaning Nigerians to continue working toward the victory of our great party,” he said.

World.title: LCFE Harps on Commodities Exchange for Transparent Petroleum Pricing, Market Efficiency
World.content:
Kayode Tokede

The Lagos Commodities and Futures Exchange (LCFE) is positioning organised commodities trading as a strategic instrument for promoting transparent petroleum pricing, strengthening competition and improving investment decisions in Nigeria’s evolving downstream petroleum market.

Following its recent licence from the Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority (NMDPRA) to facilitate the trading and clearing of petroleum liquids, the Exchange is seeking to connect the physical petroleum market with Nigeria’s capital market through a structured, technology-enabled trading platform.

The initiative comes amid significant changes in the petroleum industry, including downstream deregulation and expanding domestic refining capacity. These developments have heightened the need for reliable market information, transparent pricing and efficient price discovery.

In a statement by LCFE at the weekend, its Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer, Akin Akeredolu-Ale, said the initiative would establish a credible marketplace where petroleum products could be traded through organised mechanisms supported by appropriate trading, clearing and settlement processes.

He explained that the objective was to strengthen price discovery, improve market information and attract greater participation from refiners, petroleum marketers, traders, financial institutions and investors.

World.title: Fidelity Bank Champions Digital Adoption, Sustainable Growth for Lagos SMEs
World.content:
Kayode Tokede

Fidelity Bank Plc, has called on Small and Medium-scale Enterprises (SMEs) to embrace digital solutions, maintain sound financial management practices and adopt structured business models to enhance competitiveness and drive sustainable growth.

The call was made at the Fidelity Bank SME Quarterly Business Forum held in Lagos.

Speaking at the event, the bank’s Regional Bank Head, Ikeja, Mr. Jude Monye, who represented the Executive Director, Lagos and South-West, Dr. Ken Opara, described Lagos as a dynamic business hub with immense growth opportunities despite prevailing economic and operational challenges.

According to him, while Lagos remains one of Africa’s most vibrant commercial centres, entrepreneurs must navigate rising operating costs, intense competition, shifting consumer preferences, infrastructure limitations and working capital constraints.

“Yes, there are challenges, but that is why we are here, to see how we can guide you, support you and make sure that you bring your dreams to fruition. Building a competitive business in this environment requires more than ambition. It requires reliable products, consistent service, proper records, disciplined cost management, efficient inventory control and a deep understanding of customers,” Monye said.

He further emphasised the role of technology in improving business performance and decision-making.

In her remarks, the Divisional Head, SME Banking, Fidelity Bank Plc, Mrs. Ugochi Osinigwe, described SMEs as the backbone of Nigeria’s economy and highlighted the forum’s role as a platform for knowledge sharing, networking and business development.

“At Fidelity Bank, we are committed to helping entrepreneurs build, scale and transform their businesses into profitable and sustainable enterprises. Innovation and digital transformation are important parts of that journey, particularly in an increasingly competitive business environment,” she said.

World.title: Nigerian Bottling Company and the Business of Growing with Nigeria
World.content:
Raheem Akingbolu writes on remarkable 75-year journey of Nigerian Bottling Company, exploring how a brand born in Lagos has grown alongside Nigeria, becoming a major player in the beverage industry and a driver of value across its broader economic ecosystem

In 1951 when Nigeria was still under colonial rule, a business journey that began in Lagos would eventually become intertwined with the country’s economic story. Nigerian Bottling Company(NBC) was established by Greek-Cypriot entrepreneur A.G. Leventis, with production commencing two years later. Seventy-five years on, the company has become much more than a bottler.



The significance of that journey lies partly in its longevity. Nigeria has changed dramatically since those early years, passing through independence, political upheavals, economic crises, structural reforms and democratic transitions. Through these chapters, NBC has continued to manufacture, distribute, employ people, develop suppliers, and invest in communities, making its history a useful lens for viewing Nigeria’s changing business landscape.



There is, however, another way to understand the NBC story. A factory does not exist in isolation. Behind the products that eventually reach consumers are manufacturers supplying packaging, engineers maintaining equipment, transporters moving goods, distributors taking them to market and retailers selling them. Around this chain are thousands of people whose livelihoods depend, directly or indirectly, on the activity it generates.



That wider economic relationship is captured in a 2025 economic impact assessment by Steward Redqueen. The study examined the Coca-Cola System’s operations in Nigeria through its suppliers, distribution network, and downstream partners, rather than focusing solely on activity within factories and offices. Its findings provide an important economic dimension to NBC’s 75-year story and the value created around its operations.



The study found that the Coca-Cola System supported an estimated $1 billion in value added across its Nigerian value chain in 2024, equivalent to 0.55 per cent of the country’s GDP. It is also estimated that 160,200 jobs were supported across the value chain, showing how the economic footprint extends well beyond the System’s 2,989 direct employees.



The numbers become more revealing when the value chain is followed beyond production. According to the report, the System spent $601 million on goods and services from Nigerian suppliers in 2024. Of that amount, $482 million went into manufacturing-related sectors, including packaging materials, machinery, equipment and sugar processing, while energy and business services also received significant spending.



This is where the story of NBC becomes a story about local enterprise. Local procurement creates demand for companies that employ their own workers and purchase from their own suppliers. The effect can therefore extend beyond the original transaction, connecting a major manufacturer with businesses that may never carry the Coca-Cola name but participate in the economic activity surrounding it.

Employment tells a similar story. The Steward Redqueen assessment identified 2,989 direct employees within the Coca-Cola System in Nigeria and an additional 157,200 jobs supported across the value chain. Of these, 72,200 were linked to upstream activities such as procurement, while 85,000 were associated with distribution and sales nationwide.



The distribution network is particularly significant in a country where consumers buy everyday products through supermarkets, neighbourhood shops, open markets, restaurants and other outlets. The report estimated that 78,000 jobs were supported among distributors and selling outlets. In effect, the movement of beverages through the economy creates work well beyond those employed directly within the manufacturing system itself.



The report also offers an insight into how that economic relationship has changed. Compared with 2021, total value added associated with the Coca-Cola System increased by 28 per cent by 2024, while employment supported increased by 77 per cent. The assessment attributed much of the increase in upstream impact to a substantial rise in local procurement.



For Nigeria, this matters because manufacturing ambition cannot depend solely on the number of factories operating within the country. The deeper question is whether factories can stimulate competitive ecosystems of Nigerian suppliers, technicians, logistics companies, service providers, distributors and entrepreneurs. Industrial development becomes more meaningful when investment creates relationships that extend beyond individual transactions and strengthen productive capacity.



NBC’s physical footprint illustrates that long-term approach. The company now operates eight plants, 11 depots and more than 52 commercial territories across Nigeria. Its manufacturing presence stretches from Lagos to Port Harcourt, Benin, Asejire, Abuja, Maiduguri, Challawa and Owerri, creating a national network that connects production with consumers and markets across different regions.

Investment has remained central to that expansion. The company said it had invested about $1.5 billion in Nigeria over the past decade, directed towards expanding operational capacity, transforming supplychain infrastructure, and strengthening its workforce. More recent investments at Asejire in Oyo State and Challawa in Kano reflect the continuing push to expand production while supporting a wider manufacturing ecosystem.



Yet the economic story is not limited to factories, procurement and employment. NBC’s presence in Nigeria has also evolved through programmes addressing water and sanitation, youth development, women’s empowerment, and recycling. Its Supply Chain Academy, established in 1996, has trained more than 1,400 young people, while newer initiatives have focused on employability, entrepreneurship and practical business skills.



Water offers another dimension of the relationship between business and community. NBC’s sustainability initiatives include projects aimed at improving access to clean water and sanitation, such as solar-powered boreholes and partnerships that support water, sanitation, and hygiene infrastructure. Such programmes show how corporate responsibility can move beyond one-off philanthropy towards longer-term interventions thataddress community needs and support sustainability.



The same thinking is evident in the company’s approach to packaging and recycling. Its World Without Waste ambition includes collecting and recycling bottles and cans. At the same time, recent initiatives have included neighbourhood recycling banks in Lagos and Abuja, as well as a plastics collection hub in Apapa. Beyond environmental considerations, these efforts can create economic opportunities within Nigeria’s developing recycling and circular-economy ecosystem.



The human story behind the statistics is equally significant. The study estimated that households across the value chain received $509 million in salaries associated with the System’s activities in 2024, while the government received an estimated $267 million in taxes. It is also estimated that Nigerian companies across the value chain made $256 million in profits from their cooperation with the System.

This makes the 75th anniversary more than a celebration of corporate survival. At the Abuja anniversary event, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, represented by the Secretary to the Government of the Federation, George Akume, called for deeper local production, stronger supply chains, skills development, and investment. Those priorities provide a natural context for considering what NBC’s next chapter could mean for Nigeria.



The question now is what the next 25 years should produce. If the first 75 years established NBC as a national manufacturing and distribution enterprise, the next phase can be measured by theextent to which it strengthens local capabilities. More Nigerian suppliers, better skills, greater technological capacity, stronger recycling systems and productive jobs would give the centenary story an even larger meaning.



Seventy-five years after a business began its journey in Lagos, the most revealing part of the NBC story may therefore lie beyond the bottle itself. It lies in the factories, suppliers, workers, retailers, entrepreneurs and communities connected to its operations. That is the broader story of a company that has grown with Nigeria, and of an economy still seeking lasting shared value.

World.title: Sunbeth Global Concepts Announces N150bn Commercial Paper Issuance
World.content:
Sunbeth Global Concepts Limited has announced plans to raise up to N150 billion under its approved N500 billion Commercial Paper Issuance Programme to finance cocoa procurement for the new 2026/27 cocoa season.

The proceeds will fund short-term working capital requirements for cocoa purchases at origin, supporting the company’s international trading commitments and the procurement of cocoa inventory for its 70,000-metric-tonne-per-annum processing facility, scheduled to commence operations in March 2027.

With the new cocoa season underway, the proposed issuance will support timely purchases and the availability of inventory for export and processing requirements.

Sunbeth has secured approval for its N500 billion Commercial Paper Issuance Programme, providing a framework for accessing the domestic debt capital market to support its working capital requirements. The company has also demonstrated repayment discipline through the timely redemption of its debut Commercial Paper series.

The proposed issuance will comprise three series with tenors of 180, 270 and 364 days. The Commercial Paper will be issued in tranches, with the timing and size of each tranche aligned with cocoa procurement requirements and prevailing market conditions.

Sunbeth, in a statement, said it would maintain national-scale credit ratings from established African rating agencies, with long-term ratings ranging from BBB to BBB+ and a short-term rating of A2. Chapel Hill Denham Advisory Limited is acting as Lead Arranger for the transaction.

World.title: Towards Building Healthy Economy
World.content:
Arize Nwobu

The objectives of the economic reforms by the federal government and the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) are primarily to correct the anomalies, and towards building a healthy and sustainable economy going forward, though the policy implementations may be disruptive and distressful for a period in the timeline, but as it is said, “no pain, no gain”.

Economy is the focal point and lifeblood of the people and which is why responsible governments and all relevant institutions would do all necessary things to ensure a healthy and sustainable economy. Because of the inevitable disruptive effects of the economic reforms, President Tinubu has thus far introduced some social safety nets to help cushion the impact of the reforms towards building a healthy economy in the long run.

Basically, a healthy economy features a robust financial system, low inflation, stable prices, low unemployment/ high employment (so that those who want jobs can easily find one), and wages that match or beat inflation. Other features are moderate interest rate to channel capital to productive sectors, stable exchange rate to enable businesses plan with certainty, high consumer confidence, balanced imports and exports and growth in GDP.

CBN has thus far implemented some notable policies that have positively impacted some of the above-listed economic variables as part of the reforms towards building a healthy economy. The apex bank keyed into the envisioned US$1trillion economy envisioned by President Tinubu and has implemented a proactive and seamless banks recapitalisation policy to ensure a robust financial system.

It is expected that the recapitalised banks will channel credits into productive sectors especially agriculture, manufacturing, infrastructure, technology and small and medium enterprises to justify the essence of their recapitalisation.

After the recapitalisation, CBN Governor, Olayemi Cardoso noted that the apex bank had shifted focus to ensuring that stronger capital translated into support for productive activities. CBN has also stabilized the exchange rate and fought inflation aggressively and reduced it from it previous high levels to 15.39% and is still targeting to moderate it further.

With the reforms, Nigeria’s economy presently can be likened to a sick patient that was taken to the intensive care unit of a hospital and underwent two major life-saving surgeries for stabilization and subsequent healing and expected restoration of good health.

In the context, the economy has been stabilized after two major ‘surgeries’, namely the removal of the corrupt, costly and wasteful fuel subsidy regime by the Federal Government and the unification of the exchange rate by CBN which removed unnecessary distortions, exploitations, arbitrage and volatility in the previous multiple exchange rate regime.

The unified exchange rate has its pros and cons but CBN’s target goals for adopting the new regime are to remove the ambiguities of the previous exchange rate regime and ensure transparency, true price discovery through “willing buyer, willing seller” mechanism, curb rent-seeking and to attract foreign direct investments (FDIs). The unified exchange rate has contributed in stabilizing the economy.

The fuel subsidy removal was an inevitable, bold and courageous policy action because fuel subsidy constituted a huge financial burden and drained government resources which often led to large deficits. It also led to fuel smuggling and scarcity and corruption. The removal of fuel subsidy was a financial lifeline for the economy. It generated about N 15.8 trillion to the economy between June 2023 and December 2025.

Prior to the removal, the economy was reportedly broke and at the brink of collapse due to the drain on the resources and the alleged fiscal misadventure of the previous administration which printed money and allegedly abused the Ways and Means facility of CBN and left a colossal debt of N 30 trillion which was not repaid but securitized and which increased the debt servicing burden, triggered high inflationary pressure and aggravated poverty.

World bank noted that between 2020 and 2021, inflation left about eight million more Nigerians below the poverty line and increased the number of poor people to about 90 million.

To minimize poverty and actualize the objective and drive of the present economic reform towards building a healthy economy, the present macroeconomic stability should be maintained and inflation should be further moderated through a combination of the monetarist policy by CBN and the boosting of the supply side of the economy.

Holistically, the economy needs to be more competitive in the manufacturing sector and with policies that would catalyze industrialization and with a diversified base for greater stability and prosperity.

Nwobu, a Chartered Stockbroker and Business Journalist wrote via arizenwobu@yahoo.com. Tel: 08033021230

World.title: CHI Farms Marks Two Decades of Partnership with Aviagen
World.content:
CHI Farms Limited, a leading integrated agribusiness company in Nigeria and member of Tropical General Investments (TGI) Group is marking 20 years of partnership with Aviagen, the global poultry breeding company behind Arbor Acres®, supporting poultry farmers across Nigeria with access to breeding quality breeding stock and technical expertise.

Since 1986, CHI Farms has worked with poultry producers across Nigeria, helping them improve flock performance and meet the growing demand for poultry products. Through its partnership with Aviagen®, CHI Farms has made Arbor Acres genetics available to Nigerian poultry farmers while providing the technical support required to achieve strong results under local conditions.

Over the past two decades, the partnership has grown beyond the supply of breeding stock to include training, knowledge sharing, and close engagement with customers. These efforts have helped poultry producers improve productivity while contributing to the growth of Nigeria’s poultry industry.

Looking ahead, CHI Farms will continue to draw on its experience, market knowledge, and strategic partnerships to support poultry producers and contribute to the development of a stronger, more productive, and sustainable poultry industry in Nigeria.

World.title: Insurers Await Release of N300bn as CBN Commences Due Diligence
World.content:
Ebere Nwoji

Following the recent conclusion of recapitalisation process, insurers are eagerly awaiting the release of N300 billion in their escrow account as the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) commences due diligence.

Recently, the National Insurance Commission (NAICOM), said it has formally instructed the apex bank to release the funds.

The Commissioner for Insurance, Mr Olusegun Ayo Omosehin had at a press briefing in Lagos told the media that insurers would by the end of September receive their funds.

Addressing newsmen in Lagos, the Chairman, Nigerian Insurers Association (NIA), Mrs. Ebelechukwu Nwachukwu, disclosed that NAICOM has instructed CBN to release the funds.

She however assured operators that the funds were expected to be fully returned within this month of October.

“NAICOM has done its part by issuing instructions to the CBN. The funds will be returned to the exact accounts from which they were sent once the CBN completes its verification,” she stated.

​She urged insurance operators that crossed the recapitalisation hurdle to deploy the enhanced capital base to expand local underwriting capacity, increase retention during reinsurance renewals, and provide cover for emerging exposures such as cyber and climate risks.

She said having successfully concluded the recapitalisation exercise the regulator has come up with implementation of the Risk Base Capital model.

She said the regulator has appointed global professional services firm Ernst & Young (EY) as its consultant to guide the Nigerian insurance industry through a transparent and structured transition to a Risk-Based Capital (RBC) regime.

According to her, the Commissioner for Insurance, Olusegun Omosehin, announced the appointment during the insurers’ committee meeting alongside other crucial regulatory directives shaping the post-recapitalisation era.

World.title: [Watch] Woman fights off Cape baboon attack in viral video
World.content:
A woman fought off a Cape Peninsula baboon attack in a viral video. Images via TikTok

A video of a woman who fought off a baboon that raided her car in an attack in Cape Town has racked up millions of views on TikTok

The video was recorded at Sir Lowry’s Pass.

WOMAN FIGHTS OFF BABOON IN CRAZY CAR RAID

In the clip, posted by @buusolakhe, a group of female friends is seen trying to ward off several baboons at a picnic spot at Sir Lowry’s Pass, which falls under the Cape Town Metropolitan area.



The troop attempted to raid the car in search of food.

The woman behind the camera films herself opening her door before yanking out one angry baboon, which proceeded to bite her on her right arm.

She screams for help from her friends and a SAPS police van, parked nearby.



In the comment section, South Africans were amazed at the woman’s bravery while confronting a baboon.

She revealed that she had sought medical attention for the animal bite.

Take a look…

WHAT TO DO WHEN YOU SPOT THE WILD ANIMAL

Cape Town is well known for its Chacma baboon population. City officials have urged residents and visitors to keep a safe distance from the wild animals.



Here are a few tips on what to do when you spot the animal whilst out and about…

Stay inside your vehicle.

Keep doors locked and windows and sunroofs closed. Baboons are intelligent animals who can open car doors and may climb through windows to steal food.



Don’t leave food lying around.

Food should never be visible through the windows. Pack bags and food items in the vehicle’s boot or under the seats.

Do not chase a baboon or try to retrieve stolen belongings



If a baboon steals your bag and possessions, the City advises the public to let the animals move away after searching the bag, then retrieve your belongings.

Leave if they appear aggressive

When picnicking, pack up and leave if nearby baboons appear aggressive.



Never feed or touch baboons.

Feeding is punishable by law. The City warns that people caught feeding baboons may face a fine of up to R10,000 and/or two years’ imprisonment.

World.title: Baas van die plaas: Franco Mostert shows off his farm
World.content:
Franco Mostert at his farm. Images via IG

Franco Mostert is the latest Springbok to show off his flourishing business move – farming. The Bok lock has ventured into growing his own fresh produce and managing a guest house.

FRANCO MOSTERT SHOWS OFF NEW BUSINESS VENTURE

On their Instagram accounts, Franco Mostert and his wife, Juan-Ri, have given their followers a look at their farming business, Sous Plaas.

The company grows and sells fresh produce, like lettuce, onions, carrots and beetroot to local supermarkets.



The couple also own their own farmhouse, a self-catering holiday accommodation, called Die Mostert Plaashuis in the North West.

On its official IG account, Sous Plaas posted a clip of Franco manning a tractor in an open field during his downtime.

“Baas van die plaas”, the company said of the Springbok, who has 85 test caps.

OTHER SPRINGBOKS TRANSITIONING INTO FARMING

Franco Mostert is one of several current Springboks who own farms.



Pieter-Steph du Toit’s family owns Kloovenburg Wine & Olive Estate in the Western Cape, which produces wine, grape juice, olives, and avocados.

Kwagga Smith owns a guest farm in Mpumalanga, which also cultivates maize, soy, pecans, and walnuts.

Retired Springbok Duane Vermeulen owns a walnut farm near his restaurant in the Free State.

World.title: Ramaphosa concerned about political killings ahead of elections
World.content:
President Cyril Ramaphosa says he is concerned about the spate of politically related killings ahead of the 2026 local government elections.

Ramaphosa made the remarks while addressing journalists on the sidelines of his election campaign in Cape Town on Sunday.

RAMAPHOSA WEIGHS IN ON POLITICAL KILLINGS

This week, two ANC members were shot dead and three others injured during a door-to-door campaign in Umgababa, south of Durban, in KwaZulu-Natal.

The killings come amid growing concerns about political violence ahead of the 4 November 2026 local government elections.

“Obviously, we are all disturbed about the political killings that are targeting people who are either campaigning, who are both representatives who should be elected, and also the mass killings. The police are on the heels of all those people who are perpetrating those murders.

“We cannot be a country that has the killings of people who other people may be opposed to. We want to bring those killings to an end,” he said.

AT LEAST 43 PEOPLE KILLED IN SUSPECTED ATTACKS

The killings come amid wider concerns about political violence ahead of the November 4 local government elections.

A report by the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organised Crime, published in October, recorded at least 43 people killed in suspected political assassinations across South Africa between January and September 2026.

The report recorded 45 suspected political attacks during that period, with the number of deaths already exceeding the organisation’s full-year totals for the 2021 local government election year and the 2024 national election year.
