“Formal decisions or partial amendments to the concession agreement in Armenia’s favour are possible. However, this is a political issue. In the near future, I do not see a political solution that would not lead to a further deterioration in Armenian-Russian relations.”

Russia seeks to keep Armenia railway concession

World.title: Fidan says ‘everything is fine’ in Baku, but relations remain strained
World.content:
Strained relations between Turkey and Azerbaijan

Turkey’s Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan arrived in Baku on the evening of 14 October. The official reason for his visit was the seventh summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence-Building Measures in Asia (CICA), where Fidan represented Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan. However, the visit came amid worsening relations between the two countries in recent weeks, putting every detail under close scrutiny.

Azerbaijan’s Youth and Sports Minister Farid Gayibov greeted Fidan at Heydar Aliyev International Airport. The decision to assign him to welcome the Turkish foreign minister prompted mixed reactions on social media in both Azerbaijan and Turkey. On 15 October, Fidan met Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev. Later that day, during the summit, he left the hall along with representatives of several other delegations when Israeli President Isaac Herzog began his speech.

After his meeting with Aliyev, Fidan said relations between the two countries remained strong and unbreakable. However, his remarks also acknowledged that disagreements existed between Baku and Ankara.

One of the main factors behind the deterioration in relations has been the de facto ban on wearing the hijab in Azerbaijani schools. JAMnews examined the issue in detail in an earlier article. This time, however, the focus is on a different question:

What is happening in relations between Baku and Ankara, and how serious is the growing chill between them?

Fidan’s message: “There are disagreements, but…”

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan at a dinner hosted by Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev in Baku to mark the seventh CICA summit. Photo: president.az

Speaking to journalists in Baku, Fidan said relations between the two countries had stood the test of wars and crises, while their leaders shared an “unbreakable friendship and brotherhood”. He added that Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan had given him special instructions before the trip.

At the same time, the minister openly acknowledged that the two countries might hold different positions on certain issues. Fidan stressed that neither side should allow these disagreements to damage their strategic relationship:

“We are a people with an ancient history. We must resolve our problems as befits a people with such a past: by sitting down at the negotiating table and discussing them in a civilised manner.”

The minister also said the two sides should not turn their differences into a propaganda tool on social media. He said his conversation with Aliyev had followed this approach, with the Turkish side hearing the Azerbaijani president’s position and his assessment of the situation.

Fidan did not explicitly mention the hijab issue, Israel or Aliyev’s speech on 2 October. However, his references to “our problems”, “differences in approach” and the “use of disagreements” suggest that Ankara acknowledges the existence of tensions but prefers to address them through diplomatic channels rather than in public.

Meanwhile, photographs from the visit attracted the most attention on social media. Some users analysed Fidan’s body language, noting that he appeared relaxed both at the airport and during his meeting with the president, as though relations between the two countries faced no problems. Although such assessments are subjective, they show how closely the public watches every gesture by representatives of Baku and Ankara.

However, the most notable moment of the visit came during Israeli President Isaac Herzog’s speech. At the summit in Baku, Fidan refused to listen to Herzog and left the hall. Just a month earlier, the decision by an Azerbaijani representative to remain in the hall during Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s speech at the UN General Assembly had drawn sharp criticism in Turkey.

What triggered the tensions?

A series of events over the past three weeks has heightened tensions between Baku and Ankara:

23 September — Speaking at the UN General Assembly, Erdoğan described bans on headscarves in schools in “some countries” as an infringement of women’s rights. During the same session, Azerbaijan’s representative remained in the hall while Netanyahu delivered a speech in which he called Erdoğan a “tyrant”.

— Speaking at the UN General Assembly, Erdoğan described bans on headscarves in schools in “some countries” as an infringement of women’s rights. During the same session, Azerbaijan’s representative remained in the hall while Netanyahu delivered a speech in which he called Erdoğan a “tyrant”. 2 October — Speaking at a congress of the ruling New Azerbaijan Party (YAP), Aliyev said, without naming anyone in particular, that everyone should “know their place” and that nobody had the right to interfere in the Azerbaijani people’s way of life. He stressed that Azerbaijan had achieved its military victories without foreign patronage and had bought weapons with its own money (JAMnews).

— Speaking at a congress of the ruling New Azerbaijan Party (YAP), Aliyev said, without naming anyone in particular, that everyone should “know their place” and that nobody had the right to interfere in the Azerbaijani people’s way of life. He stressed that Azerbaijan had achieved its military victories without foreign patronage and had bought weapons with its own money (JAMnews). 9–12 October — Azerbaijani schools began inspections during which officials barred female pupils and teachers wearing hijabs from attending classes. The measures sparked protests and led to the detention of 37 people (JAMnews).

— Azerbaijani schools began inspections during which officials barred female pupils and teachers wearing hijabs from attending classes. The measures sparked protests and led to the detention of 37 people (JAMnews). 12 October — Erdoğan’s chief adviser Oktay Saral called on Azerbaijan to “correct this mistake” as soon as possible. Leyla Şahin Usta, deputy chair of the parliamentary group of the Justice and Development Party (AKP), made a similar statement.

— Erdoğan’s chief adviser Oktay Saral called on Azerbaijan to “correct this mistake” as soon as possible. Leyla Şahin Usta, deputy chair of the parliamentary group of the Justice and Development Party (AKP), made a similar statement. 13 October — YAP’s press service criticised Saral and AKP MPs, naming them individually. Its statement called on the AKP to abandon its “harmful policy” and also referred to “hegemonic ambitions” (Yeni Azerbaijan).

— YAP’s press service criticised Saral and AKP MPs, naming them individually. Its statement called on the AKP to abandon its “harmful policy” and also referred to “hegemonic ambitions” (Yeni Azerbaijan). 14–15 October — Fidan arrived in Baku and met Aliyev.

Against this backdrop, AKP spokesperson Ömer Çelik limited his response to saying that the two countries’ leaders shared a “genuinely brotherly relationship”.

Why relations are cooling: Israel, Russia and claims to the role of “big brother”

All the experts JAMnews interviewed before Fidan’s visit believe the hijab issue represents just one manifestation of deeper problems in relations between Azerbaijan and Turkey.

“The need to choose between two rivals”

Araz Aliyev | Photo: Third Republic Platform

Politician Araz Aliyev, one of the founders of the Third Republic Platform, told JAMnews that he linked the current tensions to Azerbaijan’s foreign policy.

In his view, Baku has begun to see itself as “a major geopolitical player”. However, unlike the US or China, Azerbaijan lacks the capacity to maintain close relations with two rival states at the same time:

“Over the next ten years, Turkey and Israel will be the two main rivals in the Middle East. At the same time, Azerbaijan is a strategic ally of both countries. When Netanyahu speaks, the Turkish delegation leaves the hall, while the Azerbaijani delegation cannot do the same, even if it wants to. Israel also invests in Azerbaijan and supports it. Naturally, this causes resentment in Turkey.”

Araz Aliyev notes that Azerbaijan first felt the negative consequences of its “multi-vector policy” after it backed Pakistan in its confrontation with India. According to the politician, India blocked Azerbaijan’s accession to the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, while trade between the two countries — worth as much as $2 billion — suffered a setback.

Aliyev identifies Russia as a second factor. In his view, Baku has been pursuing closer relations with Moscow since August. He sees the resolution of disagreements over the crash of an AZAL aircraft as one sign of this rapprochement. Historically, he notes, closer ties between Azerbaijan and Russia have gone hand in hand with a degree of distancing from Turkey.

Araz Aliyev also links these changes to the domestic political situation in the US. In his view, Baku’s foreign policy strategy, which has largely relied on Donald Trump’s administration, could come under threat if Republicans lose the US midterm elections in November. The politician believes concerns about this scenario are pushing the Azerbaijani authorities to seek alternative foreign policy partners.

“I don’t depend on you”

Ömer Faruk Gergerlioğlu | Photo: Grand National Assembly of Turkey

Ömer Faruk Gergerlioğlu, a member of Turkey’s parliament representing Kocaeli province and the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM), told JAMnews that he sees Aliyev’s 2 October speech as a rejection of Turkey’s claim to the role of “big brother”.

“Turkey has always seen itself as the big brother of Central Asian countries and Azerbaijan. Aliyev, however, disagrees. His message is: I don’t depend on you; I need you only as much as you need me. We have mutual interests, but ours is not a relationship between an older and a younger brother.”

In the MP’s view, Baku sees cooperation with Israel as a “lifeline” that helps it preserve its authoritarian system of government, and it has no intention of making concessions on this issue.

Gergerlioğlu also points to what he sees as contradictions in Erdoğan’s position. The Turkish president sharply criticises Israel but turns a blind eye to oil shipments from the Turkish port of Ceyhan to Israel. The oil reaches the port through the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan pipeline. The MP claims he has repeatedly presented the government with documentary evidence of these shipments.

“If tensions between Turkey and Israel escalate, I think Aliyev will openly side with Israel. For him, the principle of ‘one nation, two states’ takes a back seat. He views the world primarily through the lens of preserving his own power.”

Against this backdrop, Fidan’s decision to walk out rather than listen to Israeli President Isaac Herzog’s speech in Baku takes on particular significance. This time, Ankara demonstrated its differences with Azerbaijan over Israel directly in the Azerbaijani capital.

Growing discontent in Turkish society

Джавид Ага | Фото: личный архив

Journalist and analyst Javid Agha notes that discontent with Azerbaijan in Turkish society extends beyond the hijab issue.

According to him, Turkish businesspeople have complained for years about the difficulties of doing business in Azerbaijan, demands for unofficial payments by tax authorities and deliberate delays affecting lorries at the Georgian-Azerbaijani border.

“Turkish society has accumulated numerous grievances against Azerbaijan. However, people have only begun expressing them more openly and actively since the summer. Previously, Erdoğan’s inner circle kept this discontent in check through groups it funded, which fell silent at the president’s first signal. Now I see posts supporting protests in Azerbaijan on Instagram, TikTok and even platforms where I would never have imagined seeing such things before.”

The hijab factor: a sensitive issue for Turkey

The de facto ban on wearing the hijab in Azerbaijani schools has provoked a particularly strong reaction in Turkey. According to Gergerlioğlu, bans on headscarves remained one of the most hotly debated issues in Turkish society from the 1980s until the 2010s. Today, even voters who support the secular Republican People’s Party (CHP) consider the issue “a thing of the past”.

“Footage showing girls in headscarves being turned away from school brings back painful memories for Turkish society. Supporters of the ban argued that without it, Turkey would become a state governed by Sharia law. But the ban was lifted, and Turkey still did not become a Sharia state.”

The MP also clashed with Azerbaijani lawmakers over the issue. He said that during an online meeting of the Parliamentary Assembly of Turkic States (TURKPA), he criticised the ban. Azerbaijani MP Hikmet Mammadov then claimed that no such ban existed in the country and accused him of lying. However, according to Gergerlioğlu, a lawmaker from Turkey’s ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP), who attended the meeting, chose to remain silent.

Araz Aliyev believes Ankara’s reaction was inevitable. In his view, under Erdoğan, Turkey presents itself as a defender of “moderate Islam” and Muslims, while religious voters form one of the ruling party’s main support bases. “In this situation, Baku’s decision could not go unanswered,” he says.

Javid Agha, meanwhile, points out that Leyla Şahin Usta was among those whom Azerbaijan’s ruling New Azerbaijan Party (YAP) criticised in its statement. In the late 1990s, a headscarf ban prevented her from continuing her studies in Istanbul. Şahin Usta later lost her case against Turkey at the European Court of Human Rights and completed her education in Vienna.

“These bans did not stop her. Today, she is among those who govern Turkey. The authors of the statement should at least have familiarised themselves with her biography,” Agha says.

Sheikh-ul-Islam: “Consultations could have taken place, but they did not”

Allahshukur Pashazade, chairman of the Caucasus Muslims Board, has also commented on the situation. In an interview with Real TV, he acknowledged that the authorities had not consulted the religious organisation he heads before making the decision:

“I deeply regret that consultations could have taken place on this issue in advance, but they did not.”

At the same time, Pashazade supported the government’s position. He said the school uniform regulations do not mention the word “hijab” and that the country has no ban on wearing it. Children can study in hijabs at madrasas, he added, “but a different decision was taken regarding state schools”.

The Sheikh-ul-Islam stressed that “religion is separate from the state, and school is separate from religion”. He also accused certain “internal and external forces” of politicising the issue and trying to turn citizens against the state.

Araz Aliyev sees Pashazade’s statement as evidence that the authorities made the decision hastily:

“If the decision had been carefully considered and prepared over many years, the authorities should have consulted someone. It appears they made the decision in haste.”

For more on the legal aspects of the hijab ban, protests at schools and detentions, see JAMnews’ earlier report.

How will relations develop?

None of the experts interviewed expects Azerbaijan and Turkey to break off their alliance. However, they all believe the chill between the two countries will persist for some time.

Araz Aliyev believes the tensions will remain at the political level and gradually ease:

“Turkey needs Azerbaijan, while Azerbaijan needs Turkey even more in terms of national security, the economy and defence. Companies close to the leadership in both countries may face pressure from one another, but I do not believe their alliance will be threatened. After some time, we will hear declarations of brotherhood again.”

He notes that the two countries have weathered similar crises in the past. In particular, tensions in the late 2000s, when Turkey and Armenia were discussing protocols to normalise relations, led to Turkish flags being taken down in Baku. Aliyev believes the summit of the Organisation of Turkic States, which is expected to take place in Turkey at the end of the month, could indicate the direction in which relations between Baku and Ankara will develop.

Gergerlioğlu also does not expect Erdoğan to distance himself from Baku solely over the hijab issue. He says Ankara places much greater importance on revenue from the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan pipeline, Turkey’s ambition to play a leading role in the “Turkic world” and the support of its nationalist-conservative electorate.

“Behind closed doors, they will probably say politely: ‘Wouldn’t it have been better not to introduce such a ban?’ However, if Aliyev begins openly supporting Israel, Turkey will also start signalling its discontent with the relationship more openly.”

The MP also points to declining electoral support for the ruling party. He claims that some voters dissatisfied with the AKP’s “two-faced” policy towards Israel backed the New Welfare Party in the last election. In his view, the hijab issue could deepen this discontent further.

Javid Agha reaches a similar conclusion. He believes that no matter how often Erdoğan repeats the slogan “one nation, two states”, he will have to take into account the views of the religious-conservative electorate that forms the foundation of his political support and adjust his position accordingly.

Fidan’s statements in Baku also offer insight into this diplomatic strategy. Ankara does not deny that problems exist, but seeks to move discussions about them out of the public arena and into closed-door diplomatic channels. So far, however, there are no signs that Baku intends to make concessions either on the hijab issue or on its relations with Israel.

Strained relations between Turkey and Azerbaijan

World.title: Kyrgyz investment income payments to non-residents reach around $190M
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 19. Investment income payments by Kyrgyzstan to non-residents amounted to $189.7 million in the first quarter of 2026, increasing by 116.8% year-on-year.

This was reported based on statistical data published by the National Bank of the Kyrgyz Republic.

According to the national bank, the figure increased from $87.5 million recorded in the same period of 2025.

In absolute terms, investment income payments increased by $102.2 million.

In 2025, investment income payments amounted to $217.6 million, compared with $356.6 million in 2024, $272.7 million in 2023 and $290.5 million in 2022.

During 2025, payments amounted to $87.5 million in the first quarter, $203.2 million in the second quarter and $249.2 million in the third quarter. In the fourth quarter, the indicator amounted to -$322.2 million.

Trend estimates that investment income payments by Kyrgyzstan to non-residents could remain at an elevated level during 2026, reflecting the continued movement of investment-related income flows and cross-border financial operations.

According to Trend’s calculations, if quarterly payments during the remainder of 2026 average around $180–220 million, the annual volume could reach approximately $730–850 million. This would reflect the higher level of investment-related flows observed at the beginning of the year.

The quarterly dynamics of investment income payments can vary significantly, particularly toward the end of the year. Further data will therefore provide a clearer picture of the annual volume and the development of Kyrgyzstan’s external investment income flows.

World.title: Tanker strikes naval mine in Strait of Hormuz
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 19. A tanker struck a naval mine in the southern part of the Strait of Hormuz, causing an explosion and fire in the vessel’s engine room.

The incident was reported by the naval forces of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), an elite branch of Iran’s armed forces.

“The tanker, which violated the established rules, was damaged after striking a naval mine in the southern part of the Strait of Hormuz. An explosion and fire occurred in the vessel’s engine room,” the statement carried by Iranian state television and radio said.

According to the IRGC Navy, the vessel was attempting to leave the strait after switching off all positioning and navigation systems and disregarding the established rules for passage through the waterway.

The IRGC warned that strict and decisive measures would be taken against vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz with their navigation and identification systems switched off.

World.title: Azerbaijani judokas conclude the Asian Open Cup with 14 medals (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 18. The Asian Open Cup in judo has concluded in the Kazakh city of Aktau.

On the second day of the competition, Azerbaijani judokas won one gold, one silver and four bronze medals.

Sudaba Aghayeva (70 kg), having defeated all her opponents, claimed the gold medal. Madina Kaisynova (+78 kg) finished the tournament with a silver medal.

World.title: Breaking: Climate activists charged after Woodside offshore rig stunt
World.content:
Two Greenpeace activists have been charged after sailing out to open waters and occupying an offshore gas platform to protest Woodside's planned gas developments.

In a joint statement, the Australian Border Force, WA Police and the national offshore petroleum regulator NOPSEMA said 48-year-old man and a 52-year-old man had been charged with "interfering with offshore petroleum installations or operations".

They said the offence carried a maximum penalty of 10 years' imprisonment.

Two people being marched across the Karratha airport tarmac in handcuffs. (ABC News: Kimberley Putland)

The men are due to face Karratha Magistrates Court today.

Footage shared by Greenpeace showed activists sailing out to the Scarborough gas rig about 200 kilometres off WA's coast on Saturday morning, scaling the infrastructure and unfurling a large banner with the words "stop Woodside's dirty gas".

The banner also said "save Scott Reef", which is near where Woodside is proposing to develop its $48.7 billion Browse gas project and tap into Australia's largest undeveloped gas resource.

Authorities said they were still investigating the incident.

An image supplied by Greenpeace showed their Rainbow Warrior vessel approaching the platform. (Supplied: Greenpeace)

The proposed Browse development has been hotly contested by environmental groups opposed to new gas projects.

Greenpeace Australia Pacific CEO David Ritter said yesterday the organisation and other advocacy groups had been scaling up their activism in the face of growing community concerns.

World.title: Teen charged over Melbourne CBD crash wants to plead guilty, court hears
World.content:
A teenager has told the children's court he wants to plead guilty, after he was charged with crashing a stolen car into a woman near Flinders Street Station this month.

Witnesses described chaotic scenes as a speeding car was driven erratically through the city on October 11, near where thousands of people were competing in the Melbourne Marathon.

Emergency services swarmed the area after a 57-year-old woman was struck near the intersection of Flinders Street and Elizabeth Street.

She was taken to hospital with non life-threatening injuries.

Today, the 16-year-old-boy allegedly behind the wheel faced a Children's Court via video link.

Police alleged the stolen Ford Escape was driven along tram tracks. (ABC News: Leanne Wong)

The boy asked to address the magistrate directly after his lawyer applied to adjourn the case.

"Can't I just plead guilty today?" the teenager said.

"I've done what I've done. I want to plead guilty to all of this."

In open court, the boy's defence lawyer told him it was "something we have to talk about more carefully" before that could occur.

The boy is facing charges of reckless conduct endangering serious injury, numerous driving offences, failing to render assistance, theft and handling stolen goods.

Police alleged the stolen Ford Escape was driven along tram tracks on Flinders Street when the woman was hit.

Police and Protective Services Officers drew their firearms when the driver allegedly performed a U-turn outside the station.

The vehicle was driven along Flinders Lane and hit several parked cars, officers alleged.

The 16-year-old was arrested later that day in Albert Park.

Police ruled out terrorism or a targeted attack.

Today, the teenager complained about journalists watching his hearing on a video link, fearing they could be taking pictures of him.

His lawyer assured him that would not happen and he would not be identified in reporting for legal reasons.

"The people you're seeing on the link are people who respect those rules, they know them very clearly," the lawyer said.

The boy, who is also facing unrelated charges, will have all his cases listed together at the next hearing on November 19.

World.title: Outstations and town camps struggle with damage from 'scary' storm
World.content:
Central Australian residents say the poor quality of many homes in remote outstations and town camps has amplified damage after a storm whipped through southern parts of the Northern Territory last Monday.

Trees were uprooted, there were widespread power outages and roofs were ripped from homes as winds of up to 96 kilometres an hour, a two minute drive from the remote community of Hermannsburg, was significantly damaged during the storm.

The Western Arrarnta woman was in Canberra during the severe weather event, but said her children phoned her to tell her of the damage.

"They said it was a mini cyclone or hurricane … and it was a bit scary," she said.

"Trees were pulled out from the ground, rain just falling over the houses."

Ms Malbunka said the power went out in most outstations around the region and families were struggling to feed themselves, but electricity was restored in about two days.

Strong winds and rain destroyed Maryanne Malbunka's homeland property near Hermannsburg. (Supplied: Maryanne Malbunka)

The health worker said existing challenges with housing in many remote outstations made the homes more vulnerable to storm and many residents in the region were "struggling".

"Maybe when we get more rain or more storms like that our houses will be flown out, because we're only living in a tin shed, and some of those brick houses aren't being renovated or looked at properly," she said.

The remote location means storm clean-up will be difficult. (Supplied: Maryanne Malbunka)

Ms Malbunka said outstation residents would need to make many trips to the tip to clean up their properties, which would be costly due to the high price of fuel.

Town camps also damaged

A Northern Territory government spokesperson said four public housing properties were uninhabitable due to damage and there were 59 storm-related repair jobs across public housing in town, including five town camps.

The spokesperson said the government was "prioritising relocating" families in affected homes to alternative public housing while the houses were repaired.

Caleb Doolan says he had to throw out food after his power went out in the storm. (ABC Alice Springs: Xavier Martin)

Mpwetyerre/Abbott's Town Camp resident Caleb Doolan said his home lost power and children in the town camp were scared.

"We had to chuck everything out from the fridge," he said.

"It was hard for us."

Mr Doolan said the storm was another blow to the town camp, which was still recovering from floods earlier in the year.

World.title: RLWC quick hits: Ponga's power, Tonga's triumph and Fiji's sunny day
World.content:
The first week of the Rugby League World Cup is in the books with stars new and old making statements across the tournament.

From the classic opener between Australia and New Zealand to Tonga's statement win over England and Papua New Guinea's handy victory over Lebanon there's plenty for the international football fan to sink their teeth into.

Here are the quick hits from the opening round.

1. Kalyn Ponga holds New Zealand's hopes in his hands

Ponga scored a double for New Zealand before departing late with a broken arm. (Getty Images: Matt King)

Over the past few months Kalyn Ponga has made a transformation from someone who can play great into a great player and if his World Cup is over due to a broken arm not only will the tournament be far poorer without him he might take New Zealand's title hopes home with him.

Ponga was magnificent in his Kiwi debut on Friday night, scoring two tries and running for 254 metres as he continued the form that helped drive Newcastle to the grand final earlier this month.

World Cup opener a reminder of Australia's glory days There was a time when Test matches were rugby league's biggest, best and bloodiest spectacles, and last night's World Cup opener between Australia and New Zealand was a reminder of those days.

His battles with Australia's Reece Walsh will take some beating as the defining memory from the entire World Cup even as New Zealand fell to a frustrating defeat where they dominated every major stat but the scoreboard.

Ponga has undergone surgery and will remain in camp but if his transcendent year is over, things might have peaked early for the Kiwis.

Keano Kini, a fine fullback in his own right, was terrific in New Zealand's Pacific Championship win last year and has the work rate and running game to break any match open.

But he is not Kalyn Ponga, who is not rare but unique. That means there's nobody else like him.

2. Speed can kill for lightning Samoan backline

Fa'alogo scored four tries off the bench for Samoa in their big win over France. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor )

It's a measure of the depth Samoa enjoy that Su'a Fa'alogo, Melbourne's player of the year and one of the most dynamic attacking weapons in the sport, could only crack a bench spot for their first match.

Even so, Samoa proved they could strike from anywhere at any time and through almost any player — Jermaine McEwan's 50 metre solo effort will be one of the best efforts of the entire World Cup.

But after Fa'alogo was pitched into the action early following an injury to Deine Mariner and finished with four tries, three try assists and seven linebreaks in this thumping victory it's clear he can act as the Toa's wildcard as they look to emulate 2022's brilliant run to the final.

Just where the Storm fullback fits into the side remains to be seen — Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow is a brilliant fullback in his own right and Fa'alogo's unfamiliarity with playing wing could be targeted by more dangerous opposition.

But speed can kill and when Fa'alogo is out there Samoa have enough to run and gun with anybody.

3. Future is now for Papua New Guinea

The looming presence of the PNG Chiefs is the subtext beneath every Papua New Guinea game in this World Cup and after this impressive win it seems they've landed a good one in Gairo Voro.

The 23-year old five-eighth is coming off a monster season with London Broncos in the English second division, where he scored 39 tries in 31 games to claim the competition's player of the year award.

He took that good form into this victory, scoring a long range try and creating another with his speed and footwork standing out against a Cedars side with plenty of NRL experience.

Tapping into as much local talent as possible will be crucial and if Voro's improvement continues very well could be one of their early success stories.

4. Powerful Tongan statement a long time coming

Tonga ran roughshod over a disappointing England side. (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre)

Tonga's fourth win over a Tier 1 nation is by far their most dominant — the margin of victory is just one point more than the combined margin of all three previous wins.

Even though they've won just one of their past nine matches, have been building to a dominant performance like this for some time.

All nine of those games were against Australia, England, New Zealand or Samoa, and Tonga are now experience the gain from the pain of those defeats.

Tonga now have one foot in the semi-finals. (Getty Images: Paul Kane )

The attacking cohesion between regulars like Isaiya Katoa, Haumole Olakau'atu and veteran Tui Lolohea was plain to see, as was the defensive combinations that held England to just two tries despite enjoying far better of the field position, and shows that the benefits of regular matches extends beyond than simply winning and losing.

Tonga have hit the ground running but will still have improvement in them. With a semi-final spot essentially at their mercy after this win, it's a good spot to be in.

England, by contrast, have paid the price for the same flaw that cost them in last year's Ashes series — a lack of spark inside the attacking 20. They've scored just 30 points across their past four matches and their inability to strike has them on the verge of their earliest ever World Cup exit.

5. Fiji makes hay while the sun shines

Solomone Saukuru of Fiji scores a try during the 2026 Men's Rugby League World Cup. (Getty Images: Scott Gardiner )

With matches against Australia and New Zealand to come this might be as good as it gets for Fiji in this World Cup but you'd be hard-pressed to find a better day in the sun for the Bati than their opener against the Cook Islands.

After their women's side, the Bulikula, came within a whisker of pulling off a remarkable upset against New Zealand in just their ninth match ever they lined the tunnel to sing the men's team onto the field as they were led out by Fiji legend Akuila Uate carrying the national flag.

It was a potent mix of past and future combining in the present and didn't just Fiji duly responded, they looked good doing it.

Halves Kurt Donogohoe and Brandon Wakeham, who both played in last year's Pacific Bowl tournament together, showed the benefits of their combination with five try assists between them and Manly lock Caleb Navale was excellent in the middle of the field.

There will be harder matches to come but expect Fiji to hold the gloves up.

They haven't played a Tier 1 nation since the last World Cup but they have the talent, experience and cohesion to make Australia sweat for at least a little while.

World.title: Kenyan Ebola cases rise to eight in two weeks
World.content:
An eighth person has tested positive for Ebola in Kenya just over two weeks after the country recorded its first case.

Kenyan Health Ministry director-general Patrick Amoth said the country's eighth case was a 49-year-old person in quarantine who had attended to the first Ebola patient.

That patient died two days after arriving in the country from the Democratic Republic of the Congo via Uganda in early October.

The disease has killed at least 4,000 people in Congo since May in what has become the country's deadliest outbreak.

Ebola is highly contagious and spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person or through contact with contaminated surfaces, such as bedding and clothing.

Up to 128 people, including health workers, identified as contacts of Kenya's first patient remained in quarantine as of Sunday.

Dr Amoth said those quarantined were being tested after developing symptoms. He said six other patients were stable after receiving treatment.

Kenya's first case involved a 40-year-old Kenyan man who travelled from Congo through Uganda, arriving in Kenya on October 3. A relative drove him to the hospital, and he died on October 5.

Three of his close relatives are among those who have tested positive for the virus. Three health workers have also tested positive.

Neighbouring country Tanzania has tightened border screenings and introduced mandatory health declarations and 21-day monitoring for travellers arriving from high-risk countries.

Kenya's first case exposed gaps in screening measures at border points. The country has since strengthened screening and set up an emergency hotline for suspected contacts of Ebola patients or anyone who develops symptoms.

The country has designated a gate at Nairobi's main airport for flights arriving from 10 countries at the centre of the Ebola outbreak.

Congo's fast-moving Ebola outbreak spreads to eighth province

Response efforts are struggling to keep up in Congo where the fastest-growing outbreak of the disease reached an eighth province on Sunday.

Ebola has killed at least 4,000 people in Congo since May. (AP: Sebastien Kitsa Musayi)

Government data shows 66 health zones have been affected since the start of the outbreak.

"We see pockets of Ebola generally going down, but unfortunately geographically it's spreading out," World Health Organization regional director for Africa, Mohamed Yakub Janabi, told AP in an interview in Beni, eastern Congo.

Mr Janabi said health officials were trying to convince infected people to seek medical assistance, adding that some deaths occurred in the community outside of health centres.

Epidemiologist Serge Ngalebato told AP that health workers in the country's north-eastern Wamba health zone had introduced periodic home visits because people were too afraid to go to hospital.

Efforts to contain the virus there were initially met with resistance, but Mr Ngalebato said residents became more understanding and began reporting cases as time went on.

"Ebola is a community disease. If the community does not cooperate, it will be very difficult," he said.

He said most cases reported in his zone were around mining areas where the population moved constantly, causing many deaths.

The spread of the outbreak, caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment, is fuelled by mass population movements, rebel violence, mistrust and poor working conditions of frontline workers.

The Ituri province in eastern Congo remains the disease's epicentre, with almost three quarters of confirmed cases, according to the government health data.

From Monday, authorities in the neighbouring North Kivu province will introduce a one-week-ban on people entering the province from Ituri in an effort to slow the spread, Congo's state news agency ACP reported.

Other measures will include limiting the number of people in a vehicle to no more than two on a motorbike or four in a car, as well as suspending big public gatherings such as sports, nightclubs and political demonstrations.

AP

World.title: Small-scale florists hope to fill gap for romantics in Kununurra
World.content:
There is perhaps no easier, more sure-fire way to brighten a loved one's day than to send a fresh bunch of flowers. That is of course, if they live in a city.

It is a different story for those living in remote towns and communities.

Perth resident Gerald Contreras is acutely aware of this challenge as he now struggles to surprise his partner who lives 3,000 kilometres north of him in Kununurra.

Until recently, one major supplier of flowers serviced the town's permanent population of about 5,500 people.

Gerald Contreras and his partner Cesarina Fitzgerald live 3,000 kilometres apart. (Supplied: Gerald Contreras)

Mr Contreras said he sent his partner flowers at least once every two months, but that ended when the florist business closed.

"Being Kununurra, a very small town, there's not many options to surprise my partner with love gestures," he said.

"Not even anything like ordering a simple meal; so, flowers was one of the very few ways I could show affection, love, and surprise my partner."

End of an era

For three decades Diane and Chris Robinson were the main players in Kununurra when it came to flowers.

They would grow their own blooms when the weather permitted and trucked up flowers from Perth.

"During the wet season, when we can only grow tropical flowers. We did bring flowers from down south and gradually it just turned into all year," Ms Robinson said.

"We can't grow roses … and also the Australian native flowers are not very good here."

While demand was consistent, the pair struggled to find a long-term shop assistant to sell their flowers.

Diane Robinson sold flowers in Kununurra for more than 30 years. (ABC Kimberley: Jess Baker)

With the Robinsons are looking to retire, a decision needed to be made.

"We're going down that retirement path, so they [the flowers] were pretty easy to [let go of] because we couldn't get a florist," Ms Robinson said.

"If we perhaps had somebody that was staying, we wouldn't have shut the shop quite so quickly."

Diane Robinson says growing flowers in Kununurra is interesting, with only tropical flowers able to be grown in the wet season. (ABC Kimberley: Jess Baker)

Selling flowers on smaller scale

Meanwhile, Bianca Brown has begun assembling and supplying flower bouquets while also running an agricultural transport business.

Ms Brown said she wanted to fill a gap in the market.

"Already I'm at the point where I probably could put somebody else on and I'll probably look at scaling up next year and seeing where it goes," she said.

Ms Brown was sourcing flowers locally and from Perth, and was looking forward to seeing what types of flowers she could grow herself.

Bianca Brown recently started selling floral arrangements in Kununurra. (Supplied: Bianca Brown)

Mr Contreras said he was eager to use Ms Brown's flower delivery service.

"Beyond text messages and calls and video dates, I'm keen to try the new florist who is in a much smaller capacity," he said.

"When I did surprise my partner by flying up I was looking all over town for flowers, and couldn't find any, even in person.

"But the florist did restock the next day with a small amount of flowers. I think I bought almost half the stock."

Sophie Cooke's outback flower patch is open to the public on Saturday dry season mornings. (ABC Kimberley: Jess Baker)

There is one other option to buy blooms in the remote town, but only in the dry season and on Saturdays.

Sophie Cooke lets people visit her family farm and pick flowers themselves to buy.

Ms Cooke said her customers mostly bought flowers for their homes, but also visited the patch for special occasions.

She said a number of residents had started arranging flowers to meet the town's needs, but there was scope to grow more flowers and the industry.

World.title: Cindy Crawford 'beyond heartbroken' to lose son Presley Gerber
World.content:
American supermodel Cindy Crawford has posted a tribute on social media to her son Presley Gerber, who recently died aged 27.

"We are beyond heartbroken to lose our beloved son and brother," Crawford's Instagram post said.

"We feel so blessed to have had Presley in our lives for 27 years. He is a sweet, beautiful soul who loved and is loved, now and forever."

Loading Instagram content

The 27-year-old was Crawford's only son with her businessman husband, Rande Gerber, and the older brother of model-actor Kaia.

Gerber died in September at a rehab facility, according to the Los Angeles County Medical Examiner.

Crawford thanked fans for their support, saying: "We are grateful for the outpouring of love and support from so many who know and love our family and even strangers who feel our pain."

Sister, Kaia Gerber, also posted a tribute to "Prez" shortly afterwards.

"You know how much I loved being your sister. It has always been, and will forever be, my favourite thing about myself," she said.

" You believed people were inherently good because, Presley, you are inherently good. "

Presley Gerber worked on campaigns and did runway shows for brands such as Calvin Klein and Dolce & Gabbana.

In 2018, he appeared alongside his mother in Pepsi's Super Bowl LII commercial.

Kaia Gerber posted on Instagram about her brother. (Supplied: Kaia Gerber)

He had previously opened up about his struggles with mental health.

In an Instagram post last November, he said he started a series called Mental health Mondays, saying: "The goal was to spark real conversations about the stuff most people hide."

In August, his sister Kaia, spoke about her brother's struggles in an interview with Vogue magazine.

When something like that happens in a family, it "kind of levels everyone", she said.

ABC/Reuters

World.title: Inside the 'ghost city' designed to become Indonesia's new capital
World.content:
Loading...

Carved into the rainforests of Borneo, a brand-new city is taking shape.

It features a presidential palace, modern offices, residential towers and wide, open roads.

Loading...

This is Nusantara, the futuristic city designed to become Indonesia's new capital.

But there is one big problem.

Loading...

The city is quiet. Almost too quiet.

It was designed to hold 1.2 million people by 2029. So far, only about 10,000 have moved in.

Indonesia has spent billions on building a new capital. But there are fears the world's fourth-largest country's bet may not pay off.

Nusantara stands in stark contrast to Indonesia's current capital, Jakarta.

The heaving metropolis, home to nearly 42 million people, was last year declared the world's most populous city, overtaking Tokyo to secure the title.

Jakarta's issues are well documented. It is notorious for its poor air quality and its heavily congested traffic, which is among the worst in the world.

There are also concerns about overcrowding: Greater Jakarta has 1.5 times as many people as Australia, living in a space about 1,200 times smaller than Australia's landmass.

But the city's biggest problem is that it is sinking.

Loading...

In 2025, Jakarta overtook Tokyo to become the world's most populous city, with 42 million residents, according to UN estimates. ( )

Jakarta is infamous for its bumper-to-bumper traffic and hours-long traffic jams. ( )

Behind the towering office and residential complexes, many of Jakarta's inhabitants eke out a living in makeshift communities like this. ( )

About 40 per cent of Jakarta sits below sea level, with a sea wall in the city's north serving as a line of defence against tidal floods.

But parts of the north still regularly flood in the rainy season.

There have been many proposals over the decades to move Indonesia's capital, stretching as far back as the 1950s.

But in 2019, former president Joko Widodo, known commonly as Jokowi, made the ambitious call to build a glittering new capital city deep in the jungle of Borneo.

Utopia in the jungle

Much of the thick jungle that covered the Nusantara site was cleared to make way for the new city. ( )

The city of IKN, or Nusantara, is more than 1,200 kilometres from Jakarta, in the province of East Kalimantan.

Nusantara is seen as somewhat of a legacy project for Jokowi, who was highly popular during his time as president.

It was pitched as the true centre of Indonesia's thousands of islands and an engine for future economic growth.

It was also expected to wrest control from the Java-centric decision-makers of Jakarta.

Construction began on the forest city in 2022, with the aim of it becoming a hub for 1.9 million people by Indonesia's 100th anniversary in 2045.

It was expected to cost about $45 billion.

In 2024, Jokowi celebrated Indonesia's Independence Day at the newly constructed palace in Nusantara, after the city had been partially inaugurated and named as the new capital.

But a lot can change in two years.

One man's legacy is another's debt

Former leader Joko Widodo poses for a selfie with President Prabowo Subianto. ( )

Jokowi spent about 43 trillion IDR — roughly $3.5 billion — on Nusantara in 2024.

But after President Prabowo Subianto took office, the annual budget for the city was slashed to 13 trillion IDR in 2025 and again to 6.3 trillion IDR in 2026.

Prabowo had pitched himself as a president who would continue Jokowi's agenda, but analysts have observed a widening rift between the two men.

He has shifted large portions of the budget to his signature policies, including a nationwide school meals program, and has not spoken much about Nusantara's development.

During the 2025 State of the Nation address, Prabowo mentioned it once. This year, he did not speak about it at all.

A report in Agence France-Presse last year quoted an anonymous official involved in the construction of Nusantara, saying "Prabowo feels that this is not his legacy."

President Prabowo Subianto has been pursuing his own signature projects in recent years. ( )

When Prabowo visited Nusantara early this year, he stayed just one night in the city.

He has signed a presidential regulation that aims to make Nusantara the "political capital" by 2028, to coincide with the completion of official buildings.

But Indonesia's Constitutional Court ruled this year that Jakarta would remain the official capital until Prabowo signs an additional presidential decree.

That decision prompted considerable discussion.

Would Nusantara become a definitive new capital for 2 million Indonesians? Would it simply become a hub for different branches of government?

Or might it be abandoned in 2028, in the lead-up to a 2029 election?

Living in a political experiment

Ranty Wiyati is adjusting to her new life in Nusantara but is optimistic about the city's potential. ( )

While the wider Nusantara area, which includes dozens of villages and sub-districts, has a population of 147,000, far fewer live in the inner core of the newly developed city.

The brand-new residential towers dotted around Nusantara are home to about 1,800 public servants and defence and security personnel.

The ABC received permission to visit Nusantara from the Nusantara Capital Authority, or OIKN, which manages the development of the city.

For young OIKN worker Ranty Wiyati, living in Nusantara is a big change of pace from the bustling streets of Jakarta.

"You can't deny that it is [quiet]," she said.

"It might not be as busy as Jakarta, and there aren't as many entertainment options, but that's better for our mental health.

"We get creative with ways to stay off social media … we do things like journalling, chatting, holding book clubs."

OIKN is hiring young workers like Ranty to move to Nusantara, while government departments have been slowly transferring workers to the city.

Traffic lights and new facilities wait for the arrival of hundreds of thousands of new residents to Nusantara. ( )

Relocating young government workers to Nusantara may help others follow. ( )

Civil servants make up the majority of permanent residents in Nusantara. ( )

"I chose Nusantara because I thought it would be a new living laboratory for Indonesia," Ranty said, echoing language used by OIKN's chief Basuki Hadimuljono.

"We're hoping that more public servants can be relocated here soon to make the place a bit livelier."

The ABC met Ranty at one of the handful of coffee shops in Nusantara, before taking an electric bus that runs on a loop through the city, passing several hospitals and two hotels.

Shopping centres are slated to be built in the coming years.

Nusantara has attracted some tourists but few Indonesians have decided to make the new capital home. ( )

At an outlook in the city, tourists were singing the city's praises.

The ambitious project is a source of great national pride for Indonesians like Darmiyah. ( )

"Seeing this makes me feel really proud," Darmiyah, from South Kalimantan, said.

Yuda is among a handful of Indonesian tourists keen to see the splendour of the new capital. ( )

"We took a bus for about 12 hours," Yuda, also from South Kalimantan, said.

"The development is really grand. It makes total sense for this to be the national capital moving forward."

Ranty can drink water straight from the taps in her apartment thanks to the filtration systems installed across the city, something almost impossible to do in Jakarta without risking getting sick.

Nusantara is also aiming to be much greener than Jakarta, thanks to compulsory recycling and monitoring of water and electricity use.

"It's a real shame when people call this a ghost city, or talk like that in the media," Ranty said.

"Nusantara is a great opportunity, especially for the younger generation, to build something more ideal from the ground up.

"While we know there aren't many here right now, once the president moves here, that'll be a major turning point."

But while those inside Nusantara remain optimistic, some in Jakarta wonder whether the project will pay off.

Fears new city could become 'white elephant'

The imposing Garuda Palace is the centrepiece of the new administrative capital. ( )

The $45 billion for Jokowi's vision was expected to be covered by 80 per cent private investment, along with 20 per cent government spending.

CELIOS economist Bhima Yudhistira said investor appetite remained low due to geopolitical conditions, rising interest rates and policy risks.

"Nusantara risks becoming a 'white elephant' — an expensive project with minimal impact," he said.

"[It] could end up as a stranded asset, as the state budget may only suffice for basic building maintenance."

He said Prabowo's lack of commitment and his rift with Jokowi meant the project was now a "political gamble."

Public policy expert Agus Pambagio said funding cuts and the court decision had also slowed progress.

"It's developing, but it's not as fast as before," Agus said.

"These are different political parties, different people under the presidents … the style of leadership is different."

Agus doubts Nusantara will be Indonesia's capital by 2028, but OIKN officials remain confident.

"As the old saying goes, the dogs bark, but the caravan moves on," OIKN deputy Dr Alimuddin said.

"To this day, we have full support from the government.

"Does the government need to say in the media, 'We support this?' That's not necessary."

"What matters most is not talking, but keeping the financial support and construction running smoothly."

The network of wide boulevards that bisects the new city still remain largely devoid of traffic. ( )

Life in Nusantara's new apartment buildings is a far cry from the crowded and chaotic conditions of Jakarta. ( )

OIKN Deputy Dr Alimuddin rejects suggestions that Nusantara won't become the new capital. ( )

OIKN said private investors had so far committed $6 billion to Nusantara, and that another $10 billion had come from public-private partnerships.

A lot of people are eagerly awaiting 2028 to see whether Prabowo will issue that presidential decree making Nusantara the political capital.

As construction continues, an enormous steel sculpture shaped like Indonesia's national symbol, the Garuda, a winged, mythical eagle-like bird, watches over the city.

The next year will be a pivotal one for local and foreign investors.

Will Nusantara live up to the original dream of a thriving, populated forest city — or will the massive Garuda remain a mighty monument to a failed legacy project?

World.title: Nothing left to loot: Parisians ponder the real cost of another night of riots
World.content:
Protesters set up barricades and start fires near Place de la Republique in central Paris on Sunday.

On these smouldering streets, there’s still some sympathy with the protesters’ original demands. But it’s hard to escape the sense that these riots reflect a modern France facing troubled times.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Paris: The young men gather in the city square as if it is just another Sunday afternoon in the French capital, but they wear the uniform of the rioters who ransacked the streets the previous night. Most wear black hoodies, black sports pants, and black balaclavas. A few have ski masks over their foreheads, just in case they need to cover their eyes. They are ready for tear gas. We are in the Place de la Republique on the day after the worst French riots in recent memory, when mobs stormed through the streets to loot shops, torch cars and smash windows. And the unrest is not over because the protesters are back to assert their control of this historic square. A burnt car sits at the side of the square, not far from a burnt truck. A classic French kiosk, the sort of place you buy a chocolate and a newspaper, is now a blackened ruin. Police charge at protesters in the Place de la Republique in Paris on Saturday. Getty I have just walked past a smashed florist, a wrecked shoe store and a bottle shop that has been stripped bare and now reeks of the wine spilt from broken bottles. But I also see a group of volunteers cleaning up the rubbish around the towering monument in the middle of the square, a statue that symbolises the French Republic.



A firefighter tackles a street fire during violence on Sunday. AP Photo/Emma Da Silva One woman, Alice Boucheron, tells me she thinks many of the protesters were motivated by real problems, like the cost of living, but too many were intent on destruction. And she is angry at what they have done. Those engaging in looting and arson are the real problem, says Alice Boucheron. David Crowe “I’m really proud to be a French citizen,” she says. “So I want to clean up everything. I think that’s very important because when we clean up like this, it’s a demonstration too.” Boucheron, 33, has come in from her home just outside Paris to be here. She worries that politicians and the media will misrepresent the images from the protests. Parisian Samuel Lugassy said the previous night’s scenes felt like a “civil war”. David Crowe “We are projecting a very poor image to the world, when in reality the French people simply wanted to share their grievances,” she says.



“The real problem lies with those who engage in destruction, arson and looting.” Samuel Lugassy, a chiropractor who lives nearby, feels the previous night was like a “civil war” in parts of France. He is shocked and angry at what took place. Another pedestrian, Raphael Christophe, is about to leave for his home in Limoges, the town in the south where vandals burnt the historic town hall. He is watching the young men in balaclavas, worried about more violence. Limoges protesters set fire to the town hall in the city of Limoges in the Nouvelle-Aquitaine region of France. Hans Lucas via AFP “Look – they are ready,” he says. “They have their masks.” He is right. The group is expanding. It has outnumbered the volunteers trying to clean up the square, and it has drawn supporters displaying Palestinian and Algerian flags. Some of the group climb up the statue, as if asserting ownership of all they see. The statue is smothered with graffiti criticising Israel, the police, President Emmanuel Macron and the right-wing National Rally led by Marine Le Pen.



Protesters have repeatedly defaced the statue at the centre of Paris’ Place de la Republique David Crowe The police arrive to disperse the crowd shortly after 2.30pm. Officers with riot shields and batons advance through the square to try to force the protesters out, but it is not easy because this precinct is so busy with people who seem oblivious to the tensions. Pedestrians emerge from the Republique metro station. A jogger runs through the crowd. A group of tourists passes by on hire bikes. The crowd chants at the police, showing that the protest movement has the numbers in this square. Suddenly, the temperature rises when the police encircle a group of protesters and lead them away. A few people in the crowd start throwing things at the authorities, and they get canisters of tear gas in response. Most people start running as soon as the acrid smoke rises, knowing it will sting their eyes and burn their throats. The protests began as a response to poor conditions in schools but have spiralled into a wider movement. Anadolu via Getty Images While the protests began as rallies about school standards, the clashes in the Place de la Republique are mostly a test of strength between agitators and police. The leaders of the crowd set fire to bikes on a street, and are then dispersed by police. They put up barricades across the main boulevard to disrupt the traffic, and are dispersed with another volley of tear gas. Every action is dominated by men in their late teens and early 20s, almost all wearing their black uniforms. Young women can also be seen in the crowd, but they are in the minority among those provoking the police.



When the masks are lowered, the faces reflect modern France: the skin tones are white, black and brown. But the white faces are relatively rare. The crowd is overwhelmingly made up of young men who are new to France or born to migrant families, although there is no time to stop and ask whether their French citizenship goes back one, two, three or more generations. Loading This is a delicate subject because of the argument about whether the riots in France are caused by migration. Donald Trump insists they are; his critics say they are not. The debate about causation is surely complex. But it is important to be honest about the reality on the streets, rather than waving away what is obvious to every passer-by in Paris. Related Article Political unrest Macron addresses nation after riots, looting as Trump blames migration The streets around the Place de la Republique are full of young men from migrant backgrounds who seemed primed for confrontations with authority. They try to test the police, then retreat and scatter into small groups. In one moment they are protesters, in the next they look like bystanders. The confrontations continue into the night, and there is some opportunistic looting. Two men clamber out of a homewares store carrying brand new wheelie-bags; two boys then try to climb over the broken sheet glass to see if they can find something for themselves. If a store is not already looted, it is at least protected. Some have security guards sitting inside, watching the crowd pass by, or have metal shutters lowered. The looted stores are marked by plywood sheets to replace their broken windows.

World.title: Sydney man allegedly discussed plans for childcare mass shooting with AI chatbot
World.content:
NationalNSWCrime Sydney man allegedly discussed plans for childcare mass shooting with AI chatbot Riley Walter and Perry Duffin October 19, 2026 — 12:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A Sydney man threatened to carry out a mass shooting at a childcare centre in the city’s south during a conversation with a popular AI chatbot during which he referenced alleged Bondi Beach terrorist Naveed Akram, a court has heard. David Lan Thackray was on Monday remanded in custody for a mental health assessment after Sutherland Local Court heard the 29-year-old told Claude, an AI-powered chatbot, that he planned to shoot several children at a childcare centre near his Hurstville home. Thackray was on Sunday morning arrested after Interpol flagged his interactions with the chatbot and charged with using a carriage service to menace, harass or offend. Prosecutors arguing to keep Thackray behind bars on Monday said there would be a “catastrophic” outcome if he was released and breached bail conditions imposed. “What he intends to do is start murdering people in Sydney just like the [alleged] terrorist did in Bondi,” prosecutors told the court.



“We’re understanding what’s in his mind with his interactions with the chatbot.” Naveed Akram remains in custody charged with murdering 15 innocent people and injuring dozens of others during an attack on the Chanukah by the Sea event at Bondi Beach last December. His father, Sajid Akram, was killed in the attack. ‘What he intends to do is start murdering people in Sydney just like the [alleged] terrorist did in Bondi.’ The prosecution in court According to a police facts sheet tendered to the court, Thackray allegedly told the chatbot he would “go down to the local Westfield right now and shoot up the local daycare”. Thackray’s lawyer, Danilo Rajkovic, told the court his client had gone on a stress and frustration- induced tirade after trying to use the Claude platform to help treat an ear infection.



“There was no weight behind what he was saying,” Rajkovic said. Thackray did not instruct the chatbot to issue threats to any person or organisation and believed he was having the interaction in the privacy of his own home, Rajkovic said. Thackray had been using Claude’s voice mode, which allows users to have spoken conversations with the chatbot, the court heard. After receiving an email informing him that his Claude account had been suspended, Thackray requested to have the suspension reviewed. Thackray, who is studying international relations, has no criminal history and has lived in Australia for more than 17 years, Rajkovic said. Rajkovic said his client was confident detectives who seized his electronic devices on Sunday would find no evidence of radical indoctrination or ideological motivation.



Thackray will return to court pending the outcome of a mental health assessment. Claude is an “AI assistant for life and work”, according to the platform’s website. Anthropic, the developer of Claude, has been contacted for comment. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘That’s so savage’: Accused killer allegedly broke into TV presenter’s home hours after rejection
World.content:
NationalNSWLamarre-Condon trial ‘That’s so savage’: Accused killer allegedly broke into TV presenter’s home hours after rejection Michaela Whitbourn October 19, 2026 — 12:46pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Accused double murderer Beau Lamarre-Condon allegedly broke into Jesse Baird’s home and stole his mobile phone hours after the then TV presenter rebuffed his suggestion of a catchup, a court has heard. Lamarre-Condon, 31, is standing trial on two counts of murder over the shooting deaths of Jesse Baird, 26, a former Network Ten producer and presenter, and Luke Davies, 29, a Qantas flight attendant, in February 2024. The former NSW police officer has pleaded not guilty to the charges. Beau Lamarre-Condon sent screenshots of the text exchange with Luke Davies to a friend, the court heard. Six months before the men’s deaths, Lamarre-Condon allegedly broke into Baird’s Paddington share house and stole his wallet and mobile phone. He has also pleaded not guilty to this charge. The accused’s NSW Supreme Court trial heard on Monday that he texted Baird at 7.27pm on August 16, 2023: “Hey, sorry I had to run yesterday. I was running a tad late or I would have loved to chat for longer.



“Let’s do a walk and lunch catchup next weekend ... then we can have a proper catchup. Good seeing you though.” Baird replied at 1.49pm the following day: “It was good to see you too and glad you had fun in Euro.” Lamarre-Condon sent a screenshot of the messages to his then friend, the now senior constable Dana Schagen, who replied: “OMG. I’m dying. That’s so savage. No, it’s defs savage. “If he was keen, he would have jumped on the bandwagon.” Asked what she meant, Schagen told the court: “It’s quite evident from the text messages that Jesse had absolutely no interest in catching up with the accused at all.



“His response is the equivalent of a thumbs up. There’s no follow up to catch up with him.” Schagen texted Lamarre-Condon on August 19 to ask if he had heard back from Baird after this. Beau Lamarre-Condon is accused of breaking into Jesse Baird’s home six months before murdering him. “Yes I did hear back from him,” Lamarre-Condon replied on August 21. “He had a home invasion so he couldn’t text me that as his phone got stolen but we are catching up next Wednesday night for dinner. He said he full chased after the guy too.”



Schagen texted: “But managed to send the first message back? I don’t get it.” Lamarre-Condon replied: “Yes, because it happened after that. He isn’t lying.” Prosecutor Caitlin Diggins asked Schagen: “Did the accused tell you that he was the person Jesse had to chase out?” “No,” Schagen replied. The court heard that Lamarre-Condon called Schagen on March 28, more than a month after the alleged murders on February 19, using a friend’s mobile phone, and said: “I just wanted to tell you that I love you, and before you do anything, you need to know not everything in the news is true.



Related Article Lamarre-Condon trial Lamarre-Condon’s celebrity-chasing friend tells trial about ‘concerning’ phone request “It’ll come out in court.” Schagen said she cut off the accused and said: “You killed two people. Why would you think I would ever want to speak to you again?” She hung up and reported the phone call to her boss, the court heard. The Crown alleges Lamarre-Condon broke into Baird’s home and stole his mobile phone and wallet while Baird was home on August 17, 2023. He has pleaded not guilty to this charge. The defence case is that he used a key Baird had given him to enter the home.



Baird reported the alleged break-in at the time, the court has heard, and said he had woken shortly before midnight to a man standing over his bed. Investigating police took a photo of a bobby pin in the lock of Baird’s home, tendered in evidence in the trial. Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield, SC, alleged in his opening address to the 15-person jury that Lamarre-Condon used a key he had “stolen or surreptitiously copied to enter before putting a bobby pin in the door to give the impression that the lock on the door was picked”. It was “some six months before the two murder counts”, Hatfield said. “A wallet containing cash and ID was later found, having been discarded,” he said. “The phone was never recovered.”



The court has heard that Lamarre-Condon and Baird had a casual relationship that started in late 2022 and ended for the first time in April 2023, before they briefly reconnected in September. The Crown alleges Lamarre-Condon killed Baird after developing an “obsessive and jealous infatuation” with him that escalated when Baird ended their casual relationship permanently in November 2023. The prosecution alleges the then NSW police officer shot Davies, Baird’s new boyfriend, to eliminate a witness to his crime. The defence case is that Lamarre-Condon entered Baird’s share house disguised as a delivery rider to retrieve some of his belongings. According to the defence, a struggle ensued in which his police gun went off twice, killing Baird, and Davies shot himself accidentally in a second struggle. The accused had his Glock pistol with him because he was trained not to leave it unattended, the defence has said. The Crown has said he should not have had the weapon because he was not rostered to work that day.



The trial continues. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491. World.title: VietJet’s domestic ambitions dealt a blow after court orders global asset freeze
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesAviation VietJet’s domestic ambitions dealt a blow after court orders global asset freeze Chris Zappone October 19, 2026 — 12:46pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Low-cost carrier VietJet’s hopes of expanding into Australia’s domestic market have hit a snag, after the United Kingdom High Court granted an order to freeze the carrier’s assets as part of a fight with a hedge fund seeking to recover debts. FW Aviation, an aircraft leasing company registered in Jersey, secured court orders against the airline for $US250 million ($360 million) for four Airbus A321s in London late last week. Vietjet inaugural Ho Chi Minh City to Sydney flight in 2023. The order follows a long-running battle by a private investment fund FitzWalter Capital, which controls FW Aviation, to get the Vietnam-based VietJet to pay for the use of the four planes. UK courts have ordered three judgments against VietJet, for $18.8 million (in 2024), $182 million (in 2025) and $18.3 million (in a third trial), with the airline making a partial $2 million payment in 2025.



In the latest case, the business and property division of Britain’s High Court heard how VietJet has resisted paying, and even halted flights of aircraft to Singapore where they would have been seized under court orders. “In October 2021, following VietJet’s continuing failure to pay rent for its use of the aircraft (during the COVID lockdowns), the lenders served notices on VietJet seeking to terminate the sub-lease agreements,” the court ruling reads. “Shortly thereafter, FWA acquired all rights formerly held by the lenders,” which included the right to recover sums owed under sub-lease agreements and custody and control of the aircraft, the court said. Vietjet flight attendants dressed in bikinis. Justice Pushpinder Saini found that VietJet’s actions constituted a “risk of dissipation”, or danger that a defendant will hide, transfer, or sell assets before a court judgment can be enforced.



This masthead understands the prospect of legal judgments against VieJet would likely complicate its bid to receive permission to operate as a domestic airline. VietJet has been approached for comment. Related Article Aviation Western Sydney Airport makes play for premium travellers The low-cost carrier has applied to the Civil Aviation Safety Authority (CASA) for an air operator’s certificate, which would allow it to operate on domestic routes in Australia. It’s expected to operate up to 10 Boeing 737s on routes between Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane, under the name Cherrie Air. CASA has been approached for comment. Vietjet, which was Vietnam’s first privately owned airline when it began flying in 2011, has made network expansion a priority, operating divisions in Thailand and as far away as Kazakhstan.



The company has previously raised eyebrows for stunts featuring women dressed only in bikinis. VietJet is also expected to become the third international airline offering flights from Western Sydney International – after Air New Zealand and Singapore Airlines. It’s slated to begin flying between Western Sydney and Ho Chi Minh City on 10 January 2027, operating two return services per week, on Wednesdays and Sundays. It’s website shows prices for those flights from WSI to Ho Chi Minh ranging for $411 to $34. VietJet’s international arm – based out of Vietnam – currently operates daily return flights to Ho Chi Minh City from Sydney and Melbourne. Brisbane and Perth are connected to Ho Chi Minh City with five and three weekly return flights, respectively. World.title: Crisafulli accuses federal government of siege on small business
World.content:
PoliticsQueenslandQueensland government Crisafulli accuses federal government of siege on small business Julius Dennis October 19, 2026 — 12:13pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Queensland Premier David Crisafulli has accused the Albanese government of launching a siege on small business following the botched credit card surcharge ban, proposed cuts to worker holiday visas and reforming trust taxes. The end of the week will mark two years for the LNP state government, tipping it into the second half of its four-year term as it faces recent scrutiny over child safety concerns and its commitment to drastically cut ambulance ramping at hospitals. David Crisafulli approaches the halfway mark of the parliamentary term. AAPIMAGE While much of Monday’s speech to business leaders at a Centre for Economic Development Australia breakfast was spent on previously covered ground, Crisafulli doubled down on challenging Canberra over an “inbuilt injustice in Queensland”. Key among his gripes was his view the state receives an unfair cut of the GST pie, echoing a call from Treasurer David Janetzki for a distribution rethink.



“We’ve reached a point in the GST distribution where Western Australia has cut out an amazing deal, and I don’t begrudge that … but the beneficiary has been the states that haven’t been prepared to do the hard yards,” he said. “Somehow we are viewed as big enough to stand on our own two feet, unlike the west, but small enough that we have to cop all the bad news. “We’re not getting the upside Victoria and New South Wales get, and we have to call it out.” Earlier in the speech, Crisafulli had vowed not to use the address as a “pressure relief valve”, but the back end focused heavily on the actions of the federal government. Besides GST, Crisafulli said the removal of card surcharges at check-out and the Tax Office’s call to disallow credit card payments on tax debt, changes to how trusts were taxed, and potential changes to worker holiday visas, amounted to a siege on small businesses.





In his typical mild exasperation, Crisafulli insisted his government’s wish to mine fossil fuels while cancelling renewables projects it saw as fanciful was about economics, not ideology. “I don’t understand how we got to this point in this country where every time we talk about energy it has to be some kind of ideological war, some kind of arm wrestle where people from both camps yell at each other,” he said. With the Olympics and all the associated infrastructure, if the government could find a middle road, a “golden age” awaited for Queensland, the premier said. World.title: $300,000 on coffee: Yarra Trams’ contracts and conflicts spur whistleblower alarm
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsVictoriaTrams $300,000 on coffee: Yarra Trams’ contracts and conflicts spur whistleblower alarm Clay Lucas Updated October 19, 2026 — 12:06pm ,first published October 19, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items.
