Yarra Trams executives face accusations from senior staff of financial mismanagement and inappropriate handling of conflicts of interest, amid a raft of job losses at the public transport operator. A whistleblower report submitted to the company’s management in April by Yarra Trams’ head of procurement operations alleges millions of dollars in unusual advance payments to vendors, in a late financial-year scramble to avoid penalties for missing social procurement targets. Yarra Trams executives are facing accusations of financial mismanagement and inappropriate handling of conflicts of interest. Matt Davidson An internal investigation into the allegations was launched immediately by the company’s senior lawyer – only for the lawyer, the whistleblower and four other procurement staff to be made redundant before it was completed. The Age can also reveal that the Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission interviewed at least one other former employee, separate from the whistleblower, regarding the same allegations.



The two separate interventions come amid a tumultuous round of job losses at the company just two years into its nine-year, $7 billion state government contract to run Melbourne’s tram network. Since taking over in December 2024, a joint venture between global transport giant Transdev and big builder John Holland has made 36 employees redundant – most from Yarra Trams’ Bourke Street head office. Related Article Updated

Public transport New operator to take over Melbourne tram network Yarra Trams’ contract includes a requirement to spend a proportion of its budget with firms providing social benefits, including Aboriginal employment, disability employment, and gender equality initiatives. The operator faces penalties of up to $1.5 million a year if it misses the contractual benchmarks. The Age has spoken with 13 current and former Yarra Trams staff about the matters contained in the whistleblower complaint and report to IBAC. Though unwilling to speak publicly about the confidential material, all asserted the matters raised were legitimate.



The whistleblower alleges, in a 34-page report, that millions of dollars of contracts were inappropriately fast-tracked last June to avoid financial penalties. The arrangements include large advance payments for security services, espresso machines and barista training, and personal protective equipment. The whistleblower was concerned the process meant appropriate services were potentially not procured. “Obligations relating to social procurement are designed to deliver outcomes for disadvantaged Victorians through the channelling of public expenditure into enterprises that deliver jobs and development,” the report stated. “Proper process would have been to set evaluation criteria for the required service and give favourable weighting to suppliers who can show social outcomes.” Instead, emails, invoices and payment receipts show a last-minute effort by Yarra Trams management to hit strict social procurement spending targets before the financial year ended. To avoid fines in its contract, called “abatements”, senior executives authorised a rush of advance payments to social vendors before June 30 – logging the spending on paper to clear contractual benchmarks.



Internal correspondence reveals executives authorising payments – including $500,000 to a security provider, $300,000 for the “design, development and manufacture of [a] custom uniform”, and a $300,000 coffee deal for espresso machines to be installed in offices. A June 2025 invoice shows Yarra Trams issuing a $500,000 advance payment to a “social outcomes security group”. The security company asked for questions to be directed to Yarra Trams. A $300,000 purchase order shows money being paid to a uniform company that had not even developed the product at the time of purchase; a spokeswoman said the company had since delivered 2000 high-visibility vests, “with work undertaken at our North Melbourne manufacturing facility” that provided “employment opportunities for refugee and asylum seeker women”. Yarra Trams also entered into a deal with a coffee supplier that donates a share of it profits to charity. It supplied the tram operator’s offices with espresso machines, beans, and maintenance. Internal records show an overall contract value of $300,000, with more than $10,000 dedicated to “barista training”. The coffee company declined to respond to questions.



In a May 2025 email chain discussing the strategy, Yarra Trams’ chief financial and commercial officer Marc Walter approved the initiative, writing in response: “This is approved to proceed. No further approvals required to commence.” It is not suggested that Walter endorsed any inappropriate spending to hit the target – only that he told staff they could proceed with the contracts. The whistleblower report questions whether using public franchise funds to prepay for coffee machines and undeveloped products represented genuine value for money or was simply complying with state government social procurement rules to avoid fines. It also details the January appointment of a Brisbane-based consultant for $2000 a day. The Age has seen the contract confirming the wage, plus flights to and from his Queensland base.



The executive who hired the consultant also submitted a conflict-of-interest form acknowledging the consultant previously reported to him at mining company BHP. The form’s proposed conflict-of-interest management plan was left blank, but CFO Marc Walter countersigned the document. Responding to the allegations, a Yarra Trams spokeswoman said that all procurement processes were subject to strict probity requirements. “We have reviewed these matters and are satisfied the procurement and workforce-related decisions were subject to the relevant approval and oversight processes,” she said. She said Commonwealth legislation prevented Yarra Trams from commenting on “potential whistleblower matters”.



On corporate job cuts, the company stated that while 36 roles were made redundant, its total workforce had expanded by approximately 120 roles since December 2024. Addressing specific vendor contracts, the operator said procurement decisions were made “based on operational requirements, value for money and contractual obligations”. The company defended the coffee contract as “a trial of a managed coffee-service model, including coffee machines, coffee supplies, maintenance and training services. The coffee machines have been installed and are operational”. On the engagement of its Queensland consultant, the operator said the hire was approved through internal governance processes for “specialist procurement transformation” work.



The two annual reports filed with financial regulators since Transdev and John Holland took over Melbourne’s tram operations show the joint venture has so far made profits of $38.5 million, receiving payments from the state government of $1.254 billion – a 3 per cent return. Asked about Yarra Trams and its contract management practices, a spokesman for the Victorian government said: “This is a matter for Yarra Trams. All of our transport operators must adhere to strict probity and procurement processes consistent with their contractual obligations.”

World.title: Meet the new Kerrigans: The Castle stage show’s cast revealed
World.content:
CultureTheatreArts Meet the new Kerrigans: The Castle stage show’s cast revealed Michael Lallo October 19, 2026 — 12:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The wait is over: the actors bringing Australia’s most beloved fictional family to the stage have been revealed. On Monday, producers Michael Cassel and Working Dog unveiled the principal cast of The Castle On Stage, the upcoming adaptation of the classic 1997 film. The cast of The Castle On Stage: Ed Oxenbould as Dale, Marcus McKenzie as Steve, Christie Whelan Browne as Sal, Joel Jackson as Wayne, Justin Smith as Darryl, Roman Delo as Con, and Stephanie Graham as Tracey. Simon Schluter Loveable patriarch Darryl Kerrigan will be played by veteran actor Justin Smith (Heartbreak High, Wentworth), whose first professional role was in the 1992 Australian tour of Jesus Christ Superstar. Darryl’s wife – the sweet-natured culinary whiz, Sal – will be portrayed by Christie Whelan Browne, one of Australia’s most highly regarded performers on stage (Muriel’s Wedding the Musical, Singin’ in the Rain) and screen (Shaun Micallef’s Mad as Hell). “The hardest part about playing Sal is playing a woman whose family enjoys her cooking,” Whelan Browne said.



When asked why Darryl and Sal are one of Australia’s favourite fictional couples, Whelan Browne said, “I think they both feel like they’ve got the better deal. It’s quite simple: everything she does, he thinks is amazing, and vice versa.” Making his professional theatre debut, Ed Oxenbould (Puberty Blues, Paper Planes) is Dale: the youngest of the four Kerrigan children and a proud digger of holes, who also serves as the play’s narrator. “Dale [still resonates with audiences] because his optimism never goes out of style,” Oxenbould said. The cast of the hit 1997 film The Castle: Anthony Simcoe, Anne Tenney, Michael Caton, Sophie Lee, Eric Bana, Wayne Hope and Stephen Curry. Joel Jackson (Deadline Gallipoli, Peter Allen: Not the Boy Next Door) is Wayne, the eldest son and model prisoner; while contemporary theatre performer Marcus McKenzie is Steve, a bargain hunter and self-taught “ideas man”. Recent WAAPA graduate Stephanie Graham is the Kerrigan family’s only daughter, Tracey; and Roman Delo (Bump, NCIS: Sydney) is her kickboxing-enthusiast husband, Con Petropoulous. To say that Australians are enthusiastic about the stage version of The Castle – a David and Goliath battle between the Kerrigan family and a greedy consortium attempting to “compulsory acquire” their home – is an understatement. In May, readers of this masthead voted The Castle Australia’s favourite movie of all time. In July, the film’s creators, Working Dog, announced they had partnered with renowned producer Michael Cassel to bring the story to Her Majesty’s Theatre in Melbourne, where it will make its world premiere in March 2027.



Related Article Stage shows Australia’s favourite comedy is coming to the stage? Tell ’em they’re not dreamin’ Just 24 hours after tickets went on sale, the production broke a box office record, achieving the highest first-day sales for any play in Her Majesty’s history. Within a week, producers extended the season due to extraordinary demand – and on Monday, they announced a second extension, meaning the show will run until at least mid-May. In the movie, the Kerrigans relied on landline telephones, The Trading Post newspaper and Australian-made cars. The play will instead be set in the present day, where Wi-Fi, smartphones and electric vehicles are ubiquitous. But the central plot – and its heartwarming “vibe” – remain unchanged. Smith believes that in some ways, the story’s premise is more relevant than ever. “Look at something like Robodebt, where the everyman has been shafted by the powers that be,” he said. Whelan Browne said she and Smith were drawing on their own experiences as parents. “There’s a moment in the show where we look at each other and well up with tears every night,” she said, becoming misty-eyed. “We’re simply talking about how much we love our kids, and that’s how Justin and I both come at it – there’s a real joy in coming into this optimistic family where they believe everything is going to work out. They’re unbreakable.”



Both actors have also drawn inspiration from their parents. “My dad would prompt everyone around the dinner table to say thank you to my mum, Jude,” Smith said. “He’d say, ‘Thank you from the bottom of my heart – and thank you from Jude’s bottom, too’, which is a little bit Darryl.” “My mum, like Sal, has always got her hair done and her make-up on,” Whelan Brown added. “After she gave birth, there’s a photo of her with a full face of make-up, so I’m probably channelling a bit of my mum.” Co-creator and co-producer Jane Kennedy (who wrote the film with her Working Dog colleagues Tom Gleisner, Santo Cilauro and Rob Sitch, all of whom wrote the stage adaptation while serving as co-producers) said the team never imagined “how deeply these characters would become part of Australian life – people quote the film to us all the time.” Gleisner added: “People [also] misquote the film – for every, ‘How’s the serenity’, we get, ‘That’s not a knife’.”



Related Article Take 7 Stephen Curry knows what will be written on his tombstone: ‘I dug a hole’ Whelan Browne said she believed The Castle On Stage would attract many first-time theatre-goers: “I’ve heard AFL commentators telling people to buy tickets – I watch the footy every week, and I’ve never heard them talk about theatre. No one will walk away from this show regretting buying a ticket. It brings so much love and heart and warmth, and we’re at a time in the world where that’s what we all need.” The Castle On Stage premieres at Her Majesty’s Theatre on March 27. Tickets: www.thecastleonstage.com.au Find out the next TV, streaming series and movies to add to your must-sees. Get The Watchlist delivered every Thursday.

World.title: Nothing left to loot: Parisians ponder the real cost of another night of riots
World.content:
Protesters set up barricades and start fires near Place de la Republique in central Paris on Sunday.

On these smouldering streets, there’s still some sympathy with the protesters’ original demands. But it’s hard to escape the sense that these riots reflect a modern France facing troubled times.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Paris: The young men gather in the city square as if it is just another Sunday afternoon in the French capital, but they wear the uniform of the rioters who ransacked the streets the previous night. Most wear black hoodies, black sports pants, and black balaclavas. A few have ski masks over their foreheads, just in case they need to cover their eyes. They are ready for tear gas. We are in the Place de la Republique on the day after the worst French riots in recent memory, when mobs stormed through the streets to loot shops, torch cars and smash windows. And the unrest is not over because the protesters are back to assert their control of this historic square. A burnt car sits at the side of the square, not far from a burnt truck. A classic French kiosk, the sort of place you buy a chocolate and a newspaper, is now a blackened ruin. Police charge at protesters in the Place de la Republique in Paris on Saturday. Getty I have just walked past a smashed florist, a wrecked shoe store and a bottle shop that has been stripped bare and now reeks of the wine spilt from broken bottles. But I also see a group of volunteers cleaning up the rubbish around the towering monument in the middle of the square, a statue that symbolises the French Republic.



A firefighter tackles a street fire during violence on Sunday. AP Photo/Emma Da Silva One woman, Alice Boucheron, tells me she thinks many of the protesters were motivated by real problems, like the cost of living, but too many were intent on destruction. And she is angry at what they have done. Those engaging in looting and arson are the real problem, says Alice Boucheron. David Crowe “I’m really proud to be a French citizen,” she says. “So I want to clean up everything. I think that’s very important because when we clean up like this, it’s a demonstration too.” Boucheron, 33, has come in from her home just outside Paris to be here. She worries that politicians and the media will misrepresent the images from the protests. Parisian Samuel Lugassy said the previous night’s scenes felt like a “civil war”. David Crowe “We are projecting a very poor image to the world, when in reality the French people simply wanted to share their grievances,” she says.



“The real problem lies with those who engage in destruction, arson and looting.” Samuel Lugassy, a chiropractor who lives nearby, feels the previous night was like a “civil war” in parts of France. He is shocked and angry at what took place. Another pedestrian, Raphael Christophe, is about to leave for his home in Limoges, the town in the south where vandals burnt the historic town hall. He is watching the young men in balaclavas, worried about more violence. Limoges protesters set fire to the town hall in the city of Limoges in the Nouvelle-Aquitaine region of France. Hans Lucas via AFP “Look – they are ready,” he says. “They have their masks.” He is right. The group is expanding. It has outnumbered the volunteers trying to clean up the square, and it has drawn supporters displaying Palestinian and Algerian flags. Some of the group climb up the statue, as if asserting ownership of all they see. The statue is smothered with graffiti criticising Israel, the police, President Emmanuel Macron and the right-wing National Rally led by Marine Le Pen.



Protesters have repeatedly defaced the statue at the centre of Paris’ Place de la Republique David Crowe The police arrive to disperse the crowd shortly after 2.30pm. Officers with riot shields and batons advance through the square to try to force the protesters out, but it is not easy because this precinct is so busy with people who seem oblivious to the tensions. Pedestrians emerge from the Republique metro station. A jogger runs through the crowd. A group of tourists passes by on hire bikes. The crowd chants at the police, showing that the protest movement has the numbers in this square. Suddenly, the temperature rises when the police encircle a group of protesters and lead them away. A few people in the crowd start throwing things at the authorities, and they get canisters of tear gas in response. Most people start running as soon as the acrid smoke rises, knowing it will sting their eyes and burn their throats. The protests began as a response to poor conditions in schools but have spiralled into a wider movement. Anadolu via Getty Images While the protests began as rallies about school standards, the clashes in the Place de la Republique are mostly a test of strength between agitators and police. The leaders of the crowd set fire to bikes on a street, and are then dispersed by police. They put up barricades across the main boulevard to disrupt the traffic, and are dispersed with another volley of tear gas. Every action is dominated by men in their late teens and early 20s, almost all wearing their black uniforms. Young women can also be seen in the crowd, but they are in the minority among those provoking the police.



When the masks are lowered, the faces reflect modern France: the skin tones are white, black and brown. But the white faces are relatively rare. The crowd is overwhelmingly made up of young men who are new to France or born to migrant families, although there is no time to stop and ask whether their French citizenship goes back one, two, three or more generations. Loading This is a delicate subject because of the argument about whether the riots in France are caused by migration. Donald Trump insists they are; his critics say they are not. The debate about causation is surely complex. But it is important to be honest about the reality on the streets, rather than waving away what is obvious to every passer-by in Paris. Related Article Political unrest Macron addresses nation after riots, looting as Trump blames migration The streets around the Place de la Republique are full of young men from migrant backgrounds who seemed primed for confrontations with authority. They try to test the police, then retreat and scatter into small groups. In one moment they are protesters, in the next they look like bystanders. The confrontations continue into the night, and there is some opportunistic looting. Two men clamber out of a homewares store carrying brand new wheelie-bags; two boys then try to climb over the broken sheet glass to see if they can find something for themselves. If a store is not already looted, it is at least protected. Some have security guards sitting inside, watching the crowd pass by, or have metal shutters lowered. The looted stores are marked by plywood sheets to replace their broken windows.

World.title: Sydney man allegedly discussed plans for childcare mass shooting with AI chatbot
World.content:
NationalNSWCrime Sydney man allegedly discussed plans for childcare mass shooting with AI chatbot Riley Walter and Perry Duffin October 19, 2026 — 12:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A Sydney man threatened to carry out a mass shooting at a childcare centre in the city’s south during a conversation with a popular AI chatbot during which he referenced alleged Bondi Beach terrorist Naveed Akram, a court has heard. David Lan Thackray was on Monday remanded in custody for a mental health assessment after Sutherland Local Court heard the 29-year-old told Claude, an AI-powered chatbot, that he planned to shoot several children at a childcare centre near his Hurstville home. Thackray was on Sunday morning arrested after Interpol flagged his interactions with the chatbot and charged with using a carriage service to menace, harass or offend. Prosecutors arguing to keep Thackray behind bars on Monday said there would be a “catastrophic” outcome if he was released and breached bail conditions imposed. “What he intends to do is start murdering people in Sydney just like the [alleged] terrorist did in Bondi,” prosecutors told the court.



“We’re understanding what’s in his mind with his interactions with the chatbot.” Naveed Akram remains in custody charged with murdering 15 innocent people and injuring dozens of others during an attack on the Chanukah by the Sea event at Bondi Beach last December. His father, Sajid Akram, was killed in the attack. ‘What he intends to do is start murdering people in Sydney just like the [alleged] terrorist did in Bondi.’ The prosecution in court According to a police facts sheet tendered to the court, Thackray allegedly told the chatbot he would “go down to the local Westfield right now and shoot up the local daycare”. Thackray’s lawyer, Danilo Rajkovic, told the court his client had gone on a stress and frustration- induced tirade after trying to use the Claude platform to help treat an ear infection.



“There was no weight behind what he was saying,” Rajkovic said. Thackray did not instruct the chatbot to issue threats to any person or organisation and believed he was having the interaction in the privacy of his own home, Rajkovic said. Thackray had been using Claude’s voice mode, which allows users to have spoken conversations with the chatbot, the court heard. After receiving an email informing him that his Claude account had been suspended, Thackray requested to have the suspension reviewed. Thackray, who is studying international relations, has no criminal history and has lived in Australia for more than 17 years, Rajkovic said. Rajkovic said his client was confident detectives who seized his electronic devices on Sunday would find no evidence of radical indoctrination or ideological motivation.



Thackray will return to court pending the outcome of a mental health assessment. Claude is an “AI assistant for life and work”, according to the platform’s website. Anthropic, the developer of Claude, has been contacted for comment. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘That’s so savage’: Accused killer allegedly broke into TV presenter’s home hours after rejection
World.content:
NationalNSWLamarre-Condon trial ‘That’s so savage’: Accused killer allegedly broke into TV presenter’s home hours after rejection Michaela Whitbourn October 19, 2026 — 12:46pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Accused double murderer Beau Lamarre-Condon allegedly broke into Jesse Baird’s home and stole his mobile phone hours after the then TV presenter rebuffed his suggestion of a catchup, a court has heard. Lamarre-Condon, 31, is standing trial on two counts of murder over the shooting deaths of Jesse Baird, 26, a former Network Ten producer and presenter, and Luke Davies, 29, a Qantas flight attendant, in February 2024. The former NSW police officer has pleaded not guilty to the charges. Beau Lamarre-Condon sent screenshots of the text exchange with Luke Davies to a friend, the court heard. Six months before the men’s deaths, Lamarre-Condon allegedly broke into Baird’s Paddington share house and stole his wallet and mobile phone. He has also pleaded not guilty to this charge. The accused’s NSW Supreme Court trial heard on Monday that he texted Baird at 7.27pm on August 16, 2023: “Hey, sorry I had to run yesterday. I was running a tad late or I would have loved to chat for longer.



“Let’s do a walk and lunch catchup next weekend ... then we can have a proper catchup. Good seeing you though.” Baird replied at 1.49pm the following day: “It was good to see you too and glad you had fun in Euro.” Lamarre-Condon sent a screenshot of the messages to his then friend, the now senior constable Dana Schagen, who replied: “OMG. I’m dying. That’s so savage. No, it’s defs savage. “If he was keen, he would have jumped on the bandwagon.” Asked what she meant, Schagen told the court: “It’s quite evident from the text messages that Jesse had absolutely no interest in catching up with the accused at all.



“His response is the equivalent of a thumbs up. There’s no follow up to catch up with him.” Schagen texted Lamarre-Condon on August 19 to ask if he had heard back from Baird after this. Beau Lamarre-Condon is accused of breaking into Jesse Baird’s home six months before murdering him. “Yes I did hear back from him,” Lamarre-Condon replied on August 21. “He had a home invasion so he couldn’t text me that as his phone got stolen but we are catching up next Wednesday night for dinner. He said he full chased after the guy too.”



Schagen texted: “But managed to send the first message back? I don’t get it.” Lamarre-Condon replied: “Yes, because it happened after that. He isn’t lying.” Prosecutor Caitlin Diggins asked Schagen: “Did the accused tell you that he was the person Jesse had to chase out?” “No,” Schagen replied. The court heard that Lamarre-Condon called Schagen on March 28, more than a month after the alleged murders on February 19, using a friend’s mobile phone, and said: “I just wanted to tell you that I love you, and before you do anything, you need to know not everything in the news is true.



Related Article Lamarre-Condon trial Lamarre-Condon’s celebrity-chasing friend tells trial about ‘concerning’ phone request “It’ll come out in court.” Schagen said she cut off the accused and said: “You killed two people. Why would you think I would ever want to speak to you again?” She hung up and reported the phone call to her boss, the court heard. The Crown alleges Lamarre-Condon broke into Baird’s home and stole his mobile phone and wallet while Baird was home on August 17, 2023. He has pleaded not guilty to this charge. The defence case is that he used a key Baird had given him to enter the home.



Baird reported the alleged break-in at the time, the court has heard, and said he had woken shortly before midnight to a man standing over his bed. Investigating police took a photo of a bobby pin in the lock of Baird’s home, tendered in evidence in the trial. Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield, SC, alleged in his opening address to the 15-person jury that Lamarre-Condon used a key he had “stolen or surreptitiously copied to enter before putting a bobby pin in the door to give the impression that the lock on the door was picked”. It was “some six months before the two murder counts”, Hatfield said. “A wallet containing cash and ID was later found, having been discarded,” he said. “The phone was never recovered.”



The court has heard that Lamarre-Condon and Baird had a casual relationship that started in late 2022 and ended for the first time in April 2023, before they briefly reconnected in September. The Crown alleges Lamarre-Condon killed Baird after developing an “obsessive and jealous infatuation” with him that escalated when Baird ended their casual relationship permanently in November 2023. The prosecution alleges the then NSW police officer shot Davies, Baird’s new boyfriend, to eliminate a witness to his crime. The defence case is that Lamarre-Condon entered Baird’s share house disguised as a delivery rider to retrieve some of his belongings. According to the defence, a struggle ensued in which his police gun went off twice, killing Baird, and Davies shot himself accidentally in a second struggle. The accused had his Glock pistol with him because he was trained not to leave it unattended, the defence has said. The Crown has said he should not have had the weapon because he was not rostered to work that day.



The trial continues. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491. World.title: VietJet’s domestic ambitions dealt a blow after court orders global asset freeze
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesAviation VietJet’s domestic ambitions dealt a blow after court orders global asset freeze Chris Zappone October 19, 2026 — 12:46pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Low-cost carrier VietJet’s hopes of expanding into Australia’s domestic market have hit a snag, after the United Kingdom High Court granted an order to freeze the carrier’s assets as part of a fight with a hedge fund seeking to recover debts. FW Aviation, an aircraft leasing company registered in Jersey, secured court orders against the airline for $US250 million ($360 million) for four Airbus A321s in London late last week. Vietjet inaugural Ho Chi Minh City to Sydney flight in 2023. The order follows a long-running battle by a private investment fund FitzWalter Capital, which controls FW Aviation, to get the Vietnam-based VietJet to pay for the use of the four planes. UK courts have ordered three judgments against VietJet, for $18.8 million (in 2024), $182 million (in 2025) and $18.3 million (in a third trial), with the airline making a partial $2 million payment in 2025.



In the latest case, the business and property division of Britain’s High Court heard how VietJet has resisted paying, and even halted flights of aircraft to Singapore where they would have been seized under court orders. “In October 2021, following VietJet’s continuing failure to pay rent for its use of the aircraft (during the COVID lockdowns), the lenders served notices on VietJet seeking to terminate the sub-lease agreements,” the court ruling reads. “Shortly thereafter, FWA acquired all rights formerly held by the lenders,” which included the right to recover sums owed under sub-lease agreements and custody and control of the aircraft, the court said. Vietjet flight attendants dressed in bikinis. Justice Pushpinder Saini found that VietJet’s actions constituted a “risk of dissipation”, or danger that a defendant will hide, transfer, or sell assets before a court judgment can be enforced.



This masthead understands the prospect of legal judgments against VieJet would likely complicate its bid to receive permission to operate as a domestic airline. VietJet has been approached for comment. Related Article Aviation Western Sydney Airport makes play for premium travellers The low-cost carrier has applied to the Civil Aviation Safety Authority (CASA) for an air operator’s certificate, which would allow it to operate on domestic routes in Australia. It’s expected to operate up to 10 Boeing 737s on routes between Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane, under the name Cherrie Air. CASA has been approached for comment. Vietjet, which was Vietnam’s first privately owned airline when it began flying in 2011, has made network expansion a priority, operating divisions in Thailand and as far away as Kazakhstan.



The company has previously raised eyebrows for stunts featuring women dressed only in bikinis. VietJet is also expected to become the third international airline offering flights from Western Sydney International – after Air New Zealand and Singapore Airlines. It’s slated to begin flying between Western Sydney and Ho Chi Minh City on 10 January 2027, operating two return services per week, on Wednesdays and Sundays. It’s website shows prices for those flights from WSI to Ho Chi Minh ranging for $411 to $34. VietJet’s international arm – based out of Vietnam – currently operates daily return flights to Ho Chi Minh City from Sydney and Melbourne. Brisbane and Perth are connected to Ho Chi Minh City with five and three weekly return flights, respectively. World.title: Crisafulli accuses federal government of siege on small business
World.content:
PoliticsQueenslandQueensland government Crisafulli accuses federal government of siege on small business Julius Dennis October 19, 2026 — 12:13pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Queensland Premier David Crisafulli has accused the Albanese government of launching a siege on small business following the botched credit card surcharge ban, proposed cuts to worker holiday visas and reforming trust taxes. The end of the week will mark two years for the LNP state government, tipping it into the second half of its four-year term as it faces recent scrutiny over child safety concerns and its commitment to drastically cut ambulance ramping at hospitals. David Crisafulli approaches the halfway mark of the parliamentary term. AAPIMAGE While much of Monday’s speech to business leaders at a Centre for Economic Development Australia breakfast was spent on previously covered ground, Crisafulli doubled down on challenging Canberra over an “inbuilt injustice in Queensland”. Key among his gripes was his view the state receives an unfair cut of the GST pie, echoing a call from Treasurer David Janetzki for a distribution rethink.



“We’ve reached a point in the GST distribution where Western Australia has cut out an amazing deal, and I don’t begrudge that … but the beneficiary has been the states that haven’t been prepared to do the hard yards,” he said. “Somehow we are viewed as big enough to stand on our own two feet, unlike the west, but small enough that we have to cop all the bad news. “We’re not getting the upside Victoria and New South Wales get, and we have to call it out.” Earlier in the speech, Crisafulli had vowed not to use the address as a “pressure relief valve”, but the back end focused heavily on the actions of the federal government. Besides GST, Crisafulli said the removal of card surcharges at check-out and the Tax Office’s call to disallow credit card payments on tax debt, changes to how trusts were taxed, and potential changes to worker holiday visas, amounted to a siege on small businesses.





In his typical mild exasperation, Crisafulli insisted his government’s wish to mine fossil fuels while cancelling renewables projects it saw as fanciful was about economics, not ideology. “I don’t understand how we got to this point in this country where every time we talk about energy it has to be some kind of ideological war, some kind of arm wrestle where people from both camps yell at each other,” he said. With the Olympics and all the associated infrastructure, if the government could find a middle road, a “golden age” awaited for Queensland, the premier said. World.title: $300,000 on coffee: Yarra Trams’ contracts and conflicts spur whistleblower alarm
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsVictoriaTrams $300,000 on coffee: Yarra Trams’ contracts and conflicts spur whistleblower alarm Clay Lucas Updated October 19, 2026 — 12:06pm ,first published October 19, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Yarra Trams executives face accusations from senior staff of financial mismanagement and inappropriate handling of conflicts of interest, amid a raft of job losses at the public transport operator. A whistleblower report submitted to the company’s management in April by Yarra Trams’ head of procurement operations alleges millions of dollars in unusual advance payments to vendors, in a late financial-year scramble to avoid penalties for missing social procurement targets. Yarra Trams executives are facing accusations of financial mismanagement and inappropriate handling of conflicts of interest. Matt Davidson An internal investigation into the allegations was launched immediately by the company’s senior lawyer – only for the lawyer, the whistleblower and four other procurement staff to be made redundant before it was completed. The Age can also reveal that the Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission interviewed at least one other former employee, separate from the whistleblower, regarding the same allegations.



The two separate interventions come amid a tumultuous round of job losses at the company just two years into its nine-year, $7 billion state government contract to run Melbourne’s tram network. Since taking over in December 2024, a joint venture between global transport giant Transdev and big builder John Holland has made 36 employees redundant – most from Yarra Trams’ Bourke Street head office. Related Article Updated

Public transport New operator to take over Melbourne tram network Yarra Trams’ contract includes a requirement to spend a proportion of its budget with firms providing social benefits, including Aboriginal employment, disability employment, and gender equality initiatives. The operator faces penalties of up to $1.5 million a year if it misses the contractual benchmarks. The Age has spoken with 13 current and former Yarra Trams staff about the matters contained in the whistleblower complaint and report to IBAC. Though unwilling to speak publicly about the confidential material, all asserted the matters raised were legitimate.



The whistleblower alleges, in a 34-page report, that millions of dollars of contracts were inappropriately fast-tracked last June to avoid financial penalties. The arrangements include large advance payments for security services, espresso machines and barista training, and personal protective equipment. The whistleblower was concerned the process meant appropriate services were potentially not procured. “Obligations relating to social procurement are designed to deliver outcomes for disadvantaged Victorians through the channelling of public expenditure into enterprises that deliver jobs and development,” the report stated. “Proper process would have been to set evaluation criteria for the required service and give favourable weighting to suppliers who can show social outcomes.” Instead, emails, invoices and payment receipts show a last-minute effort by Yarra Trams management to hit strict social procurement spending targets before the financial year ended. To avoid fines in its contract, called “abatements”, senior executives authorised a rush of advance payments to social vendors before June 30 – logging the spending on paper to clear contractual benchmarks.



Internal correspondence reveals executives authorising payments – including $500,000 to a security provider, $300,000 for the “design, development and manufacture of [a] custom uniform”, and a $300,000 coffee deal for espresso machines to be installed in offices. A June 2025 invoice shows Yarra Trams issuing a $500,000 advance payment to a “social outcomes security group”. The security company asked for questions to be directed to Yarra Trams. A $300,000 purchase order shows money being paid to a uniform company that had not even developed the product at the time of purchase; a spokeswoman said the company had since delivered 2000 high-visibility vests, “with work undertaken at our North Melbourne manufacturing facility” that provided “employment opportunities for refugee and asylum seeker women”. Yarra Trams also entered into a deal with a coffee supplier that donates a share of it profits to charity. It supplied the tram operator’s offices with espresso machines, beans, and maintenance. Internal records show an overall contract value of $300,000, with more than $10,000 dedicated to “barista training”. The coffee company declined to respond to questions.



In a May 2025 email chain discussing the strategy, Yarra Trams’ chief financial and commercial officer Marc Walter approved the initiative, writing in response: “This is approved to proceed. No further approvals required to commence.” It is not suggested that Walter endorsed any inappropriate spending to hit the target – only that he told staff they could proceed with the contracts. The whistleblower report questions whether using public franchise funds to prepay for coffee machines and undeveloped products represented genuine value for money or was simply complying with state government social procurement rules to avoid fines. It also details the January appointment of a Brisbane-based consultant for $2000 a day. The Age has seen the contract confirming the wage, plus flights to and from his Queensland base.



The executive who hired the consultant also submitted a conflict-of-interest form acknowledging the consultant previously reported to him at mining company BHP. The form’s proposed conflict-of-interest management plan was left blank, but CFO Marc Walter countersigned the document. Responding to the allegations, a Yarra Trams spokeswoman said that all procurement processes were subject to strict probity requirements. “We have reviewed these matters and are satisfied the procurement and workforce-related decisions were subject to the relevant approval and oversight processes,” she said. She said Commonwealth legislation prevented Yarra Trams from commenting on “potential whistleblower matters”.



On corporate job cuts, the company stated that while 36 roles were made redundant, its total workforce had expanded by approximately 120 roles since December 2024. Addressing specific vendor contracts, the operator said procurement decisions were made “based on operational requirements, value for money and contractual obligations”. The company defended the coffee contract as “a trial of a managed coffee-service model, including coffee machines, coffee supplies, maintenance and training services. The coffee machines have been installed and are operational”. On the engagement of its Queensland consultant, the operator said the hire was approved through internal governance processes for “specialist procurement transformation” work.



The two annual reports filed with financial regulators since Transdev and John Holland took over Melbourne’s tram operations show the joint venture has so far made profits of $38.5 million, receiving payments from the state government of $1.254 billion – a 3 per cent return. Asked about Yarra Trams and its contract management practices, a spokesman for the Victorian government said: “This is a matter for Yarra Trams. All of our transport operators must adhere to strict probity and procurement processes consistent with their contractual obligations.”

World.title: Meet the new Kerrigans: The Castle stage show’s cast revealed
World.content:
CultureTheatreArts Meet the new Kerrigans: The Castle stage show’s cast revealed Michael Lallo October 19, 2026 — 12:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The wait is over: the actors bringing Australia’s most beloved fictional family to the stage have been revealed. On Monday, producers Michael Cassel and Working Dog unveiled the principal cast of The Castle On Stage, the upcoming adaptation of the classic 1997 film. The cast of The Castle On Stage: Ed Oxenbould as Dale, Marcus McKenzie as Steve, Christie Whelan Browne as Sal, Joel Jackson as Wayne, Justin Smith as Darryl, Roman Delo as Con, and Stephanie Graham as Tracey. Simon Schluter Loveable patriarch Darryl Kerrigan will be played by veteran actor Justin Smith (Heartbreak High, Wentworth), whose first professional role was in the 1992 Australian tour of Jesus Christ Superstar. Darryl’s wife – the sweet-natured culinary whiz, Sal – will be portrayed by Christie Whelan Browne, one of Australia’s most highly regarded performers on stage (Muriel’s Wedding the Musical, Singin’ in the Rain) and screen (Shaun Micallef’s Mad as Hell). “The hardest part about playing Sal is playing a woman whose family enjoys her cooking,” Whelan Browne said.



When asked why Darryl and Sal are one of Australia’s favourite fictional couples, Whelan Browne said, “I think they both feel like they’ve got the better deal. It’s quite simple: everything she does, he thinks is amazing, and vice versa.” Making his professional theatre debut, Ed Oxenbould (Puberty Blues, Paper Planes) is Dale: the youngest of the four Kerrigan children and a proud digger of holes, who also serves as the play’s narrator. “Dale [still resonates with audiences] because his optimism never goes out of style,” Oxenbould said. The cast of the hit 1997 film The Castle: Anthony Simcoe, Anne Tenney, Michael Caton, Sophie Lee, Eric Bana, Wayne Hope and Stephen Curry. Joel Jackson (Deadline Gallipoli, Peter Allen: Not the Boy Next Door) is Wayne, the eldest son and model prisoner; while contemporary theatre performer Marcus McKenzie is Steve, a bargain hunter and self-taught “ideas man”. Recent WAAPA graduate Stephanie Graham is the Kerrigan family’s only daughter, Tracey; and Roman Delo (Bump, NCIS: Sydney) is her kickboxing-enthusiast husband, Con Petropoulous. To say that Australians are enthusiastic about the stage version of The Castle – a David and Goliath battle between the Kerrigan family and a greedy consortium attempting to “compulsory acquire” their home – is an understatement. In May, readers of this masthead voted The Castle Australia’s favourite movie of all time. In July, the film’s creators, Working Dog, announced they had partnered with renowned producer Michael Cassel to bring the story to Her Majesty’s Theatre in Melbourne, where it will make its world premiere in March 2027.



Related Article Stage shows Australia’s favourite comedy is coming to the stage? Tell ’em they’re not dreamin’ Just 24 hours after tickets went on sale, the production broke a box office record, achieving the highest first-day sales for any play in Her Majesty’s history. Within a week, producers extended the season due to extraordinary demand – and on Monday, they announced a second extension, meaning the show will run until at least mid-May. In the movie, the Kerrigans relied on landline telephones, The Trading Post newspaper and Australian-made cars. The play will instead be set in the present day, where Wi-Fi, smartphones and electric vehicles are ubiquitous. But the central plot – and its heartwarming “vibe” – remain unchanged. Smith believes that in some ways, the story’s premise is more relevant than ever. “Look at something like Robodebt, where the everyman has been shafted by the powers that be,” he said. Whelan Browne said she and Smith were drawing on their own experiences as parents. “There’s a moment in the show where we look at each other and well up with tears every night,” she said, becoming misty-eyed. “We’re simply talking about how much we love our kids, and that’s how Justin and I both come at it – there’s a real joy in coming into this optimistic family where they believe everything is going to work out. They’re unbreakable.”



Both actors have also drawn inspiration from their parents. “My dad would prompt everyone around the dinner table to say thank you to my mum, Jude,” Smith said. “He’d say, ‘Thank you from the bottom of my heart – and thank you from Jude’s bottom, too’, which is a little bit Darryl.” “My mum, like Sal, has always got her hair done and her make-up on,” Whelan Brown added. “After she gave birth, there’s a photo of her with a full face of make-up, so I’m probably channelling a bit of my mum.” Co-creator and co-producer Jane Kennedy (who wrote the film with her Working Dog colleagues Tom Gleisner, Santo Cilauro and Rob Sitch, all of whom wrote the stage adaptation while serving as co-producers) said the team never imagined “how deeply these characters would become part of Australian life – people quote the film to us all the time.” Gleisner added: “People [also] misquote the film – for every, ‘How’s the serenity’, we get, ‘That’s not a knife’.”



Related Article Take 7 Stephen Curry knows what will be written on his tombstone: ‘I dug a hole’ Whelan Browne said she believed The Castle On Stage would attract many first-time theatre-goers: “I’ve heard AFL commentators telling people to buy tickets – I watch the footy every week, and I’ve never heard them talk about theatre. No one will walk away from this show regretting buying a ticket. It brings so much love and heart and warmth, and we’re at a time in the world where that’s what we all need.” The Castle On Stage premieres at Her Majesty’s Theatre on March 27. Tickets: www.thecastleonstage.com.au Find out the next TV, streaming series and movies to add to your must-sees. Get The Watchlist delivered every Thursday.

World.title: Wildfires have destroyed one-third of small PNG island, responders say
World.content:
Small island villagers in Papua New Guinea are appealing for international help to fight wildfires, which they say have burned through one-third of their land.

As winter turns to spring under El Niño drought conditions, bushfires are battering communities all over PNG, with local fire and response teams often powerless to fight it.

In Manus Province, Lou Island has battled wildfires for the past week, in what locals call an "unprecedented" disaster.

Ngenge Sasa, from Rei village in the island's north, told RNZ Pacific that the impact has been devastating.

Speaking from a high vantage point, he said at least one third of the island appeared scorched and flat, and that an entire forest appeared to have vanished.

"It's a clean sweep," he said.

"On the Eastern side ... all the trees that we use for building our houses, the roads and some of the gardens, all our resources have gone. This is one of the only forests that all of the island used for sawn timber."

He said the fire seemed to have tempered by around 7am local time, with smoke visible on the southern end, after it had spread island-wide the day before.

"It's the first kind of fire that islanders have experienced in their life."

Kireni Sparks-Ngenge, a fellow coordinator, said locals have relied on whatever they had lying around to fight the fire, but it was nowhere near enough.

"Community members have been working tirelessly, risking their own safety, to try to kill the fire, but latest reports say that the spread of the fire is out of their control," she said.

"We believe that the best equipment to put out this wildfire would be monsoon buckets, but have yet to find anyone who has and will deploy this equipment urgently.

"Other critical support could include assessing fire boundaries and coordinating containment lines, and use of high volume water pumps directly onto active fire."

Sasa said re-enforcements from Manus Island arrived yesterday, with firefighters up until 3am, while locals island-wide kept up their efforts.

"There's people from all around Lou Island, they're all coming today. Everybody will get one litre, two litres, five litres of water, and walk up to the mountains and try to killed the remaining fire now.

"But big damage has been done to our traditional land. These forests here were untouched forests from our great grandparents... now it's all gone on this side.

World.title: Some New World customers may have been overcharged due to 'pricing issue' impacting North Island stores
World.content:
A pricing issue is affecting several New World supermarkets across the country and may have led to some customers being overcharged for items.

A Foodstuffs spokesperson said refunds would be issued to anyone who had been affected.

At least two supermarkets, one in Auckland's Takapuna and the other in Willis St, central Wellington, are closed.

Do you know more? Email iwitness@rnz.co.nz

At others, self-checkouts have been closed and staff are checking the accuracy of prices for all items.

A sign at New World Mt Roskill said a system update had not yet been loaded into the checkout system and expired specials may still be displaying at the checkout, while new promotional prices may not be showing correctly.

A sign at New World Metro on Willis St said the store was temporarily closed because of the problem, and its team was working to resolve the issue.

Customers outside the Willis St store. BAZ MACDONALD / RNZ

Members of the public reported to RNZ that New World in Paremata, in Porirua, along with New World Stonefields in Auckland had remained open but had closed self-checkout services.

A Stonefields local said there were "massive lines" and staff at every checkout were double checking prices against the website/online systems.

The Foodstuffs spokesperson said a technical issue was found on Monday morning which meant some promotional prices weren't being applied correctly in North Island stores.

The issue had been resolved at Pak' n Save and Four Square, the spokesperson said and staff were working urgently to restore the affected promotions at New World.

"We're sorry to customers affected and thank them for their patience while we get this sorted.

For any customers who have been overcharged, we will refund the full amount paid for the overcharged product in line with our Refund Policy."

Club+ customers who scanned cards and were overcharged would automatically be refudned, the spokesperson said.

World.title: Te Pāti Māori's Oriini Kaipara on gangs: 'I see whānau'
World.content:
Te Pāti Māori MP Oriini Kaipara is doubling down on her support of gangs saying "I will not ever turn my back on whānau in need".

The MP for Tāmaki Makaurau promised to "restore mana" to Mongrel Mob gang members when she visited a gang pad alongside other MPs from her own party and the Greens earlier this month.

Speaking to Midday Report with Guyon Espiner, Kaipara said she can understand people might see her actions as an endorsement of gangs, but engaging with that community is more important than any perceptions people might have.

Audio player for " Oriini Kaipara discusses visit to Mongrel Mob gang pad " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics_election-2026/2018789%2Fte-pati-maori-s-oriini-kaipara-on-gangs-i-see-whanau

Oriini Kaipara discusses visit to Mongrel Mob gang pad Midday Report Download MP3 7m

"I think what we need to clarify first Guyon is the fact you see Mongrel Mob, I see whānau. I see mums and dads, I see uncles who have been trapped in intergenerational trauma who have not been listened to, especially in the last three years by this government who continuously target those behind the patch."

"We do not discriminate against anybody, and especially where Māori are over represented, and in the gangs we know that there are many Māori whānau in gangs."

Responding to those comments, National leader Christopher Luxon told RNZ he was proud there were 2000 more people in prison, with half of them gang members.

"They are not Probus or the Lions or Rotary, they're not a community organisation, they peddle misery and death and suffering."

Kaipara accepted there was a harrowing history of sexual violence against women in gang culture.

"I am not dismissing the stark realities and the violence and the crimes committed by many a gang, not just this one," she told Midday Report.

She said, however, when you look at the definition of victims "it goes without saying that gangs exist because of systemic failures, because of the government of the time creating state care abuse".

Luxon said the findings of an inquiry into Abuse in State Care about intergenerational trauma isn't "an excuse" for gang behaviour.

"Abuse in State Care has had a whole bunch of challenges in a whole range of areas, but actually it's a little bit too cute, because here's what happens - gang members go get people hooked up on meth and drugs, that is their business model."

He said both Te Pāti Māori and Green Party MPs were "making excuses".

"They're hanging out with gang members who caused pain and suffering, and do the bashings and do the beatings. Did any of them ask the gang members they were hanging out with how they got their gang patches?"

Labour, meanwhile, has rejected suggestions a left-leaning government would "restore mana" to Mongrel Mob gang members.

Leader Chris Hipkins has ruled that out, saying it's "all the more reason to vote Labour".

"No, I think gangs are a scourge on society," he said. "They do enormous harm.

"They peddle drugs, they perpetuate violence. I've dealt with victims of gang violence, including women who have fled gang relationships, where they have been the subject of violence.

"I have no time for the gangs. They will not get any support from any government that I lead."

Hipkins said Labour also would not support changes to the gang patch ban.

"Other parties can promote that, we will not support it."

Green Party co-leader Marama Davidson said it was for Te Pāti Māori to answer to its comments about restoring the mana of the Mongrel Mob.

"Oriini Kaipara made those comments, not the Green Party, and that is for Te Pāti Māori to answer to."

National's justice spokesperson Paul Goldsmith also weighed in saying Kaipara's comments were "outrageous".

"There is no excuse for gang sympathy. They peddle misery and havoc throughout New Zealand.

World.title: Explainer: What are the US midterms and why are they a big deal?
World.content:
Audio player for " Explainer: What are the US midterms and why should we care? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/world/2009371%2Fexplainer-what-are-the-us-midterms-and-why-are-they-a-big-deal

Explainer: What are the US midterms and why should we care? Afternoons Download MP3 9m

Explainer - American voters will soon get one more chance to cast their verdict on US President Donald Trump - quite possibly for the final time.

The US midterm elections are coming up on 3 November (expect results to come in after midday 4 November NZ time), and millions of dollars are being spent as candidates sprint around the country seeking votes. Early voting has already begun in many states.

But what exactly is being voted on? Here's what to look out for, and what Trump may face after results come in.

What are the midterms anyway?

They're a key part of the American political process where, halfway through a president's four-year term, voters get to pick their local congressional representatives and many senators and governors.

All 435 members of the House of Representatives and 35 of the 100 Senate seats are up for election this year, as well as 36 state governors.

The midterms are usually seen as a referendum on how a president's term is going and determine whether the US Congress is led by the Democrat or Republican party.

RNZ's Tim Watkin, executive producer of podcasts and series, is a keen observer of the American political scene.

The midterms are the biggest deal for the final two years of Trump's presidency, he said.

VINCENT FEURAY / AFP

"It will change the balance of power in America."

If Trump's Republican party loses badly, "It will give Democrats the power to question Trump in a way he's never been questioned this term," Watkin said.

Explain to me again how America's Congress works?

We can try.

Instead of a Parliament, they've got Congress, which consists of two separate chambers - the House of Representatives and the "upper house", the Senate. Bills must pass both houses to become law.

The House has 435 members who are divided proportionally among the 50 states based on their population (so bustling California has the most reps, 52, while wide-open Wyoming has only one).

The Senate has 100 members and every state, regardless of size, has just two senators. The US Vice-President acts as a 101st member to break any 50-50 ties in the Senate.

The US Senate is considered more prestigious and powerful. Representatives only serve two-year terms, while senators serve six-year terms.

The current makeup of the House and Senate is very tight - there's a single seat majority in the House and six seats in the Senate. They've both been under Republican control since the 2024 election.

How big a deal is this for Trump?

Trump has operated the last two years under a Republican House and Senate and broadly exercised executive power with little pushback from fellow Republicans. That could well change after 4 November.

During his first term, when Democrats ran the House of Representatives, Trump was impeached twice, but both times the Republican-controlled Senate failed to convict him, which would have forcibly removed him from office.

US President Donald Trump speaks at a rally in Clarksville, Tennessee. ROBERTO SCHMIDT / AFP

If Democrats control both houses of Congress, look for an awful lot more talk about investigating alleged corruption, and perhaps even another go at impeachment.

While Trump has made lots of allusions to seeking a third term - which is illegal under the US Constitution - the reality is that an 82-year-old Trump probably won't be running again in 2028.

"It's Trump's last election," Watkin said.

"Once the midterm's done, especially if he loses badly, the next two years Republicans are going to be running a mile from him, and he's going to be standing there going, 'But I'm Donald Trump'."

US Speaker of the House Mike Johnson hits the gavel during a Joint Meeting of Congress in the House Chamber at the US Capitol in April 2026. SAUL LOEB / AFP

Is history on Trump's side?

Not really.

Whether or not one supports Trump's policies, history is against him.

Over the last 80 years, the president's party has lost seats in the midterms 18 times out of 20.

"A sitting president gets held to account for not achieving the promises they made a year and a half ago," Watkin said.

It's almost inevitable that any US president, by the last few years of a second term, starts to enter "lame duck" status. Trump, who has defied a lot of political gravity in his career, is racing into that timeframe.

The current New York Times average of several political polls finds Trump's approval rating sits around 37 percent.

Watkin said that a faltering economy and the impact of the Iran war have hit many Trump supporters hard.

"Those men who have been his base are now pissed off because they're now paying [US] $6 for diesel in their trucks.

"He was supposed to be the businessman."

Current predictions by the influential nonpartisan Cook Political Report and others foresee the Democrats likely to take back control of the House of Representatives, while the Senate will be a closer call.

"They've given up in the House," Watkin said. "The idea that they could hold on to majorities is gone. The Senate's the thing that people need to watch."

And of course, nobody really knows how Trump will react if his party loses badly at the midterms.

"Assumably - he will claim corruption, right?" Watkin said.

Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico with supporters at the conclusion of a campaign rally in Kerrville, Texas. BRANDON BELL / AFP

What are the big races to watch out for?

Despite all 435 seats in the House of Representatives being up for election, only a handful are truly considered competitive. The New York Times and Cook Political Report currently list just 21 seats as toss-ups that could go either way, and another 21 as leaning somewhat towards Republicans or Democrats.

Because the margin of the current majority is so slim in the House, it would take only a handful of seats to flip to give Democrats control.

The Senate currently has a 53-47 Republican majority (two independent senators caucus with Democrats), and will be harder to flip. Democrats need to win 51 seats to achieve a majority as Vice President JD Vance can cast votes to break 50-50 ties in the current House.

The Senate, with its smaller membership, longer terms and more powerful legislative powers, is key. If Democrats capture the House and Senate, Republican Trump will lose any leverage to get his legislative priorities passed. CNN has ranked 10 seats that may flip in 2026.

There are several big Senate races to watch:

Texas - Democrat James Talarico is facing Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton. Normally Texas is deep red, but Paxton has been dogged by a series of scandals including a fraud indictment and impeachment. Polls show Talarico doing better than Democrats usually do there, but Republicans are pouring money into what will end up one of the most expensive Senate races of all time.

Maine - Democrat nominee Graham Platner's campaign imploded and replacement Troy Jackson hasn't quite gone so viral, but incumbent Republican Susan Collins has been in office since 1997 and is in danger due to the Trump backlash.

Republian US Senator Susan Collins campaigns in Fryeburg, Maine. SPENCER PLATT / AFP

Ohio - A popular former senator, Democrat Sherrod Brown, is running to get back into office against Republican Jon Husted, who replaced JD Vance when he became vice president.

Michigan - One of the most combative races is between Republican Mike Rogers and progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, who could become the first Muslim US senator.

Alaska - Remote Alaska would seem as Republican as they come but former Democrat Congresswoman Mary Peltola, the first Alaska Native elected to Congress, is running a close campaign against Republican Dan Sullivan.

Other important races are in North Carolina, Kansas, New Hampshire and Iowa. Many of the tight races are in states Trump won by a wide margin in 2024.

So are the Republicans doomed?

Well, we live in unprecedented times, and few political observers would've ever predicted most of what's happened in America in the past 10 years. America's deep political polarisation isn't likely to be resolved no matter what happens at the midterms.

Two big things still work in the Republicans' favour - the controversial redistricting of multiple states' congressional districts, which has seen both Republican and Democrat-controlled states trying to rejig electorates to ensure their party gets more votes. Republicans are generally seen as having created more possible seats for their party.

The second is money, which is the petrol running the US political engine. At least US$10 billion is believed to have been spent so far on advertising, by political parties as well as by big-pocketed donors such as the AI industry and Elon Musk.

Republicans are believed to still have more than US$1 billion to spend, and will pour money into places such as Texas' Senate race.

This year's election will break records, the nonprofit Brennan Center For Justice told The Washington Post recently.

"Having tons of money doesn't guarantee victory," US government ethics expert Meredith McGehee told the Post. "But the contrary is true - not having 'enough' does guarantee defeat. And no one ever really knows what 'enough' is."

And in case you're already dreading the endless carnival of the 2028 US presidential election, bad news - the race to succeed Trump will pretty much begin the day after the midterms. Expect candidates from both parties to start announcing their plans by early 2027.

Once again, when are those midterms?

World.title: Coalition by Christmas? Don't bet on it
World.content:
Audio player for " Weekly interview with Prime Minister, Christopher Luxon " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics_election-2026/2017956%2Fcoalition-by-christmas-don-t-bet-on-it

Weekly interview with Prime Minister, Christopher Luxon Morning Report Download MP3 7m

Christmas could come and go before New Zealand gets a new government, with neither Christopher Luxon nor Chris Hipkins willing to promise a coalition deal before the festivities are over.

On Monday, both prospective prime ministers refused to put a deadline on coalition talks, raising the prospect of Christmas being swallowed up by political horse-trading.

Asked on RNZ's Morning Report about the timeframe, Luxon was non-committal.

"I'm hoping that we can get something put together before Christmas - would be ideal. But frankly, it'll take as long as it takes."

Luxon indicated formal negotiations would likely wait until the final vote count was released on 27 November, nearly three weeks after polling day.

"We'll probably need to wait for that to come back, and then you'll see negotiations commence," he said.

"That's why I'm asking New Zealanders first and foremost to think very intentionally about how they want to vote."

Hipkins was similarly reluctant to make promises, telling reporters at Parliament it would depend on what voters delivered.

"We've got to play the cards that the voters deal us. If you want a good, decisive outcome, vote for one. Vote Labour.

"Give us the strongest possible hand in those post-election discussions."

On Sunday, Hipkins said he would make it a priority to get a deal done before Christmas, but he could not guarantee it.

"It's one of the later elections that we've had in recent times, and that could, depending on the outcome, make it more challenging."

In 2023, it took National, ACT and New Zealand First 41 days after voting day and 21 days after the final count to sign their coalition agreements.

The same timetable this year would take us to 18 December - just one week before Christmas.

World.title: Wellington family shaken after pedestrian breaks windscreen of car with them inside
World.content:
A Wellington family has been left shaken after a pedestrian threw an object at their car while they were travelling through Mount Victoria Tunnel tunnel.

Olivia Fuller was in the car on Sunday around 5pm with her two young children while her mother was driving from the airport through the tunnel towards the Basin Reserve.

She said she saw a pedestrian throw something at their windscreen about a third of the way through the tunnel.

"And then the next thing I knew it just smashed into our windscreen," she said.

Although no one was injured, Fuller said her six-year-old daughter was upset by what happened.

"We had sunglasses on and things, which was lucky because there was glass everywhere."

Fuller said glass had gone 'everywhere' but no one had been hurt. Supplied

The family continued driving out of the tunnel before heading home and contacting police.

"My daughter was very scared and she tends to stress out about stuff, so I didn't want to freak her out. I tried to stay calm and just get her inside before I called the police."

Fuller said she fears the consequences could have been much worse if the object had broken through the windscreen, potentially injuring or killing someone in the car.

Fuller said she was concerned others could be hurt. Supplied

She said her mother was visiting from out of town, and she had honked the car's horn in the tunnel for her kids - as driver's often do.

The incident has left the family shaken.

Fuller regularly uses the tunnel about four times a week and is concerned another motorist could be seriously hurt.

"It just concerns me that people were doing that and they might hit someone else and they might not be as lucky as we were," she said.

She is trying to get CCTV footage from the tunnel.

Police said the report is at assessment stage and that it is fortunate no one was injured, given the potential consequences.

World.title: FNRL clears $300k debt and pays World Cup player allowances
World.content:
The Fiji National Rugby League (FNRL) says all players and officials competing at the 2026 Rugby League World Cup (RLWC) have been paid for their pool game commitments.

FNRL executive chairman Rajesh Singh confirmed to RNZ Pacific that every one of the Fiji Bati and Fiji Bulikula players and officials were paid before the teams left for Australia last week.

He said the FNRL is now debt-free, after the organisation cleared its outstanding debt.

Singh said the pre-tournament payment of allowances and clearing of debts were two positive achievements for the FNRL following financial restructures in the past six months.

"We've cleared our debts, which was around $300,000 (NZ$225,000)," he said. "And the players and officials have been paid for all their pool games at the World Cup. If they advance to the next round, we'll make sure they'll get paid for it."

Singh said the results have come after the streamlining of expenses and restructuring of the organisation's financial system following audits.

"I'm grateful to the dedicated staff at the FNRL office for their commitment and sacrifice," he said.

Fijian players huddle ahead of the Men's Rugby League World Cup Group A match between Fiji and the Cook Islands at McDonald Jones Stadium in Newcastle, Sunday, 18 October 12026. AAP / Photosport

The Bulikula took the New Zealand Kiwi Ferns to the wire in their opening clash in Newcastle, Sydney on Sunday, only losing 18-12 in the end, with the Kiwi Ferns managing a converted try two minutes from fulltime.

The Bati defeated Cook Islands 40-12 to open their campaign with a convincing win.

Singh said the initial performances were promising, although he believes the second round of matches will be tougher for both teams.

The Bulikula will take on Papua New Guinea in Port Moresby on Saturday. The PNG Orchids won their first game with a 58-4 thrashing of France at home on Saturday.

The Bati take on world champs Australia, who pipped New Zealand 24-22 on in their RLWC opener last Thursday.

Disparity addressed

Meanwhile, Rugby League Players Association president and Dolphins' forward Feleti Kaufusi has told Australian media that the pay disparity between Australian and other international players needs to be addressed.

Australia is paying AU$40,000 to players for their World Cup commitment, which is an agreement between the Rugby League Players Association (RLPA) and the Australian Rugby League Commission (ARLC).

Other international teams have been tagged at A$850 per match.

Kaufusi said he would formally address the issue in the next Collective Bargaining Agreement (CBA).

"I want more equality in the prizemoney. It is something we will raise in the next CBA," Kaufusi was reported in the Australia media as saying.

"Australia is always going to get first preference, which is fine, but we need to get to a stage where it is a lot more even.

"It may not be the same, but it should be somewhere thereabouts."

Meanwhile, the Pacific Island teams are in action again this upcoming weekend.

In the women's competition, Fetu Samoa, who played brilliantly despite losing to Australia last weekend, will take on Wales in Sydney on Friday evening.

PNG hosts Fiji at home in Port Moresby on Saturday.

World.title: Labour pledges social media ban for under-16s
World.content:
*Correction: An earlier version of this story incorrectly said Labour promised to implement the ban in its first 100 days

Labour is pledging to get an under-16 social media ban to select committee in its first 100 days and set up an online watchdog that can fine technology giants that break new rules.

If back in government Labour says it will give people more control of their internet feed by platforms to allow users to choose between an algorithm-driven feed or posts only from accounts people follow.

The new rules would mean users could switch between those feeds at any time.

There would also be a new 'Digital Duty of Care' law that would require platforms to "identify risks and protect Kiwis from harmful content and addictive designs".

Any breaches of these new rules would be assessed by a new independent online regulator, which would have powers to "enforce safety standards, investigate harmful practices and take action against companies that break the rules'.

The new duty of care law would cover stronger protections for under-18s against harmful content, bullying and design features that encourage excessive use or damage self-esteem, the party says.

It would also have "stronger protections against deepfake abuse, including non-consensual sexual images, and powers to take down harmful nudify apps and sites".

Lastly the new law would cover reponsibilities for companies and make platforms identify risks, detail what they're doing to keep people safe and fix the problems when things go wrong.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins says big technology companies have too much power when it comes to New Zealanders' online experience. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

The government introduced a bill to ban social media for under-16s in August but it did not have support from National's coalition partners New Zealand First or Act.

It was introduced so close to Parliament rising for the election that National's Christopher Luxon and Erica Stanford said it would not get its first reading this term.

Labour said it would support the bill at first reading to allow it to go to select committee but the Leader of the House Louise Upston made clear it would not go before the House as there wasn't enough time.

Addressing reporters at Parliament, Labour sought to differentiate its proposed social media ban from the National Party's policy.

Labour MP Reuben Davidson said National's efforts were little more than "a PR exercise" given it refused to progress legislation before the end of this term.

"We're committed to having that first reading of the bill within the first 100 days. To getting that into the select committee process. To getting things started.

"It can't just be announcements. It has to be action."
